blocks.x: SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Horace Henderson
Reels One - Six
Part One
Interview by Tom MacCluskey

Washington, D. C.
April 9 - 12, 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S

We are on. We're rolling. This is April, 1975, talking with Horace Henderson in Denver, Colorado. Horace, actually, I'd like to get a little bit of biographical material. We have a certain amount that is available to us, but I think that one thing particularly interests me and all of us is basically, what got you involved in music and how old were you and what were you doing when you really first started in music?

Well, naturally, the number one thing -- I was 100 percent influenced, Tom, by my brother, you know, and even before I could play a note, he was playing, and he was going to school at that time in Atlanta University which wasn't too far from home. And he would come home about twice a month, I guess, and he'd play the piano, which we still have in Georgia, with my sister, and he would just sit down and play, and we would have selections to call, and he would just play anything -- anything that we asked for. We used to -- this just amused me to no end, you know, and I said one day, I'm gonna try and do this, you know.
Um-huh. Had he taken lessons prior to going to college?
Well yes. My father actually was instrumental, number one, in starting my mother on the piano,

and of course it rubbed off on Fletcher, and they had a music teacher there in Georgia that my brother first -- began his first lesson, we'll say, and my father and mother told me this later on, in later years, that they used to lock Fletcher up when he was six or seven years of age in the front room and make him practice, and they would hear the noise and hear the noise and after a while there was a silence. They'd open the door and there he was curled up in the middle of the room asleep.
Oh. Was he taking lessons that early?

That time, yes. My father started him real early, and of course, my father knew about the piano and how heavy you should play on that piano. He'd tell you if you were hitting it too heavy. So many ounces, and you're overdoing it.
I see.
(Inaudible). He knew the fundamentals of it. He didn't pursue that, naturally. He didn't pursue that profession.
But did he play somewhat himself?
Yes. He knew all the scales and he knew how to read, and of course, my mother knew how to read, and of course my sister, she was the best.
Did any of them play popular music
All classical and church music.
Ah-hah. When you say church music, again, was that music that they were reading or --

Yes, you know, like you would have a choir, like the books when you go to church they would pass out the hymns and what-not, and they're six-eight time, and (unintelligible) those things like that. They'd play those things. No jazz.
I see. Well now, when Fletcher came back from college and you say you requested him to play things, was this still classical music or by this time was he playing --

No. He went to Atlanta University and somewhere along the way he picked that beat up. He always had it of course, but -- the popular music, you know -- we got so we'd buy the sheet music, and Fletcher would know all the tunes, and of course, he had a little band going to school in Atlanta University, and he used to play there, and of course, when he would come home, why, we would look forward to hearing some of these things that the band played, and he would sit down and play them and tell us about them and what-not. And it was jazz. It had a beat, and of course it had that strut, you know, like the late and great Thomas "Fats" Waller.
Right. Earl Hines.
Earl Hines, and (inaudible)
James P. Johnson, you bet.

So, Fletcher had that. Of course, from that he -- I imagine, he kept it going right on until that was the beginning of his Swing Era, I'd say, Fletcher's, (inaudible), and, of course, it rubbed off on me because I was fascinated.
Um-huh.
After I heard him, I wanted to get there quick.
Yeah. Well, had you studied classical piano prior to that time? In other words, he had been taking lessons as a boy, had you also? Had some lessons?

Yes. My father had a music teacher in the school that I attended, in the grade school even. My first music teacher was a Mrs. Mills from Savannah, Georgia. She was an excellent pianist, and that was my first music teacher.
Do you remember how old you were when you -- or what grade you were in, or something like that?
Oh, Tom, you're putting me on the spot. Let's see, I gotta go back.
Well, was it like before high school would you say?
Oh yes. It was before high school, it was in grade school, because my father had things in school

like a music class with certain division -- this particular teacher that was my first music teacher had classes for all the children in singing and playing, and of course, I wanted to learn the piano, of course, and my father paid her extra to teach me.
I see.

So, it was quite a thing, because in those days, all the teachers that my father hired for his school had a house which belonged to my father, and, of course, this particular music teacher lived in that house. There was a piano there, and of course, I used to do a little overtime, you know. She knew that I was bent on playing the piano and that she knew that I loved Fletcher and that I loved his works and that I was going to pursue that and that was all there was to it. So she took an extra few hours every week to give me her attention, and she was quite a pianist. She didn't play much jazz, but she could play a beat. She could tell you what to do, and this was it, and I picked up from the things that I had been talking to my brother about -- it all worked out together.
I see. So -- let's see -- by the time he was in college then you were around junior high age or --
Yes. Yes. I was --
Thirteen, fourteen?
About that age. Yes.
: Uh-huh. So that's really when you got started in sort of jazz playing?

Yes. And of course, let's don't forget that my sister helped me a lot too. She was an excellent reader, and she taught school, and she taught music, and she was head of the musical department in Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, and she would come home twice a month and boy, would I ever heckle her, you know, about different things to show me how to read -- I wanted to learn this thing quick. There was no such thing, I found out later. You have to, you know, take it by steps, and she in no certain terms told me this. But I was hard head. I wanted it, and I bothered her, I -- between my first music teacher and my sister, I bugged them. I just kept on because I wanted to get there. I could see nothing else. In fact, I was about to neglect the other fundamentals that you are supposed to get in high school, you know, like reading, letters and things like that, so this is where my father stepped in, so I had to --
: --keep up with everything. Had you by that time decided that you really wanted to make a career in music?
Yes. There was nothing else for me.
: Uh-huh. Did you in high school have any sort of a group or play in any group?
Not in Georgia. Not in (inaudible) Guthbert,

Georgia. I went to school to Atlanta University where my brother went -- where he graduated. One year only. And I got some information through some very good friends in Atlanta that Wilberforce University was a better school for what I wanted to do -- among musicians that were in that school in Ohio. So the next year, my father saw that I was bent on this, so he let me transfer to Wilberforce University.
He then didn't have any opposition to your going into music as a career.
No he didn't.
Even jazz or whatever.
No. He saw that I was just intent on it, and he said I guess my sons are just gonna make music a career.
That's great. When you were first learning to play jazz, were you -- do you recall how you went about that?

Yes. In transferring to Wilberforce University in Ohio, which is right out of a little town called Xenia, Ohio, my brother at that time was playing in New York City at (Unintelligible) the Roseland Ball Room at 51st and Broadway. And he used to send me arrangements, piano parts of things, and of course, I have to bring Fletcher into these things because it borders on answering (inaudible) your questions. Fletcher had a band that was uncanny in playing arrangements and memorizing them

quick. And as soon as they would memorize these arrangements, Fletcher would take them up and send them to me. And I -- this was at Wilberforce University -- and I would study these things, and I found out that the people that recommended this particular school to me were so right in saying that there were a lot of musicians that went to Wilberforce. So this is where I found my band called the Wilberforce Collegians, and we sounded horrible. Nobody knew anything about intonation. The guys could read. A lot of musicians went to school there from Birmingham, Alabama. I had quite a few musicians from Birmingham, Alabama that went to school under a professor named Professor Watley that turned out a great number of musicians, like Theodore and Caster McCord -- the McCord brothers -- you remember them. In fact, Caster McCord is still (He died in 1963 - ed.) living and he's doing terrific in New York. That was one of my original musicians from Birmingham, Alabama, and he was with my Collegians, and we had a fella there that later went on to fame. He was our valet in the band. You know who that guy was?
I don't believe I do.
Ben Webster. Yes.
No kidding? Far out.
All he was Played with a little [F-stop piano. sharp] or anything,
He didn't think anything about the saxophone (inaudible), but he idolized Coleman Hawkins. So Ben wasn't much for

classes so he disappeared one time. He was our valet. He used to go around, set the band up and everything, help -- so he disappeared -- we didn't see him for almost a year, and the next time we saw him he had a horn, and he was doing pretty good on it. He always had that tone, from the very beginning. And he said, "Coleman Hawkins is my idol. I'm back to Wilberforce, and why, he went right up. Well, that helped us. I had quite a few musicians, as I mentioned before, from Birmingham, Alabama. We formed the Wilberforce Collegians. I think we had three saxophones, two trumpets, a trombone, a tuba, drums naturally, and I had a vocalist. I'll get to that vocalist later, but I think he came -- if I can recall -- he joined the band later. These were the original Wilberforce Collegians I'm talking about. I had a drummer with me named Jimmy King was our first vocalist. Bless his soul, he's passed now, but nevertheless this was the beginning of my first band, the Wilberforce Collegians, and we played all through the state of Ohio. We'd play the one-nighters and come back. Sometime we'd go as far as Cleveland, and we'd come back 7:00 in the morning, just time enough to make that 7:45 class, you know. But some funny things used to happen, you know.
We had a couple of cars. We used to get snow bound sometime, and we'd just make that first class back. I had a little guy with me. I think you remember. He was one of my trumpet
players. He was a great salesman. I guess you've heard the name Freddie Jenkins.
I believe I have, you bet.

Well, he was at Wilberforce, and the funny thing about it -- we didn't have any uniforms or anything - not many clothes at that time. We were struggling. But Wilberforce University had a fire at one time, and everybody loved Freddie Jenkins so much after the fire; he had a wardrobe that was more extensive than any six guys, you know. And we kidded him about it. But He could play. He was always a salesman. But there was only one thing that I regretted about him -- he would do -- invariably do. We would go and play a job on a percentage, and he would play like mad. I mean nobody in the house but about 15 people, and he'd just swing play at everybody comin' down, and the next three or four days, we'd get a job where there'd be two or three hundred people, and he would sit up and just barely blow, you know. And I never could understand that. But funny things (inaudible) would happen. Don't know what got into him. He was moody, you know.
What year were you in school, like freshman, sophomore, or whatever, when you began this?
I was in my freshman year.
When you got the band together?
Yes.
And you started the band yourself,
No, I wasn't playing with somebody else.
You organized the band.

The only experience that I got which I was gonna get to -- every summer I would look forward to going to New York, and I would go right to the Roseland, I'd sit right by my brother on the stand and pick up pointers and things to go back to school in September again. And he would help me out this way, and I would watch every guy. I had my notebook and everything -- would watch the way his original guys did. You know the original band that Fletcher had consisted of Don Redman, Coleman Hawkins, and Buster Bailey. That was his reed section. I know them real well as if it were yesterday. Those three sounded like six, because they didn't double on instruments, they tripled. They did everything. Don Redman played everything. He used to go around to pawn shops and pick up old kazoos and everything because his daddy was an old band master, you know, and Don could play all these things, and some of Fletcher's earlier records had these different sounds on 'em. And that was from Don Redman from the pawn shops. And Coleman Hawkins played the saxophone, the bass sax, the baritone, and Buster Bailey played the tenor, and of course the clarinet. That was the reed section. Then he had Kayser Marshall on the drums that
sock cymbal invented the (unintelligible). He's the one that started this.

He had a guy named Escudero that played the tuba, and he was a foreigner, excellent tuba man. This was before the days of the great late John Kirby. And his brass section consisted of a guy that was three-fourths Indian called Big Green from Nebraska, Omaha, Nebraska. I'm telling you these things for a point. And he played trombone. One of the greatest trombonists that I've ever heard play a waltz. Then he had a trumpet player by the name of Elmer Chambers. He had another trumpet player named Scotty. (Howard Scott-ed.) -- he had 3 to start with. This was his brass section (inaudible). And later came another guy that got into that section which -- I think his name might be familiar -- Louis Armstrong.
I believe I've heard of him, somewhere along the way.

Somewhere along -- picked that whole band up. This was during the Summer months that all this transpired. And I had my notebooks, and I'd fill them full every -- I used to watch them every night. And when I didn't understand things, I'd ask Fletcher, 'What are they doing, what is he doing, how did this happen?' He would have an answer for me for everything. He said, 'You remember this, because some day if you intend to pursue this is gonna come in handy.' And boy, was he ever right.
Do you by any chance have those
notebooks or any of them? Somewhere?
You know, we're talking back now.
Oh yes.
I have Fletcher's personal library downstairs. Somewhere that -- those things might be in there. I'm gonna have to look for those.
You know, that would really be a very interesting thing to see those.

I was scribbling real fast, because as he talked to me, I was writing and looking at him, and I had nothing but admiration for him. I mean And I thought he was God, which he was to me. And every question that I asked, he never had to stutter about it. He knew the answer. Then I would -- I would get paid, you know, he'd give me something just for sitting there. Of course, he let me sit in. I could read pretty good all of the time, you know, and he had his arrangements. Everybody had the arrangements and things, and they had the individual parts, and the piano parts in those days consisted of not the chords, like the G minor seven or one of those things. They were the actual notes.
They had it all written out.

Yeah. Everything was written. The only thing that was tough -- they were in D flat. Fletcher liked to write in D flat, F sharp, and D natural. He wrote a tune called D Natural Blues, and all these things. But

actually it was a musical education to play in those keys, I found out later, you know. And of course during the course of years, his personnel changed, you know, some -- because of death, because of other guys wanting to be leaders, you know, and what-not. And they were -- he always managed to get great guys in his band, though. And this also amazed me, and I'd go back to school, and I'd do a little changing too, you know, because we had other guys, and I used to have little auditions and things, and he'd tell me how to do -- it really helped.
So we had these Collegians for three years in Wilberforce before we actually got -- I mean could, you know, real good, and we got so they knew us in the State of Ohio. We had regular jobs.
What sort of money did you make with those kind of jobs?

Well, we had -- let's see. I think I had about eight or ten piece band, and if we'd go to Cleveland, Ohio, which wasn't too far from there, I could get $150 a night, which was 350 a night now or 450, you know, because you could do as much or more with that $150. And there was no such thing as union deals, you know, then, you know, and we would just divvy up the money. We'd take out the money for transportation, you know, and we were buying cars, you know, they had 2 cars for transportation. (Unaudible) But it was more or less like a family. And we'd
always have money enough in our pockets, you know. It was a lot of money in those days, you know.
You bet. As leader, did you have extra pay or did you divide it equally?

No. We'd divide everything equally, you know. We'd go to Cincinnati, Ohio and play a place there. In fact, today I just thought of the name -- I'd been trying to think of it all the time -- a place called Crystal Ballroom on 5th Street, and we used to -- we were so good, we played there every Sunday. And that guy paid us $200.
No kidding.
That was a lot of money.
Now, were most of the people that you were playing for -- were they blacks or whites or was it mixed or how was that?
These were strictly blacks.
Every job you played.
No. I thought you meant in Cincinnati.
No. Wherever you played.

No, no. No, no. Because we played in Columbus, Ohio and played a beautiful club there called the Valley Dale. That was a gorgeous place. It was an excluded -- exclusive, excuse me, place, and I had to augment my band for that, but by that time, we go so that we knew
what intonation meant because even Coleman Hawkins and Don Redmond would write little notes down to my musicians, how to get certain vibratos, you know, anticipating... (inaudible)
On the horns, yeah. Get it in tune.
Yes. So -- but we had some notes that were -- I tell you -- I hope I can find those things.
It would be great if you could.

It was really something. And from these greats -- these guys that we're talking about were creators of jazz, Tom, in those days. We didn't know that at that time, but they were the creators. They weren't imitators, see. So we got this first hand. We got this -- so we were just like going to school. Boy, when I come back to school in September, we'd hold night classes -- music classes on our own, and we'd try things out, and there was such things in those days as making, you know, little discs. They were 78's, you know --
Little wax --

-- wax, yeah. And I made quite a few of those. I brought them back because we'd play 'em back, you know, and let the guys hear 'em, and then we'd pick out a certain tune, and we'd just go to school on this thing. We spent more time on that than we did our books, our studies. I don't know how we ever graduated. But, let me say one thing. I'll tell you how we did. We were popular on the

campus, naturally, because we were a jolly bunch. All the girls liked the boys, naturally, and even the men liked the guys (unintelligible) as great musicians, the chefs that they had there, even the professors and everybody. I would say that they used to lean a little bit for us, because I'll tell you why. Can I give you one instance?
Sure. Love it.

Like we'd get in from Cleveland, Ohio at seven o'clock in the morning, our first class is 7:45. There was a professor there, I'll never forget him, named Prof. David, we called him. And he was a psychology teacher, and were in that -- and most of the time, there would be discussions. We'd get in his class, and we'd start a debate purposely, and after we'd get it started, in about 15 minutes, you could tell the guys in the corner asleep.
Oh, yeah.
The debates are going on, you see. We'd do this, we talked thought this up, It's very terrible, to say this, but -- this is what happened, and it worked.
Sure.
And -- but one day, professor caught on to it, you know, and he says, "I know what you guys are doing." He says, "It's okay as long as we're getting results." But he was 100 percent.
You were majoring in music.
Yes. But I went to Wilberforce -- my father wanted one of his two sons to be a scientist, a bachelor of science. Fletcher started out that way.
He was a chemist, wasn't he?
A chemist, yeah. I meant chemist.

So he got to swinging, and he changed over. So my father said, 'Well, maybe my next son will do it, so why don't you go to Wilberforce.' He knew they had this there. I changed over from BS to bachelor of arts, and I didn't tell him about it, until the day of my graduation. And I'll never forget the look on his face when on graduation day, he was sitting right up front. He always had excellent ears, see, he could always hear. So when they handed me my diploma -- I had my gown on, my hat -- they said, 'Horace Henderson, AB.' I looked dead at my father, and he looked right at me, and he didn't say a word. We got through -- till the sermon was over and what-not (inaudible) -- exercise. He called me and we took a walk in the woods right at Wilberforce. We didn't say a word for about a half mile, and he stopped me and he put his hand on my shoulder, and he said, 'Son, how come?'
You knew.

I knew. Then I had to go through misery and everything to explain to him why I did it and of course my only answer was that had I gone to bachelor of science I would have had to spent a lot of time in the laboratory, checking these unknowns, and (inaudible) these deals, and I

knew that I wouldn't have had the time for my music. So I said, "Father, I want to be a musician like my brother. He's succeeding with where he is on Broadway. I want to do this, and I know if I told you about it -- I wrote you about it, you wouldn't have agreed. So I had to take this chance." You know he took it beautiful, and you took about a relief --
I'll bet.
I thought I would inject that. But this is --
That's great. Do you feel that the musical training you had in the school helped you with what you were doing or did you find it at odds, or how do you feel about that?

It did give me the foundation, Tom, a little bit, you know, but my greatest experience came from being in New York, seeing these giants of jazz execute it, and being able to ask them questions and them givin' me the correct answer. There weren't too many books out, as you know, during that time like they are now. So this came from, as we say, the horse's mouth. And these guys would tell you just exactly how it is and how it was done. Plus the fact -- I will inject this here -- I remember when we had dinner a couple of weeks ago, I don't know if you recall my telling you that we used to have jam sessions up to Coleman Hawkins' house. (Inaudible)
Right.

Well, I would look forward to that more or less as a lesson for me because it was a great experience and all I did was play the chords for these giants. You know, and listen in. I realize now how much jazz came into my ear, you know, from these guys, you know, and --
Why don't you tell us a little bit about that? We did talk about it before, but --

Yes, well, Coleman Hawkins had an apartment in New York City, what they call up on Sugar Hill, 80 St. Nicholas Place. I'll never forget it. And we used to go up and have jam sessions at his apartment, after they finished playing the Roseland, and this constituted the fellas in Fletcher's band, of course. The trombonist, Jimmy Harrison; Buster Bailey, the clarinetist; and Coleman Hawkins, of course; and Louis Armstrong; and the trombonist Big Green; and they would sit down and call out the standard tunes to play, and I would take Fletcher's book up. He had two sets of books, incidentally, there. He would have the numbers from one to one hundred -- the stock arrangements, you know, of standards. Then he would have the things alphabetically listed, like A1, A2, A3, B, B1, B2, B3 of the arrangements, because he had -- oh, gobs, gobs of arrangements. I used to borrow the stock books and take up there, because these guys would call out these standard tunes, naturally, I didn't know them all.
Were the stock books published at
that time or --
Quite a few, you know. The great Archie Blyer --
Yes.
-- was successful in making a lot of guys sound good, you know, the band's sound good, you know, a lot of standards. Russ Morgan made a lot of stocks.
This is in the mid-Twenties?

This was back then -- when the stocks -- well they were just coming out. I got all those things downstairs now, you know. Like 'Limehouse Blues,' during that era and all those things. So these guys would call out these things -- 'Basin Street,' 'Stardust,' and all these things, you know. And I wouldn't know them, you know, but I could read, you know, the chords and everything else. So they would call out a tune and I say, 'Wait a minute, wait a minute.' Fletcher always kept his book in order, (inaudible), and they'd tell me to take a four-bar introduction, and I say, 'What do you mean?' And I'd do it a couple of times and then Hawk would take a four bar (inaudible). One tune would last sometime 20, 25 minutes, or longer, you know. Guys take different choruses, you know. Then when we finished that, we would stop like we'd recorded something -- stop and discuss what had transpired during that session, you know, that particular tune. And, man, that was a lesson. Those things don't happen any
more now like this, and they was regular sessions, and I used to ask some time why -- I say, 'You guys are too good to do these things. Why do you do it?' They say, 'Well, a lot of reasons.'

'We want to be familiar with each other's styles,' so this was the answer -- how to blend more together then, see. Even in those days, as quick as they were, they were never satisfied. They were always wanting to reach -- as you know in music is never conquered.
Right.

There's always something. So if those greats did that, some of these youngsters today, boy, I don't know. But this is one of the things that I would look forward to -- going to Coleman Hawkins' house. And of course at that time of morning -- we're talkin' about three, four, and five, and six, because musicians were night-lifers anyway, you know. And Coleman Hawkins in his great apartment -- I'm not going to tell you what he had in his apartment.
Tell us. Now you have us curious.

Well, Coleman was married to a beautiful girl one time, but he was more interested in music, and he never would come home except on the times of the jam session. His wife was named Gertie. And he would come in at seven, eight, nine in the morning, and he would stop off at a place called Big Johns, somewhere up in Harlem, and everything,

and he'd have his uniform on and Gertie would meet him at the door, and I remember him distinctly saying this. He said to the guys one night, 'You know, I got in nine o'clock in the morning, and Gertie met me at the door -- she called him Poopsie -- 'Hello Poopsie, how are you? Can I fix you something?' He said, he'd get mad. He would want her to be mad at him for being late. She'd never get mad. And it bothered him no end. So he thought that she didn't love him, one of those things, and they begin to become distant, and she was a real beautiful girl, but she was so nice and easy, she didn't worry about anything. Finally, they divorced, and so she took the furniture. And of course, Hawk never replaced it, except just the essential things, like when you walk in -- I think he had a four room apartment -- as you walk in the front door, there's a couch in the first room past the living room, and the piano. That's it. The couch. No chairs. The dining room had a small table and two chairs. That's all in the dining room. In the bedroom was a bed, and he had a small dresser with a mirror. That was it. He didn't want all that stuff -- no rugs, no nothin'. And the man could have had a mansion. This is just Hawk -- cause he stayed out all the time. They called him Bean too, you know, the boys called him B-E-A-N, Bean.
That's another thing Fletcher used to do. Instead of writing first trumpet, second trumpet, somethin', he would write the guy's first name, you know, like Joe, John, Bean,
Hawk, they call him, you know. And they would call Don Redmond -- he had a real funny -- Tater, T-A-T-E-R, because he was short and chunky like a --
Potato.

And these are funny things. I've got some arrangements of Fletcher's, his original library downstairs, and a lot of those things are on there. They've got these names like we're talkin' about, and sometimes I go through and I laugh like mad, because I remember these names, you see. They're classics.

When you were having these talk sessions -- jam sessions and so on at Hawkins' house -- apartment, what sorts of things were talked about? I mean, like you say, you play through something, and then they would say, 'Okay, we did this, we did that.' Do you recall some of the things that were really said?

Yes. Yes. I'll tell you why. Coleman Hawkins was a thorough musician, chordwise, you know. He'd played the melody in his own accompaniment in order to do that, so to speak, like they played 'Body and Soul,' remember and go around and dip down how he used to play the melody (inaudible) and play these chords. A lot of the fellas respected him in Fletcher's band. So much so that they would like to know what notes were in that particular thing, and Hawk would -- on his chorus -- would we would be jamming something, and Jimmy Harrison had a great

ear. Jimmy Harrison was a great trombonist. He knew nothing about chords or anything. He just played the way he felt in his heart, but he wanted to learn how -- what notes were in certain chords, and Hawk would tell him, you know. And other guys would ask -- the trumpet player -- Henry Red Allen, incidentally, was in on this session too. And he was one of the few trumpet players that I know of that could run a diminished chord against a major and make it sound good. He'd invert it on the end and come back to the chord. But he didn't know what he was doin'. But it sound good. Like you would play like a E flat chord, like (Sings Chord). Red would play (Sings Chord), and turn it in, you know. So Hawk said -- would tell him, "That's wrong, but it sounds good, keep it in." He'd say, "Well, what am I doing?" We'd ask those things, you know. Guys would ask those things. And I didn't write that down, you know.
