And I had another guy with me -- excuse me -- that -- during my Wilberforce days in fact, I had two other guys with me left out before -- their names -- one of the greatest guys -- that I think he's a genius -- a musical genius.
You bet.

He took the trumpet up, and he plays good trumpet, and he's an excellent arranger. He was excellent, and of course I had the late and great Rex Stewart playing cornet with me in Wilberforce. I took Rex to
Wilberforce. I took Benny Carter to Wilberforce.
Where did you find them? How did that come about?
I found Benny Carter in Pittsburgh. I took him back to Wilberforce with me, after my engagement there.
Did he actually go to school, or he just came there to play with your band?

No, he took up some things there. In fact, Benny Carter -- I've got forgot to mention this -- we were in Wilberforce, and he was taking up something there. Rex Stewart wasn't, but he joined the Collegians, and the work was that steady to have those guys at that time. And of course Benny was helpful in arranging, even those days with the band. In fact, do you remember a tune that was popular -- it's getting away from me -- Singing the Blues?"
Yes --

Alto was prominent in this particular tune. We played a battle of music in Detroit, Michigan at the Graystone Ballroom, and we had seven thousand people there. Out in the gardens. There was a garden there too. And McKinney's Cotton Pickers was our opponent. I had Rex Stewart and Benny Carter in that band, and we played Singing the Blues, and we broke it up. We got the cup and everything and we went back to Wilberforce. But those -- the band was playing then though.
Oh, we had a great band.
When they had those competitions, how did they make the judgment? I mean by crowd appeal --
The audience that made the most noise and what-not. This is how they arrived at the winner.
Were those competitions quite common in those days? Or just --

Battles of jazz were great in those days. We don't have those now. They were great. Like Fletcher Henderson and Glen Gray and his Casa Loma band (unintelligible) did thirty-one one-nighters of jazz in battles of music in the universities all over the country, like the University of Illinois, University of Michigan, and actually, they had two bandstands set up, you know, and I followed Fletcher on these things too. And of course, we played a battle of music with one band. I'll never forget it. The University of Michigan. Against Les Brown who had Randy Brooks as a trumpet player there. He had just left some small band that he had been with for quite a few years. This is the first time that we had ever heard -- when I say we -- Fletcher's band -- this is including Coleman Hawkins. Randy Brooks played so much. He played first, to hot and everything, in Les Brown's band at that time, second, and third trumpet (unintelligible). In fact, Fletcher's band played first. I'll never forget this. This is the University of Michigan.
This -- in the forties?
This I will have to check, but this is such a story -- I don't want to lose it.
Okay. Yeah. Go ahead. Right.

Les Brown struck up his band right behind Fletcher's last number, and they started off with something -- Randy Brooks featured on trumpet -- The guys started to get off, you know, like musicians get off on their breaks.
Yeah.

They looked over there and heard this guy. They sat down. The whole 45 minutes. This guy was such a genius, 'til he intrigued everybody, and I never heard nobody play like that in my life. And one of the things I remember we he played -- because I got the record of it now -- of course he played it with Les Brown -- was 'Tenderly,' which his band later made. (unintelligible) His solo in 'Tenderly' was like Jack Kennedy with 'Stardust,' (unintelligible). that eight bars.
Yeah.
But anyway, I feel probably ahead of myself, but I didn't want to lose that deal, but we're getting back to -- we'll go back to Wilberforce again.
Okay. Well we were talking about Rex Stewart and Benny Carter. You had mentioned Shelton Hemphill.
Shelton Hemphill was another one of
those trumpet players that came from Birmingham --
Birmingham?

-- Alabama, from the same school that the McCord brothers came from, and he turned out to be a great reading trumpet player. In fact, from my band he went to the great bands, like he played with Duke Ellington for quite a spell. He played with Lucky Millinder and his great band, and we called him Shad. That was his nickname, Shad or Scad -- I believe it's Scad. But anyway, he was a little humpback guy with great shoulders. When I say humpback, I mean he could play close up, you know, pumping. When you say pumping, he'd play those little -- he had great broad shoulders. Very seldom missed. He was at Wilberforce, you know. He was one of the Wilberforce Collegians, and I was quite proud of him. He graduated too. The great band.

I think one time you told me a little bit about how you had met Rex Stewart. Maybe I'm thinking of somebody else, but you told me the other night about somebody that came and nobody thought he could play, and then he suddenly just boomed out, maybe --
Let's see. There's was somebody that asked to sit in, I think, or something.
Right. Maybe in Pittsburgh.
Was that Rex? I wonder -- I don't know if that was Rex or Ben Webster. You know, Ben disappeared
and when we saw him again, he put down the F sharp piano for that tenor. He wanted to sit in or something. I don't know if that was Rex -- did I say Rex before?
It seemed to me you did, but maybe I'm not remembering well.
Well Rex was in the Collegians. He was in that band.
Well, you said that Rex was playing cornet.

Yes. He always liked to play the little cornet. In fact, it was a long time before I saw Rex with a trumpet. He looked real funny with a trumpet, you know? But the little cornet -- it seems like he always -- you know Rex was one of the few trumpet players that could hit a blue note -- a sour note, as we call it -- and sell it and I remember in Detroit during that battle of jazz with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers, he'd snatch a note, say (Sound), and it'd be all out of tune, out of everything else, and the people'd just
Eat it up.
Howl. Eat it up. And he'd be mad when he'd get through and he'd snatch his horn down, you know, but he would sell. He'd sell that blue note, you know? People bought it. He -- I don't know.
When you were playing in those days,
did you have many problems with club owners telling you how to play or how to work with crowds or anything like that?

You know, I was pretty lucky that way. I didn't have any trouble. You know, they -- as I say -- we would have to make the auditions for the job, and these club owners, in those days, weren't struggling like some of these guys now, you know, like now you -- I don't care how great the band is, if the business isn't there, the first thing the club owners do is blame it on the musicians. They didn't do that in those days. They just -- in fact, business wasn't bad. Things were booming, you know. But nowadays, if people observe some particular week, like Lent, or one of those kind of things, first thing the owner will do is cut the musicians out, you know what I mean? Cause they're gonna blame them, you know. Do you know this?
Yes.

But, I was fortunate enough to play for club owners that -- well, they believed in you, and of course the crowds were terrific, cause people loved to dance in those days. I think more so than now. And I mean they danced, because the people that I'm talking about in those days, they are the mothers and fathers of these kids now, but they danced, see. And the money was better. The jobs were better. People were working. We didn't have that Depression, you know. And of course, as long as you drew the people in,
which we did, your job was safe you know. You stayed on the job then for months and months and years. Things that -- that's unheard of now except in a few cases where you were lucky.
In those days, was the Collegians -- were you working with contracts usually, or how were the arrangements made?
Well, the job --
-- for the one-nighters.

Yes. We'd have to have a contract, but it wasn't the union deal. We'd write it out on our-own paper, two pieces of paper, you know. After all, a man's word was his bond in those days. You know what I mean even on a piece of paper. I remember a guy telling me, he says, 'contract is fine. I can make a contract on my white cuff here, but if I don't keep it,' he says, 'that's no good.' So it's one of those things. But the guys paid off 'cause the people were there, like I said a few minutes ago. But I remember a couple of times, I experienced an unpleasant thing that unfortunately wasn't with my band. It was in Fletcher's band and we were touring in the State of West Virginia playing one-nighters and Fletcher was getting 900, a thousand a night then, which was excellent money, you know, and he -- because Fletcher had his men salaried whether they worked or not, so he had -- But I remember one night we played -- I don't know if it was

Charleston or Huntington, West Virginia -- the guy had 3,000 or 4,000 people in the house, and they were charging 2.50 and $3.00 a head. They got the money, and the guy took 'em in and ran off. So I remember, Fletcher took a break, and we started playing around 9:00 -- Fletcher took a break about 11:00 and went to collect some money. He came back on the bandstand and told the people, "I'm sorry, we didn't get paid, and we're not going to play any more tonight." And, you know, it was almost a riot. "You're not going to play and I paid my $2.50 and my $3.00. They said, "You better not get off of that stand." And the place packed with people. Boy, you should have seen the guys there. We were elevated. You were targets, you know.
Right.

We were targets. So, this guy -- not this particular guy, any guy that did that -- knew that the band was booked, you know, on one-nighters. You couldn't stay around and look for him for a week. You had to move on. So only thing you could do is -- then the (unaudible) union was active at that time. Only thing you could do was put the guy on the unfair list. All he's got to do is change his name and get somebody else -- go on and put somebody else in. And he knew you couldn't stay around to hunt him for a week. You had to move on 500 miles, and one of those things, so there he was. So the only thing you could do was put something in
and whether the people believed it or not, that the paper (inaudible) was up to the public.
Did that happen very often?

No. No it didn't. This wasn't because -- but it happened enough to make the promoters -- the booking agents, I'll say, not the promoters, begin to demand half the amount of the contract -- put up half the amount of the money before the band got there, and then the bands got so that they would take an early break -- like they would have a four hour gig or five hours -- they would play an hour and a half. The band leader would go down and collect his money. Get the balance. And they would have -- this is where I think the beginning of the road managers for the bands came in. The road managers followed these guys around like they were twins, you know, that they wouldn't escape. So they (inaudible) they dispersed with it, so that it got to be obsolete.
When you were working with the Collegians did you have somebody serving as the manager and the agent and so on? Or did you do all that yourself?

I started out doing that and it begin to tax me, so I made my bass player the manager, a guy named Hutchinson. He was a tuba -- played the tuba, but he was a good mathematician, could figure, so he took that up, off of me, where I could, you know, concentrate on the musical end of it.
How did the fact that you were quite popular off campus as well as on campus -- did this have any effect directly with your professors and the school

Well, we'll say (unintelligible) through the had to naturally--just now and then we'd State of Ohio, which we actually (unintelligible) get into West Virginia, but that would be more or less on the weekends. But through Ohio, we became real popular, and of course, the news got back, and of course it got in the papers. We got so we were celebrities.
Celebrities. Yeah.

Yes. The professors began to treat us as such. They knew we were trying to do two things, and the professors in those days were swingers, man. They were -- we had a Professor McGinnis there, and Professor David, who I mentioned to you earlier in this session. Man, they were swingers. In fact, I'll tell you what set the thing off. We used to play for the university in the gymnasium some nights, and play free, and set it off, that you know, for...
Sure.

-- different things. So, we had to be cool, but they understood what we were doing, and they encouraged us. And as long as you at least did half your work in the books, you know what I mean, to actually earn your degree, that was all they required. And they knew the handicaps, they knew we'd been ridin' all night, and all these kinds of things, to get back in, so they would laugh. There was only one guy -- there was a guy named Bruce Green at Wilberforce. He was the
that were - bachelor of science (16) one that had the students (unintelligible) and as the laboratory. He didn't dig jazz at all. He wanted -- the only jazz he did was mixing up the --
-- chemicals.

-- chemicals. Yes, and he would even walk out of step in order (inaudible) and all this kind of stuff. He didn't care, you know. But the guys avoided his class. They didn't go into that. This is why I changed, you know. They said, Bruce Green gives you nothin'. You earned this, you know what I mean. We stayed away from that, so -- (inaudible) we took the courses that we figured we could handle, you know. We weren't trying to cheat. That was going to be our profession, and to teach. We just loved music. That was it. (Inaudible). We knew we had to have a degree, too, because in later years we knew it would come in.

It would help out, right. With your own arranging, as you said, that you began doing more and more of that in later years, did you -- well, I know for a fact that you did contribute some arrangements to Fletcher's band. I've read someplace that some people were -- have come to the conclusion that a number of the arrangements that were attributed to Fletcher were in fact your arrangements. Can you talk about that at all?

Well, I think a lot of people that said that -- Fletcher was so prominent during that time, as an arranger, until they just figured that -- (inaudible) well, when you played this tune, Fletcher arranged that, one of those things, until they found out later that that were learning to arrange and were making little things there were other guys in the band (unintelligible) and so

they began to give us credit for it. One of my biggest thrills was a tune that I wrote and we recorded it called "Big John Special," and how it came about -- I got the name from -- there was a guy in New York City that owned a tavern where most musicians and professionals hung out up in Harlem on a 141st and Seventh Avenue. Anybody that was somebody always hung out in Big John's. Musicians didn't play. He just had good food there and beer and all that stuff, and so anybody they wanted to find they'd go find at Big John's. It was Like the Metropole, you know, downtown. And so I wrote this particular tune, and I told Big John I was going to write a tune and name it after him. I looked up on the wall there and I saw something about special -- a certain drink, you know. I said -- it occurred to me -- I says, I should call this tune "Big John Special," so it hit me, and I went to Big John and told him I was gonna name it after him. He was flattered, you know, so I really did, and we recorded it, and the thing was a hit. Benny Goodman recorded it, and Fletcher recorded it, and I think -- and I had met some great guys that played great solos in there like Henry "Red" Allen, which to my way of thinking, sold the record. And of course, (unintelligible) -- and incidentally I wrote that tune when we were on a plane, and Fletcher, during those days -- not only Fletcher -- they used to travel in a bus called the Newark Charter Company, and it was -- everybody used that

because you had to pay by the mile and it wasn't like the Greyhound -- expensive like that -- so they gave 'em rates, and this particular bus broke down one time, and we had to take a plane to the next job, and while I was up in the air, I was scared anyway, so I took my little stuff out and started writing this particular tune. I hadn't named it Big John then, but this is how it turned out.
This was then when you were with Fletcher.
Yes.
One of the times. When you played with Fletcher, did he do much playing or were you doing most of the playing? How did that work out?

I did three-fourths of the playing, except there were a lot of special tunes that would feature the piano, and naturally, Fletcher being the leader -- like "Honeysuckle Rose", and all those things, when we would get down to the piano chorus, I would step aside, and I'd direct the band, and Fletcher would play the solos naturally, because we were featuring Fletcher Henderson and his band, and I loved this, you know, because it gave me a chance to --
To get out in front.
-- wave and find out how you do this thing, you know. And there were quite a few tunes. Plus the fact there were a lot of things that Fletcher wrote that they

were in difficult keys, and a lot of them I didn't play in at that time, you know. Like D Natural Blues. He wrote this thing, and the type of piano part that he would write sometimes would be what we call a skate, you know. A skeleton. Just real quick, you know, write down. He'd just say piano solo, so and so, D natural, write down a couple of chords. Start out anything, and then the rest of the 32 bars were up in the mind, he didn't have piano parts to a lot of those solos. you know. So (unintelligible)
You mentioned earlier that they were not using chord symbols in the beginning. They were writing out all the notes. When did this begin to shift over in arranging?
Well, you'll have to help my memory in this thing. I would say in the late forties.
That late?
Maybe a little earlier. I don't know. But this is -- you know from the stock arrangements.
Right. I was just thinking, when I first started playing stocks they were always written out.

Yeah. Now, Archie Bleyer was instrumental in this of the chords and deals, you know. So I think during that era -- now, we would have to check when Archie Bleyer and his -- I remember one of his stocks called Business in F. Did you ever play that?
No.

Man, it made a lot of musicians sound like -- I mean, bands sound like they were special arrangements, you know. It was a great thing, you know. Things like "King Porter Stomp," Jelly Roll Morton. (unintelligible). These were great things. And the chords, if I'm correct, I think were there then during that era. They begin to come in.
Chord symbols, you mean?
Chord symbols, yeah. And in later years, the notes began to disappear.
Yeah. Guitarists were playing from chord symbols.
Yes.
But not pianists.
But not pianists, so I don't know if it was a lazy man -- arranger's lament or not, you know, because a lot of times, you know -- as you know, it takes time to write the notes.
Sure it does.

When all you got to do is write the name of the chord. Boom. So this made the piano player, whoever he would be, find out what that chord was and how you make it, you know. So it really -- it was helpful to the arranger as far as the time element is concerned to write the piano part for chords. In fact, the guitar player -- you could just make two guitar parts and write piano in. If a guy
couldn't read chords, of which I found out there was a lot of guys who couldn't, you know, and he was really hung, you know.
Nowadays, it's the other way around. You find guys that read chords all the time, but nobody that can read notes.

That's the truth. So I don't know whether this hurt the guys or not, you know, musicians. I'm not gonna quote on that, but I'll tell you one thing, though, while we're talking about the musicians. The younger guys, with all due respect to them, I know having been here in Denver and a few other towns around -- it's a pathetic thing when you ask a young guy to play the melody of 'Stardust' and he can't.
I know.

And if you write it out for him, he sounds like a high school kid. In fact, he doesn't sound as good as some of these high school kids. He's struggling. For instance, I've heard tenor players have to read 'Stardust.' They've had beautiful tones before and as soon as they read them, they lose their intonation.
They forget the tone. Yeah.

Now, to me, this -- I don't know. This is the only thing about the young kids that -- it's too bad, and if you talk about the verses of certain tunes, for instance, like 'Stardust' -- one of the most beautiful verses that was ever written, they've never heard of that. They can't

play it, which back in those days like Hawk, and that's why I say these guys were the creators of jazz. I happen to have been around when these things were happening, so there's no comparison, as far as I'm concerned, you know, in the musicians of that era and the ones nowadays, you know, because those are creators of jazz, and a lot of guys we got know are imitators. And there's a lot of difference between creation and imitation.
For sure. A while ago you mentioned Jelly Roll Morton. Did you ever meet him?

Yes. I knew Jelly Roll Morton. He used to hang around a place in New York City on 132nd and Second Avenue called Bert Hall's Rhythm Club where all the musicians hung out, and they had jam sessions there. They had a piano as you walk in, you know, and guys like the great Fats Waller and J.P. Johnson, and they used to jam. Willie Smith and all these guys, and Jelly Roll Morton used to stand around and he'd crack his jaw to these guys, and he'd say, 'You might play more piano than me, but I write more tunes,' he says, 'I wrote King Porter Stump.' I mean, he was a pop-off. He was like Dizzy Dean in baseball. He'd say things, but he'd go on and do it. He meant it. He wrote great tunes. But he'd walk in and say, 'I'm Jelly Roll Morton, you know.'
Take off your hats, boys.

He and Fletcher were great friends. Fletcher's -- one of his greatest arrangements as far as I'm concerned and one of the greatest tunes that band played was "King Porter Stomp," (unintelligible), because Fletcher won quite a few battles of music with King Porter Stomp." And Jelly Roll Morton knew this, and he used to go and say, "I made Fletcher Henderson." And Fletcher used to laugh at all these things and say, "You did," you know. He wouldn't argue. He was a great guy. He was a weird sort of little fellow. You had to understand him.

Did you listen to many records in those days? Did you learn from that, or -- you know, a lot of people in later years -- Forties, Fifties, and so on -- have learned a lot from records. Was that as prominent in those days?
You mean prominent in the Thirties or --
Well, even Twenties or Thirties.

Well, I didn't do too much record listening, because I was one of the few fortunate ones to have been in person with these guys so much, so I sacrificed the record deals where probably other musicians would lend an ear. In later years, I've had to listen to records, because I didn't travel too much, you know, and I wanted to listen to some of the up coming guys, you know, that we've had. Now, I used to listen to a lot of Bird's things, because I didn't get a chance to see Byrd much. I knew him, you know, met him, but I was
fortunate enough to get in on the ground floor with these the greats.

I'm trying to note here -- after you had been -- after you left school and went to New York and then we got into talking about Chicago, about when was it that you went to Chicago and spent a lot of time there? Was that the late twenties or --

No, this was in the thirties. You know, Fletcher went to Chicago. In fact, he took his band into Chicago where and this was when I was with Fletcher, and I stayed with Fletcher, I believe, better than a year in Chicago, and this is when I formed my own band and went into Swingland, and Fletcher was at the Grand Terrace.
You had been with Fletcher first, and then formed your band, or you had your band first and then you went with Fletcher?
Well, both. I was with him first, and then I had my band for a while.
And then you went back with him.
And then I went back with Fletcher. Yes. But those days in Chicago were the Thirties.
Is this when the so-called Chicago style was really getting itself together with --
This was when I had the pleasure of playing the 400 Club when I had personnel with me like Ray
Nance -- Ray Nance just before he joined Duke. I was playing the 5100 Club, and one of the performers that was on that show was the great Danny Thomas.
(End of Reel 2.)
Oh yeah. You just started to talk about Danny Thomas.

Oh yes. That was in the 5100 Club in Chicago, and I had a big band then. There was a fellow there that played the violin and the trumpet. And his name was Ray Nance. He was quite an inspiration to us, and he was always a salesman. A Chicago boy. And Duke Ellington came to town and heard Ray. (Inaudible). He loved Ray and wanted Ray to join him. You know, Ray didn't want to leave the band? He wanted to stay with us, and I had to get mad with Ray. Ray will tell anybody this, and finally, we showed him where it would be a great advantage, and one of those things, and he joined Duke, and you know the story from there on. This was in the 5100 Club in the Thirties, and there was some other things that happened there in Chicago.
You know, my brother began to write more and more for Benny Goodman around this time.
Did he -- was he playing with Benny at the time he first started writing, or was he just writing arrangements for him?
He was Just writing in the beginning. He
did a playing stint with Benny.
I know he did later on, but I was --

-- later on, but he first started writing, because Benny would wake him up at ungodly hours -- four and five in the morning, you know, to write one of those things, and this is where I came in. Fletcher was so swamped, you know, and Fletcher said, "I just can't do it. Can you make something up for Benny?" So I was tickled to death in thinking that Fletcher asked me to write something for Benny Goodman. In fact, I'm thinking, "For goodness sake, that's an honor, you know. So I did do things during that era when Three Little Words, I made " " " " Japanese Sandman, Walk Jenny Walk, and the last thing I did for him was String of Pearls, and I think that was around '35. I got this down here.
Now, when you wrote -- these were written for Benny Goodman.
For Benny. I made the scores.
And Benny Goodman was aware that you had written them or did he think that Fletcher had written them?
I think Fletcher told Benny. I don't know whether he did it immediately or later on, I don't know. But Benny did find out.
He knew.
This is while I made more. I made one
first, then of course I made Big John Special for him, one of those things, too which came later.
Did you -- when you wrote arrangements, did you put your name on them?
No.
The arranger did not sign them.
Later on, I found out it was an advantage, and my wife had a stamp made, because we found out that the union said that you had to have a stamp (unintelligible) But in the beginning, no.
How much did you get paid for an arrangement like that in those days?
I got -- I think starting out, I got $100.00 for the score.
Was this for a big band or a small group, or --
This was for the big band. It might be five brass, and then four saxophones (unintelligible) And, of course --
Some of those are recorded aren't they? I mean, Benny recorded those.
Yes, all the things I mentioned are recorded.

You never saw the score again, and, of course, the good part about that you didn't have to extract your score. They had the copies, naturally, and of course, Fletcher's wife was quite instrumental in that; she was an excellent
And she did most of Fletcher's, and she copied mine. Fletcher scored in concert, which is rough on a copyist.
Right, cause they had to transpose.
Transpose. But I never did. I've never scored in concert yet.
Really?

I've always scored in front of the instrument as you copy what you see, because I had -- I'll tell you what started me doing that too, I later got some copyists, and they begin to ask me is it a concert or so and so, and if it was a concert, they'd turn you down. A lot of them didn't know how to transpose, actually, but they had things set up for that.
Yeah. Did you write most of your arrangements at the piano or how did you do -- how did you go about it?

To begin with, until I got a clear picture of the keyboard in my mind, and in fact, I think I told you a little story over this one time. I used to walk down the street, you know, I'd get to hummin' a riff, a picture where it would be, and I'd walk down with my hands stretched, with my five fingers out, I'd say well, here's five lines, and four spaces and this thing, and I was walking down the street one day, and a lady looked at me as if I were crazy, you know,

and all of a sudden I realized, and I turned around to her, and I said, 'Lady, I'm not crazy. I'm just picturing a musical version.' It was funny. So I quit that. At that time it helped me to concentrate, you know, to picture. So now I can do it without the piano. In fact, it's been quite a few years; I can do it without (unintelligible). Every now and then I might want to check some. I'll get stuck, if it's something difficult, you know, maybe difficult chord or one of those things. I might just play it. Go to the piano, and strike the chord, just to see. I remember one instance. I was with Charlie Barnet as his arranger. I had the good fortune of being on his staff along with Billy May (unintelligible) one time, and I remember bringing in an arrangement, and I had started to rehearse the band, and there were a couple of chords in there, that was a dischord. Charlie Barnet loved it. He said, 'Remember what you did?' I says, 'No, I don't know.' 'Right there, you remember what you did?' 'Let's Go back.' And I says, 'No, I don't; I says, a dischord.' 'Keep it in, Keep it in.'
He liked it.
That guy's crazy, man, but he was out of sight. But he liked weird deals, you know.
Were those dischords the result of mistakes, or you planned them?
Actual mistakes, yeah. Like you know, you'd have an F sharp on top of an F, you know, one of those things, and you didn't mean that. You meant it to be an A flat,
"Keep it in! Keep it in! I like it, you know. "Keep it in." How you gonna think that way? Oh that was funny.
Before you would write an arrangement, would you sort of sketch it out on paper, just basic things, or did you just start from measure one and go on?

You know, if I was gonna make an arrangement, I'd like to set a little pattern first, you know, figure in my mind what I'm gonna do, and I'll sketch it out, you know, like what my first chorus will be, and what my next chorus, and the next. Now usually, if it's a swing thing, I'd always try to -- timewise have four choruses, you know, for the out chorus, you know, one of those things. And then a lot of times -- well this is for the swing things. Now for ballads it's different, like two and two and a half, but when you have to write a lot of 'em, then you got to really sit down and figure so it won't all sound the same, you know. And that was a hard thing with Barnet. I used to have to make two arrangements a week for him. And of course he was carrying 19 pieces then.
When was this? I always hit you with dates.
Well, '39 and '40. Got that down.
In where? Chicago? Wherever you --
This was in New York. Yeah.
Were you writing only for him or
were you playing also?
I was writing only for him. Yes.
Were you playing with him? In the band at all, or just arranging?

I played a short period with him when -- he had a little piano player named Bill Miller. Excellent pianist. He's out in Hollywood now in one of the studios -- arranging and playing. Bill got sick for about a month and we were doing one-nighters, and then I played. But I was used primarily as an arranger, because a lot of times the band would be on the road, and I would stay home and write, but I'd make the arrangements, and a lot of times he'd be up in Boston, and that vicinity around, and I used to have to go up to rehearse the band on certain days and take up arrangements, you know.
Did you have to copy your own arrangers -- arrangements? Or you said, they had a copyist.
I had a copyist. He paid me for the copyist. I had my own copyist, and that would ease it up.
Were you making about the same kind of money for writing for him as the ones --
I was salaried with him.
Uh-huh. What kind of salary did you make? If you can remember.
I think sometimes -- I think it averaged around $225 a week, which was real good.
Sure it was.
Real good. But he was carrying 19 people, pieces.
Yeah. That's a big group.

That's a big group, and I had to make two arrangements a week. This was in the contract. This was rough, but I never got a chance to go anywhere. (Inaudible). Now I did a little writing for Jimmy Dorsey, too. Now the difference between he and Charley -- and God knows Charley could have stood this better than Jimmy, because Charley's family was wealthy and so was Charlie, you know, and what he cared about a dollar was less. He wasn't cheap at all, but he wanted those two arrangements a week. Jimmy Dorsey was just the opposite. Now I stayed with Jimmy for a few months, but Jimmy always told me this: "Horace, if you feel like writing, you write. If you don't, don't do it because whichever you write, your mood's gonna be on that paper." I thought that was great, you know. And sure enough, it was like that way sometimes. You didn't feel good and you'd write and it wasn't up to par, you know, and he'd still pay you.
Jimmy would, you mean.
Jimmy Dorsey. He would still pay you.
In other words, you were salaried with him also.
Yes. Yes, I was with Jimmy -- not so long as Charley Barnet, but I had a lot of fun with him.
Did they make any suggestions as to how you should write these things, or did they leave it entirely up to you?

It would be left entirely up to me, but they wanted me to come and hear the band play, and hear the soloists, so I would know who to give this to, and hear the strong men in the trumpet section, and what I used to do, like if I'd write my first chorus ensemble, and it would be pretty busy -- the arrangement -- all through the arrangement instead of having guys (unintelligible) lay out -- when I say pretty busy, it'd keep the band going. Then I would switch a strong trumpet player for the out chorus, you know, to build up. You understand this because you write. And this -- that way we'd keep the thing fresh. So these are some of the things that they wanted me to come and hear the band. In fact, I used to come and hear the band and sit in the back and listen to them, you know, all night long, because this was during the time that I first joined the band, 'cause I wanted to know who I was writing for, and I've always found out, even from my own groups, if you write according to the ability of the individual, your arrangement will sound much better.
Sure.
Even if you have to simplify it. Which I found out with groups that I've had, if a guy doesn't read real well, and he reads slow, all right. Then you make
easy passages, and they sound good. If you write something complicated --
They don't come off out.
As the boys say in the musical term, it's gonna be scufflish.
Right.

But a lot of guys don't do it. Like I had a couple of arrangers make some things for me, you know, just to find out, you know, what I'm missing, and one of those things. I wanted them to hear the group. I had them hear the group, and they still come in and they put the kitchen stove in the arrangement.
Everything.

And it sound like scrambled eggs. It was just horrible. I had a certain guy, however he's a terrific arranger, and he's -- I'm not going to call his name, but he made a couple of things for me. He's a Chicago boy. A very good pianist, and he played with locked hands and everything. Wow! But he would write that same way, and they'd be jumpin' all --
So it'd be tight, yeah.
It didn't make sense, so I just paid him for the two arrangements, and that was it. We just put him in the back of the books. But I figure, if you write
according to the way the guys ability is, you're gonna get the best results.
Did you listen to other bands? Did you get a chance to listen to other bands and other arrangements, and in a sense, steal things, or --
Oh, when I was writing for Barnet and those, I used to make the rounds, man. Go out and hear, sure. That's where you get your ideas. If you don't, you find yourself in a bag, man.
In a rut.

That's bad. You'll be writing the same things, the same arrangements -- and different arrangements, I mean. And that's really bad, so I used to go the Savoy down to the Hotel Clinton, many and had everything, and hear these bands, you know. I even went to hear Guy Lombardo one time. I found something there. I used it.
Well that band was always a good musicianship band, whatever style they were playing.

Yes sir. In fact, there were a couple of things I did for Barnet -- I've forgotten what the things were -- but I heard Guy Lombardo, and there was a little whining goin' on. Him and Charley le Barnet would -- he liked to play corn a lot too, you know what I mean? Just putting people on, you know.
Right.
And this is where some of the Guy Lombardo things came in.
Put it to use.
Yes. It was funny. I made the rounds. In 'The Home of Happy Feet,' man, (Unintelligible) you could always get ideas, at the Savoy Ballroom.
Did Fletcher, you know, do approximately the same thing? I mean, he was busy playing a lot. Did he have a chance to get out and hear other --

No. Fletcher didn't go around much. I used to try to make him go around a lot. Not-- I just wanted to get his mind away from music a lot, because he was working real hard. I used to be in New York at our house on 39th Street, -- 139th rather -- and I'd come in from my job -- oh, I'll say 3:30 in the morning. I've been off for two hours, and there's poor Fletcher at the piano. Benny'd just called up and says, 'I need an arrangement for tomorrow morning for nine o'clock. We're recording so and so.' This is for 12, 15 pieces we're talking about. Poor Fletcher, and he's sittin' up all night, man, and sleepin' at the piano, you know, one of those things, and I'd wake him up sometimes and help him undress. He's tired. He says, 'I gotta finish this for Benny, at least gotta copy it by morning.'
Benny would think nothing of calling you up, man, four in the morning, telling you I gotta have this by ten. Oh. He's an arranger's nightmare.
But you got 'em out.
Yeah. And they'd turn out to be good, you know. Quick things, you know, and what you would do, though, is make -- you've heard the band that you're writing for.
Sure.

So you make little skeleton things, you know, and Benny they would understand that, and your copyist would understand it, you know, and you'd, you know, being an arranger you know this. After you've written for so long, if you've got to have something fast, then you've learned the short-cuts.
Sure.
-- in writing.
Patterns, and -- Did you ever sometime come in and say -- and find Fletcher half asleep and finish an arrangement? Did you ever finish any arrangements for him?

Many a times. In fact, I happened to have been on one of the rehearsals that he went to sleep and he was writing, and he forgot what key he was in, and all of the sudden, the band is swinging down, and they go into something else, and the guys looked, you know, one time, and Fletcher says, 'Oh my gosh, this was when I fell off asleep.' It
was funny. Man, everybody turned around and looked at each other. It didn't happen often, you know what I mean, but -- of course, the copyist didn't know this.
So he just wrote it out.
Like Flip Wilson says, what you see, is what you get.
Right.

But, this is what happened, and it go to be -- it was funny. It broke the spell. Everybody was tense, you know, they -- I think this was one of the tunes that they had played last, or next to last at the session, you know. I think usually on a session that time we'd do four tunes.
How were the recording sessions in those days? Like what was the set-up? Did they use one microphone, or -- they probably --

I think they had more than one. They would switch them around, and this echo chamber wasn't popular during that time, you know, that they would have a soloist or something go in, and then they'd play something and then they'd have the leader come in and back in the sound room -- (unintelligible) and the (unintelligible) -- what do you call it? -- and play it back, but they would have the engineers come out, and I'd see them push the bass player up here, and the guitar player -- put the drums away in the rear, and all that stuff, you know. It was funny. And I remember one time, Fletcher had a recording session with

Chu Berry and Coleman Hawkins was his saxophonists, and in this particular arrangement -- I've forgotten what it was -- they both had to play something. Now Chu Berry was a great saxophonist, and you know Hawkins, but this was a unison thing, -- Chu played sharp, he had a tendency to play sharp and Chu played so sharp (inaudible) on a melody that flowed, you know, especially when they was playing unison to it. It sounded like he was in another key.
Half step up.

Half step. So you know what they did? They put Chu in the back. Way in the back of the room, just for this particular deal. I remembered that, but it was done diplomatic so it didn't hurt his feelings, and what not. He played sharp, and that brought Hawk closer to the mike where he was prominent with that big tone, you know, so he actually covered Chu. I remember this. I've forgotten what tune it was, but it was a session. And I used to hear a lot of arguments, sometimes fellas arguing about musicians, and I remember these things, but when they would begin to compare Coleman Hawkins with this guy Chu Berry, I'd walk away. They'd ask me how come I walk away. I wouldn't say anything, but There's no comparison, see. I didn't want to embarrass the man.
In those days, mainly when you were recording they were just three-minute recordings, cause you were still using old 78?

Right. Right. And they would watch that clock. That second hand would be going like mad, you know. And a lot of times they'd do this. We'd run over. We had to cut out the end a little or something, just to make it -- like you play the first chorus and make an interlude, a modulation, or one of those things --
Right. You just --
-- going into another key. You had to make it abrupt.
Change.
Change key, you know. So those are the things you'd have to learn. It's good experience for you.
Yeah. Well usually, as the arranger, you could pretty well plan that out so you --

You would know your own score, what you did that in. In fact, now sometimes you know, in this little small combo that I have, we jump right from this key right into another one. Abrupt change, man. And it's pretty funny. We've got something we play now, where my saxophone player changes keys immediately. We go into another key, and it's naturally brilliant. But I did it thinking about these things the way we used to cut, you know. And I don't go into a long thing with them to tell them why, but they like it, see. It's a brilliant change, as far as I'm concerned. Plus the fact that it helps
the musicians to play in different keys, as you know. These young kids need to do it more --
Yeah. Did you play a lot of blues in those days?
I tried to play a lot of blues in those days.
Why do you say tried? What do you mean?

Well, I was still thinking in that Earl Hines era, you know. And Earl was swing, you know. But I began to think blues when -- this is where the Grand Terrace came in. The floor shows -- we began to bring in guys like -- what's the big guy -- the Kansas City name -- Joe Turner.
Yeah. Big Joe Turner.
Big Joe Turner. Mr. Clean Head. This is all they could sing, the blues. We brought in Witherspoon.
Yeah, Jimmy.

The great Spoon, as we called him. And so they began to sing the blues. 'Ain't Nobody's Business' -- Lady Day had blues things. Not only, cause she had everything, you know, but these particular guys sang the blues, and the boss of the club would book these guys in, so we began to lean toward these blues patterns. (unintelligible). But you know who could play the blues in the band? Coleman Hawkins. Yes sir. He could play some of the filthiest -- and you had to like it, you know. And the

guys would -- we had trumpet players and all that, but Hawk would -- he'd growl, you know, and you begin to think in that vein. And the blues singers loved the thing. So you just begin to think blues, and we had a guy on trombone, as I told you, Big Green from Nebraska. He could play the blues. Och. So it rubs off on you, you know. After you hear the guys, you'd walk down the street and little riffs (unintelligible) begin to come to you. I love blues.
But you really hand't played blues much prior to that time.
No. No. I was too busy learning the fundamentals, but I found out later I had to get with it, you know. I love the blues. I play 'em a little better now.
Obviously. Well, one thing -- we started off this tape -- we were gonna talk about Danny Thomas and somehow we never talked about Danny Thomas. You were going to tell me --
Oh yes. This was at the 5100 Club in Chicago when I had that big band, and I followed a band that was playing in there named Mark Fisher -- does the name ring a bell?
I'm afraid not.
He had a band there at the 5100 Club.
This is Mark or --

Mark. M-A-R-K. Mark Fisher. Well I followed his band into the 5100 Club, and this was around '39 and '40, and I played for a guy there named Harry [Eagle] who had Danny Thomas there as the star of the show. And from there, you know where Danny went.
Yeah.
I wish I'd been his valet, anything, to follow him.
You bet.

But he played the 5100 club there which became famous. And I talked this guy into broadcasting from the 5100 Club. This guy was a millionaire that owned it. He wouldn't owe you a dime, and he wouldn't lend you a dime, one of those things. He was one of the few Chicago cash whiskey buyers, nightclub owners, and he was like that. But I felt as if I had done something great. I talked the guy into bringing WBBM in there and (unintelligible) but it paid off. And I had a great band there. This is when I had Walter Fuller, trumpet, Ray Nance, and I had a little guy from Ohio named PeeWee Jackson, Harry Jackson. Excellent reader. He's dead. But that was my trumpet section. They were great. I had Omer Simeon (unintelligible) with me. He played a beautiful clarinet. We did a great job broadcasting.
You mentioned also Bob Hope, that

Oh, this was during the time that I played with Duke Ellington's band. I was in the pit, and so was the band, and Duke was directing the band, and he had to direct the show at the Loew's State Theatre in New York City, and I've got the date here on this one. November, 1932.
Yes. And we had a guy on their as extra added attraction, and I think his name was one that you might recall -- Bob Hope.
You bet.

And Bob Hope was on the stage and when he took his bow and got through -- this is funny -- the boys in the band started to laugh, and we were in the pit like Johnny Hodges and Otto Hardwick and those guys. Bob Hope seat of his pants had a hole in them, and we laughed like mad. This was Bob Hope.
'32 yeah. Duke --
Forty-three years --
We showed it to Duke, and Duke fell out. It was the funniest thing. I've never forgotten it. That was one of my greatest thrills.
And you were playing with Duke at
Duke hired me to play the piano. That was one of the greatest thrills of my life.
You bet. How long did that go on?
The entire week. He was booked in the theatre for a week stand at that time, like at the Apollo, you know, so this was in 1932 in November. I never will forget it.

This is April 12, 1975 in Denver, Colorado, interview with Horace Henderson. Horace, we're just checking out some of the information that we've gained from other books, and one book that I have indicates that -- let's see, in the year 1931, Don Redmond, who apparently had been playing in your band, became the leader for a period of time, and that you continued with him for about another year and a half, up until 19 -- early 1933. Is that correct?

No, that isn't quite correct. I'll tell you. Don Redmond first was the director and arranger for the great McKinney's Cottonpickers Band in Detroit, Michigan, the Graystone Ballroom. And Don has been -- (inaudible) I should say, because it's past tense now -- was always aggressive in getting a good job. Don got a contract in New York City in a nightclub called Connie's Inn. He got the contract first, and began to search for the band, McKinney's so he gave his notice with the Cottonpickers as director. So

he found out that I was playing in a place in Columbus, Ohio called Valley Dale. I had an excellent band there, and he came over and came out and heard the band, and loved it. Then we talked about what he had in mind, and he said, "I have a contract in New York City at Connie's Inn, and he said, 'It's gonna be a long time contract. The Mills Brothers will be a feature there, and he said, 'You'll have to relinquish your ownership of the band, and naturally your name, but I would like to use you in the band as pianist, and arranger, and he said, 'What I have in mind -- you have a 12-piece band now, and I would like to augment the band to 17 pieces, and he said, 'I would pay you very well for the loss of your name, plus the fact I would pay you for the arrangements that the band is currently playing now.' So it was one of those things where I had the band and he had the job, and the contract, so we compromised and we did go into Connie's Inn, and we were quite successful, because after having opened up at Connie's Inn, we also got a commercial out of this thing for the Chipso Hour for 14 weeks.
For the which?
Chipso.
What was that?
It was a soap deal, you know, in New York, and we played for that, and we got paid extra besides playing regular at Connie's Inn. So it worked out real good,
plus the fact that -- and the Mills Brothers were on this too, and this was the original Mills Brothers with John, one of the fine bass players that passed.
Yes.

That was before the Mills Brothers' father took his place. And we made a tour after we had played in Connie's Inn for about a year, or a year and a half, and it was a successful tour then, so I didn't lose anything by compromising with Don.
Right. When you say you were playing this commercial, does that mean you had a regular radio broadcast, or how was it? What do you mean by a commercial?
Yes. It was 14 weeks, once a week the band played, and it was radio, naturally, during that period.
Was this a broadcast from Connie's Inn where you were playing, or a special -- you went up to a studio --
We had to go up to a studio to do this.
I see.
The Chipso Hour, they called it. It was quite successful. It was a 14 week run, you know. So they paid very good, even in those days, you know.
Sure. Okay, good. Then also, we talked about this before, but it was during that period in

November of 1932 where you worked for Duke Ellington for one week. ^ Yes, that was in New York City downtown at the Loews State Theatre, and I knew most of the fellas during that time, in Duke's band, you know, having been around with Fletcher and those boys. And Duke needed a pianist because he had to conduct on the stage, see, the acts at this time. One of the acts was a fellow that I think he's pretty well know, you know -- Bob Hope.
Yes, right. We did talk about him. That's when he had the holes in his pants. That's funny.

I got a kick out of playing for Duke for that week, because he had his great band there, you know, Sonny Greer, and Braud on the bass, and Otto Hardwick, the alto saxophonist. The original There is no guys -- 'cause Johnny Hodges was there too, you know. It was a great thrill, and they played things like It's Glory, you know that old record?
I don't think I know that one.
Oh, ^ It was a swinging thing. And Sonny Greer was on the drums. So that was another great experience.
Tell me a little bit about Don Redman. How did you find him as a person to work with?

Don was excellent to work with. In fact, he knew everything in music that you wanted to know about music. You would ask him questions about how you would phrase things, and, of course, Don played the alto saxophone in his

big band, of course. He led the section. We had five horns, and man, you talk about phrasing. But the greatest thing I admired Don for is his rehearsing the band. He rehearsed the band so hard on an arrangement till when he finished rehearsing his band, you knew that new arrangement by memory, almost. This was how thorough he was. He could hear a mistake even if it was a whisper, and he could point right out and tell you, and I learned a lot of things from him like distributing the chord, you know, and he would tell the trumpet -- like if you wanted your D flat and you want to put your G on top, he would tell the trumpet his note. Tell the alto his note --
The transposed note.

-- transpose right away, and then he -- after he would give one of those notes, -- this wasn't written on paper. This was a quicky, you know, and then he would direct it, and hit it, and man, it would sound like a symphony. So I learned that -- how to do that, because in later years when I had a big band, I used to do those things. But he was one of the greatest rehearsers, thorough rehearsers of a band. More so than a lot of big leaders that I know, you know. He was great.

Now you say that he was using a number of your arrangements that you had had with your own band, and then he augmented that band. Did you do -- continue arranging while you were working with him or was --

Yes. He let me write anything I wanted to, and of course, my book was quite instrumental in keeping the job because we had to build a new library. Only thing that happened -- I had to make the extra parts for the extra men when he augmented the band. In fact, one of the guys is quite active now that was in that group -- Benny Morton, the trombone player.
Oh yes.
Well, Benny was in that great band. We had three trombonists -- Claude Jones, a guy named Freddie Robinson, I don't know if you remember him; he had a great tone.
Is that Robinson or Robertson?
Robinson.
Robinson.
Three bones. And of course, Benny Morton was there, and Benny did most of the jazz, which he's noted for. So he's one of the few remaining original Don Redman members.
Was this Don Redman's first band, in a sense?
This was his first band. His own band.
Yeah.
He arranged and directed the McKinney Cotton Picker's Band, but it was already organized when he
came in. But Don really claimed this as his first band. And boy, could he write!
So both of you, in a sense, were writing arrangements during that time. Do you recall who the other personnel were, like --
In his band?
Yeah.

Yes. He had an excellent clarinetist and saxophonist -- alto saxophonist that is -- and he's a very good friend, a guy out of Detroit named Edward Inge -- I-N-G-E. Excellent clarinetist, and my tenor player was Bob Carroll out of Louisville, Kentucky, he went onto the band, and the other saxophonist was a foreigner, a little guy named Rupert Cole. This is what we called him, anyway. His last name was Cole. -- five. That constituted the reed section. We had a trumpet player named Sidney DeParis, one of the DeParis brothers -- remember Wilber De Paris?
Wilber. Yes.

Well, Sidney played trumpet, and we had another trumpet player -- I'm thinking real hard now -- named Clay, Shirley Clay. He was one of the few trumpet players in those days that could play a verse and play a lot of soul with that verse, you know. Don found this out, and this is the way he featured him.
I see.

He was quite a trumpet player. And we had a first trumpet player that was originally with the McKinney Cottonpickers. He was a professor. I was reading about him the other day. Right now his name skips me. (Langston Curl - <d.))
That's okay. We can dig that --
This was it. And of course --
How about drums?
I'm trying to think. Isn't that funny how that is gotten away from me. I'm trying to think of the drummer -- a guy named Bill Beason.
Beason?
Yes. B-E-A-S-O-N.
Had he been with your band or with --
Yes. He was with my band. And Don -- we had a bass player. He was terrific. I shouldn't forget his name. You'll have to come back to me.
Okay. We can dig that out.
That was a great band. 17 pieces.
Yeah. That must have been.
Claude Jones was one of the trombone players who later was with Fletcher's band too. He was an excellent trombonist. He was one of the original McKinney's Cottonpickers, so Don brought him over.
I see.
He was quite a guy.
So then you worked mainly at Connie's Inn and did some touring as well, or other local gigs?

Yes. We had a great show down at Connie's Inn, incidentally, and I would like to make mention of the fact there was a great dancer that I remember called Earl "Snakehips" Tucker. He was the one that invented that when you dance, you know, the snakehips. But he was quite famous. Like they say, you know, this guy with the twist -- what's his name?
Chubby Checker, originally.
Earl Tucker was the dancer that way. Snakehips.
I see.
He was primarily known all in Harlem as the king, and he was.
When you were doing shows that way, did you have much opportunity to really play jazz as such for the shows, or was it more between shows that you played jazz, or how did that usually work out?

Yes, we had a chance to play a lot of jazz and a lot of solos, because a lot of times we had to stretch the show, you know. Like when the girls would dance, and we'd play a first chorus ensemble, and then we'd go into ad lib things, and these revues would last sometimes an hour and fifteen minutes to an hour and a half, because we'd do

three shows a night, and when they had the blues singers, then Don used to let the jazz men come out and surround the blues singers, right on the floor, you know. They'd play jazz and play a chorus and she'd sing different blues, you know. So the boys didn't have to stick entirely to the script, you know. They could ad lib.
Yeah. Did the show change very often, like weekly, or monthly, or --
No. It was a set revue, and when you said monthly, you might have rung a bell, (unintelligible) yes. They would change numbers, but not the --
personnel. I see.
We had a great dance team there -- Paul Meeks and his wife -- they were terrific. We had, at one time, there was a special added attraction. The great Bill "Bojangles" Robinson.
Oh, great.

And naturally, he was tap dancing down there, so I had the pleasure of playing' stop time for him. And he always used to dance by things like "I'll See You in My Dreams," you know, which is a perfect tune for tap dancing.
For stop.. -
(Singing)
Right. To stop time that way.
So it was a great experience. It really was a great experience.
Where was Connie's Inn located?
At 131st and Seventh Avenue. And incidentally, they have a mark there now that was dedicated to Bill "Bojangles" Robinson.
Oh, really?

Right in the center of the street, which is a little parkway, like, you know, and there's a big stone there with his picture on it, and everything else, and it was right next door to a great, famous theatre called the Lafayette Theatre. See, Connie's Inn was downstairs. That's where the jazz really, you know --
-- was happening.
Things were really happening there, you can say that.

Following your work with Redmond's band -- or he actually combined your band and his band -- according to some of the authorities, approximately May, 1933, you went back and played with Fletcher's band, and this was known as the Decca band. Is the reason for that is that you were doing a lot of recording at that time?
For Decca Records. Yes. Fletcher had a contract with Decca. I've forgotten some of the tunes that (inaudible)
I have some lists some place.
(inaudible)
Probably if you call them out, I'll remember some incidents that occurred during that time.
Let's see. Now we're talking about 19 -- what did I say? -- 33 and 1934. These dates I have are later.
Now I have a thing here where Fletcher recorded Christopher Columbus on March 27, 1936, and he had personnel in his band like Roy Eldridge and Choo Berry, Buster Bailey.

Let's see. Here's the Connie's Inn orchestra. It's 1932. I guess that's Fletcher. Fletcher though -- Fletcher had been at Connie's Inn prior to your being there with Redmond, is that -- let's see -- December, 1932, Horace Henderson was playing with Fletcher, and you recorded "Honeysuckle Rose, New King Porter Stomp, Underneath the Harlem Moon, Yeah Man, Queer Notions, and so on. Those -- that goes on into -- that's all Fletcher's, but you were playing with Fletcher at that time too.
Yes. I think the band that preceded Don Redmond at Connie's Inn was a great band . . .
(End of Part One)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Horace Henderson

Washington, D. C.

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE

PROCEEDINGS
You just recalled the name of the trumpet player that had been with that Don Redman band. What was his name again?
Langston, I believe was his first name. Curl.
Langston Curl.
He was quite a first trumpet player. I remember him distinctly, because he was not an ad lib man; (inaudible), if you took the music from in front of him, you got silence.
And he had come from McKinney's.
Yes. He was with the McKinney's Cottonpickers in Detroit at the Graystone Ballroom. (unintelligible).

Okay. Getting back to Fletcher's band in '33 and '34, you were playing with them, and actually we do have an account of a number of the records they were making at that time. I'd like to move on to 1934. In fact, we covered some of this on the previous tapes, but in 1934, according to the authorities, you reformed your own band, and in 1935 then you played with Vernon Andrada. Is that right?
Yes.
-- in New York City. Then -- and we covered some of that material the other day -- 1936 you joined Fletcher's band, and this was at the Grand Terrace for
a period of time, if that's correct.
In Chicago, yes.
Right. And then in July '37, you reformed your own band, and went into the Swingland.
In Chicago.

In Chicago. Right. We have talked a little bit about that, but let's go into that a little more, if you will. Who were some of the people that were playing with you at that time in the Swingland in '37, if you recall?

Yes. That was a place where we broadcast in Chicago, from Radio Station WBBM, and Swingland was a nightclub similar to Connie's Inn in New York City, because they had some great revues. We played shows there, and I had a big band at that time, and we used to come on at night at 11:30, right behind Lawrence Welk and his seven piece band, and Lawrence was on the squeeze box.
Right.

This was a thing that happened four nights a week on the air, you know, and we played for a great little guy, who All the theatrical people in Chicago know. He recently passed -- and we used to call him the little king. His name was Benny Skoller -- S-K-O-L-E-R, and he -- during his period -- his life period, I should say, owning two or three different nightclubs, he had such people as the great Nat King Cole perform for him with his trio at Swingland. And he

turned out some beautiful performers. They had quite a show there. This particular thing was a production. We had a great producer, and he recently passed. His name was Sammy Dyer, and we would have like an opening number, and then we would have a tap dancer come on. We'd have a singer. Then we'd have what we call a middle number for the line of girls, you know, and these girls could really dance, and then we'd have Dusty Fletcher, the comedian, remember "Open-the-Door, Richard?" routine
Yes. Right.

He was in this revue, and he was doing that same act that he became famous later on by -- right in Swingland. Open the Door, Richard." And I remember distinctly one night we had a visitor sitting right at the door. The place was packed on Saturday night, and the MC, whose name was Rubel Blakely -- that just came to me. He was quite a guy, and he happened to recognize this particular guy in the audience, sitting near the door. You know who this guy was? Steppin' Fetchit.
Oh. Really.

So let me tell you what that guy did. They announced him, and they put the spotlight on him. You know what he did? He got up and turned his back to him and walked out. He was quite a guy. Oh, he was something. He had that lazy look. He became famous by it. And that was the second time that I had run across Steppin' Fetchit. The first
time -- I've got to mention this. Can I take you back to New York?
Sure.

You know, at one time at Connie's Inn we had Bojangles down there. He was tap dancing, and he was doing such a terrific job, and the audience was real silent. He had done this at Connie's Inn, the band playing. So all of a sudden, the audience began to laugh, and everything, and Bojangles didn't know if something had happened to his uniform or something, you know. And we happened to look over in the corner, and there Stepin' Fetchit slipped on the stage, put a chair out, dropped his head like he was sleepin'. It was a funny thing, and Bojangles looked back and saw that man -- you talk about somethin' goin' on. That was a funny thing. Now that was the first time I'd ever seen Fetchit. Then this Chicago incident was the second time. So I began to form my conclusions about him, you know. He didn't want to be introduced, you know. But getting back to that revue. That was an excellent revue, and it kept the band steadily employed. We stayed there for like two and a half, three years, no change, and we broadcast three and four nights a week. So this was a great thing for me in Chicago.
Sure was. Who were some of the people playing in the band at that time?
I'll have to lean on the fellows that

later went on to fame like the great trumpet player, Walter Fuller, and the great drummer, Alvin Burroughs. I had an excellent little saxophonist named Bob Crowder. C-R-O-W-D-E-R. He was quite a little arranger too. I had another saxophonist who came out of Earl Hines' band called Willy Randall.
: Willy?

Willy Randall. And I had a guy that played flute and saxophone and sang beautiful, named Leroy Harris. I had the great "Streamline" on trombone. John Ewing was his name. He's in Los Angeles. I'm pretty sure he's still out there. I had another trombonist. He's from Chicago, named Ed Fat, and he had a lot of drive. He was quite a guy. I also had that great lead alto saxophonist with me, Omer Simeon. Used to play all that dixieland on his clarinet. So I had a real good band with me.

: Yeah. That's great. I'd like to ask some questions before we really continue on the years here. Something about -- some musical questions. When you were playing these ballrooms such as this -- of course, you were doing reviews, did you play only the show or did you play for dance music in between, or concertized, or -- how did that work out?
Well, at Swingland, we're talking about that now -- well, the band would come to work, you know,

like at 9:00, and we would play for 45 minutes, you know, dance music, and then we'd take our fifteen minute break, and the first show of the evening would go on. Then we would play the show, which would last anywhere from an hour and fifteen minutes to an hour and a half. It all depends if the audience was quite responsive, naturally you stretch it out, you know. Then just before the break, we would always play a couple of numbers for dance set, dancing, and then make our usual announcement that the band was going to take an intermission, and we'd be back with you very shortly. "And ^ Don't forget, we have another show entirely different from the one that you've just seen," you know. And that show would come on until the last hour of the morning, that is, to hold the people, see.
Right.

Well, during that time we would play dance music, and it would give the people a chance to dance, and sometimes we'd have some nice dancers, even, just from our guests that were there, you know. ^ Had some fun. They'd do all this swing, and a lot of them would do the twist and all that stuff. I think I would like to inject one thing while we're talking about that band. This is an important fellah. My bass player, in that band, was named Harry Gray, G-R-A-Y, whom we campaigned, and almost had to fight to run for the presidency of the musicians' local in Chicago. This was Harry Gray, and he played

bass, and he was always a figurehead. He was a good man. I used to have him pay the fellows off, you know, and keep books and all this sort of stuff, and he was a good figurehead. He was pretty accurate, and he was a well-to-do man, and we campaigned for him, and he won the presidency in Chicago, and he did an awful lot there. Naturally, I had to get another bass player, and the bass player that followed him was a guy named Jesse Simpkins. He was an excellent bassist, and he was from my home town. He was a little kid, I remember, when I was coming up, and he could play.
Did you quite a lot of rehearsing at that time, or did it involve --

Oh yes. We would have to rehearse because I used to have to turn my programs in to WBBM, you know, a week in advance to have them cleared, you know, like what were the original things and the tunes that couldn't be broadcast at that time, and I would make arrangements, you know, musical arrangements. This is for the band, and we would have to rehearse so they would be pretty clean on the air, you know, and we got a chance to rehearse quite a bit by broadcasting three or four times a week, you know, you have to change your program. Usually they were half hour shots, and, if I remember correctly, that we would broadcast on there programs, it would constitute about eight tunes, and I used to have to send these into the librarian, and her name I'll never forget.
Helen Keppler. She would even call me in and I used to have to send the programs in by the week, you see, so they could have time to clear --
ASCAP.
Yes, or BMI. (Inaudible) So this is why we had to rehearse.
Did you have regular rehearsals scheduled, or did you just say, 'Okay, tomorrow we'll rehearse at such and such a time,' or --
Well I would always try to make it to the boys' convenience, you know, sometimes some guys had other things to do. Maybe an appointment for their family to go somewhere. It was always agreeable.
Did any or many of the musicians with you at that time have day jobs, or were they --
They couldn't, man. We worked seven nights a week.
Yeah.
No. No day jobs. In those days, I guess the musicians would have thought that would have been an insult, you know, to work days and then come and play seven nights a week.
Sure.
But they were serious about their music, and they pretty well stayed right with their music,
because this is all they knew, you know.
Do you recall what sort of money you made at that time, or how much you paid the guys in the band?
You know, I think these guys were getting around 75 or either 85 dollars a week. This is what the deal was at that time. And that was a lot of money, though.
Oh sure. That went a long way.
That's equivalent to 150 now.
Yeah.
I think that's what -- you get guys for 75 and 90 dollars, man, in those days, they thought they were making a fortune, you know? You could do more with your dollar, you know.
Right. Were -- you were doing most of the arranging for the band, or were you doing all of it? Was anybody else writing?

No. I had another fellow with me that was quite an arranger, and he was a pianist. He used to play piano sometimes on the things I'd direct, and he wrote for quartet, and he was quite a little arranger. Bob Crowder, my saxophonist, was an excellent little writer, and this particular arranger that I'm talking about, his name -- it's slipped my memory because this question came up -- but, Specks.

That's all I know him by, I can remember now, his name is Specks. Spencer was his first name, and he used to do a little writing for the Charioteers. He could write, and he was pretty thorough. Played very good piano, and he used to write some of the things for the show, and he had more time than I did, because he was more or less a handy man to the producer for the shows there which was Sammy Dye. And also, he would get paid extra when Sammy Dye would have rehearsals for the girls, you know, they had to have music, you know.
A pianist, yeah.

And he was the pianist for them, and of course, he'd play a few bars, and Sammy wanted him to stop, and one of these things. He'd get paid by the hour, so it was a full time job. Spencer Odum. Came to me.
Odem? O-D-E-M?

O-D-U-M. And we called him Specs because he did wear glasses. He was quite a little arranger. Now I think he's still living. And he went on to New York, and he did well. He was writing exclusively -- I have to push this tooth back up again -- for this group of excellent singers.
The Charioteers?
Yes. He did quite a bit of work.
Were a lot of the things that you played standard tunes or did you have some originals, or --
It was mixed. I had a few originals,

not as many as I accumulated, you know, in later years, but we stuck more or less to the standards, and of course, in those days, you know, a lot of guys used to come around with arrangements, and they wanted you to try 'em out to get 'em on the air. They'd do anything, you know, make you any kind of deal if the tune was all right or if you put it on the air, and said that this was his original tune, you know, one of those things. Well, --
These were song pluggers?

These were song pluggers, yeah. And of course, as you know, when you were broadcasting, the music publishers would bring some of their current tunes for you to broadcast, and they would give you a fee for doing it, you know. And that was permissible in those days.
Yes.
And that helped out quite a bit, and it encouraged the arrangers to write more actually.
Sure.
If a guy would bring a tune to me, and say, 'This is a tune that hasn't been published yet. We want to get it plugged on the air, and I'll pay for the arrangement,' you know, and --
There was early payola.
Yes. Right. And if you put it on the air a couple of times a week, so and so, we'll pay for
" this and that and the other thing. It worked out like that, and some of that was stopped though.
When you did that, did you sometimes find good tunes and then decide you'd like to keep those in the book?

The melodies of some of the things was real good. Of course, some of the chords didn't strike too well, but naturally, you know, you can change the chords. And by having a band with four saxophones and a full brass section, you could distribute those things around. You could make the sound good tunes, especially with a little arrangement, you see. And these guys got real interested. Even the other arrangers. It go so that they would like to write, and a funny thing about it. We created a certain style, you know, a regular swing deal, and I used to tell the boys that were writing, "let's try to write according to the way the style of the band is, even with these new tunes." And then we wouldn't sound like a different band, you know. And they caught on real well.
What are some of the characteristics that created that style, you know?

I'll have to say this terrific drummer and bass player that we had, Alvin Burroughs had the drive, beat with the you know, and Walter Fuller would play on the trumpet that punching deal like Jonah Jones, go --
(Singing)
Yeah. Right on the head. And it just had that beat, and so we kept it going, and it was easy for the dancers to dance by. So we were successful, and we just decided to stay with that pattern.
Was there any kind of special voiceing you used in the saxophones, or anything that way, or the brass in writing the arrangements?
Yes, we experimented a little bit with a closed chord, you know, in harmony, and then we'd experiment with opening it up, like with the mths.
Big sound.
And we found out in moving, that as long as the passages were moving, we'd write play it close, you know, instead of spread out the harmony. But on the ballads, we'd spread it.
If they were sustained.
Yeah, sustained. It would be pretty, you know, and you wouldn't have any notes clashing with each other, like the F sharp on top of the F --
Right. Yeah. Flat nine.
Yeah. Right.
Did you have a singer with the band at that time, or because of the show, you didn't have your own singer?
Yes. I had the great Arthur Lee
Simpkin.
Ah. Sure. That's right.

Yes. And he sang right on the floor, and of course, he was on with the broadcasting deal too, the sessions, you know, and he sang all the tunes, and he was great at learning the tune quick. This is what you had to do naturally, when you're (unaudible) broadcasting, and the guys were bringing in new numbers. He had quite an ear, and he had an uncanny memory, which helps all singers in learning lyrics quickly.
Right. Getting back to the arranging style, were you playing -- this is say 1937 at Swingland -- were you playing basically four beat music or two beat music, or did you mix it?
No. This was more or less four beat. Yeah. We played four.
What sort of piano style were you using at this time?
Trying to think of Hines during that time, and you know, having been in Chicago and Earl having been at the Grand Terrace, and I think his theme song was 'Deep Forest', wasn't it?
I believe that's it. Yeah.
I just loved that thing, and of course I used to listen to Earl play those solos, and I used to just pattern some other things, and I found out you could imitate

EARl the best of your ability that is, by playing a lot of things in swing with minor riffs, you know, like a lot of times instead of us playing a 12 bar blues pattern with the major chord, we'd play it in the minor strains, you know, and it would work out like mad, you know, in swing? And then on the out choruses you'd have the band -- if you're playing something like in C -- we'd have a C minor chord, like (Singing) and then resolve it, you know, and come on down. And it made good taste. We were experimenting, so like Charlie Barnet said, 'Remember what you did.' Keep that in, you know. It was a lucky thing.
With -- getting back to the piano style, and you say the closeness to Earl Hines' style, were you doing quite a lot of chording or was it still a certain amount of stride bass, or --
I would play chords when the ensemble thing was going, but as soon as you got to the solo, it would be the -- sometimes the one finger, and of course, Earl would play like in octaves, you know.
Yeah.
It would move. It would swing. It was a rather awkward thing to do, especially if you wanted to make some fast passages, and you would have to go back to the one-finger stuff.
-- the single line. Yeah.
But mostly, if you had a tune like
"Sweet Lorraine", you know, and you'd be --
(Swinging and Singing)
Well, then you could use your octave.
Something fast --
(Singing)
-- you had trouble.
