Were -- there was something I was gonna ask about that -- oh, in the arrangements -- when you're writing arrangements, did you consider a lot modulating from key to key, or did you tend to stay in one key? Now, I'm not thinking about having singers, but say, just a straight instrumental.

Instrumental? I find out -- I found out rather that if you would make little interludes after you're, say, first or second chorus and change keys -- have your out chorus in different keys -- the arrangement would sound more brilliant, and especially if you brought it up from say two or three steps up from the original one that you started out in. And a lot of times, you'd play with modulations going into that. It would lead you into that change of key, which would make the arrangement more interesting. I used to like this, plus the fact that it would give you a chance to play in more keys, and the musicians would like this because they wouldn't be limited, you know, to just plain E flat, or F--
Did you use -- sometimes did you
use strange keys like B or --
Or D natural.
Or D natural, yeah, A natural.
We didn't do too much. I left that up to Fletcher, you know. This was his bag, but we would play in D flat a bit.
Well five flats is --

Yeah, five flats, and that's a hard thing. And then some of the tunes that were written in those days, even A flat was, you know, you had to keep your faculties about you. But everybody could play in C and F and B flat, you know, that was the crips (unintelligible), you know, but the guys go so that they wanted challenge some other keys. So I wrote a couple of things in D natural, A natural, and for a while, it sounded like scrambled eggs.

Right. A natural puts your tenors and trumpets in B natural. Yeah. That would be a problem. Did you -- when you were rehearsing, did you really concentrate a lot on intonation and good sharp cut offs?
Yes. Well, (I knew the individuals in the band, unintelligible)
Clean attacks?

-- that had the best tone, and the guys that didn't have -- generally, you know, in those days, the third alto had the worst tone, as a general rule, you know. So we'd put him in the middle where his note was important
but yet didn't stand out. And I used to have a little alto player. His name was -- I called it before here -- Willy Randall.
Yes.

And the only trouble I had with him -- a lot of times we had trouble with him over shouting the five saxophones in the reed section. That third alto is very -- those notes that he has sometimes important, and has to be treated (Unintelligible). So sometime, he would play them so loud that he would make the chord sound like it was a dischord, you know. And I used to tell him, I'd say, 'Willy, you're overshadowing your lead man, first alto player.' I said a chord is supposed to be built like this, like an angle. The first man on top, then there you are, and then there's your tenor, and your tenor support, and then it would sound mellow. I never could get that over to him for a long time, except one time I did exactly what we are doing now, I taped something for him once and played the reed section chorus back, and Willy -- I was hoping that he would play loud like we'd had trouble -- he did. And I played it back, and he heard himself. From that day on, I had trouble with him bringing it out.
-- playing loud enough.
That was the greatest teacher, you know. So he said, 'Is that me? Man, that can't be.' I said, 'Well, listen to the notes, Willie.' I said, 'That's you. That

Simeon. " Simeon's isn't Simeon. Simeon's the lead alto player. He says, "Now I hear, I see how bad I sounded." It was fun. We made that thing, man, and we made jokes out of everything. Nobody got mad, you know, but it was a constructive criticism, you know, so it worked out real fine. And I got so I could get that mellowness that I wanted, you know, in the section.

When we were talking the other day, you had said that in the beginning everything that you played was written out -- piano parts were generally written out. By this time again, 19 -- mid-thirties, were pianists still having everything written out? I mean on the stock arrangements, we do see them written, but what about your own arrangements?
Well, I used to make a skeleton piano part, because --
Just chord symbols?
Yeah, chord symbols.
Punch chords?

A lot of the things that -- like, for instance, when we'd play a thing like "I Got Rhythm", well I know that so I (inaudible) one chorus I Got Rhythm, and then just say, write it on the piano part modulate, you know, so and so, and I just (unintelligible) save time.
Sure.
Because in broadcasting like that,

you wouldn't have the time to, you know, write out a real part, plus the fact that they weren't paying you for copyists copies during those days, and one of those things, so you had to find a short cut. And this was it.
That's sort of like Bach when he was writing a new cantata every week, you know, he had to borrow from other composers and other of his own music, and everything else.
Sure.
In your improvisation, were you at that -- or by this time thinking pretty much of just improvising on chord changes or still relating to the melody? It probably varied, I would assume, but --

It varied. Yes. But we tried both, because we wanted all the experience we could get, and I knew that eventually it was gonna come to, you know, the chord deal, so -- There were quite a few guys that came into town, and we used to have the opportunity to listen as these things came about, and we just figured that eventually this was the way it was gonna be.
Do you recall how early that began? I mean, say like going clear back to Connie's Inn or something, how was the improvisation going in those days? That was in the late twenties.
Well, we knew that it was inevitable, because, you know, like -- I hope I'm answering your question right -- as you know, in music there's always a challenge there to try something new.
Right. Become more complex, in a way, more sophisticated.
And we just figured eventually that this was where it was gonna wind up. And it did just that.

Talking a little bit about traveling, how far out during those various years that you were traveling out of either Chicago or Ohio or New York -- how far out did you really go? I mean, did you travel, for instance, in the South or in the West or --
Well --
Were they mostly one-nighters by car?

Well yes. We did a few one-nighters. We went down in Missouri. You know, after having played on the job for a long time, sometimes the boss would want you to go out for a month, and, you know, he said take a little vacation and when you come back, you won't be stale to yourself, one of those things. So we decided to try other cities to see how we would be accepted, you know, and there weren't too many booking agents during that time, and sometimes we were told different

guys in different towns who would run dances, you know, these one nighters, and we would have the guys in the band -- in fact, we would have a secretary in our band, you know, one of those things that was -- he was pretty smart on keeping books, like we'd have the kitty, you know, and the guy keeps all the tips and all this stuff, and you right it down. This particular guy used to write these individuals like down in Kansas City and St. Louis and say we'll be available and we would try to get a series of one nighters that would lead us directly into this place so that expenses wouldn't be great, you know, and this is how we'd do. We would have an opening next month, between the fourteenth of the month and the seventeenth, could you use . . . (inaudible) The guy used to buy up a week, and then what he'd do is play the other little towns, you know, and he'd just buy the band for the week and pay us a flat deal, and, of course, we'd play the one nighters. So it worked out pretty good. That was our first venture about -- I think around St. Louis and Kansas City, Joplin, Missouri, places like that.
: I've played there. Were these mostly for white audiences or black or mixed or --
Both. For both.
: Were there many -- there probably weren't many mixed audiences, were there?
No, except one time, we did venture away from home in North Carolina, and we played, believe it or
not -- we played a warehouse, in the warehouse, and they had one of these kind of floors that you put in -- dance floors just for this particular case. Now what do you call that?
: Portable floor, I don't -- That's the word I wanted,

(Unaudible) and this was a mixed audience, and we would drive the bus -- we had a bus at that time that we could rent, you know, and we could drive the bus right up into the warehouse, you know, right next to the --
: -- dance floor.
-- dance floor.
: Unload.

And unload, right in there, and when we'd take our intermission, the guys want to go sit in the bus, right there, and you still -- overhead you're covered. And the people would pay $2.50 and $3.00 and a half a head to get in. And you talking about some dances, and some of them were really comedians dancing, you know. And a lot of people, they had grandstands, like sections in the baseball games, you know, outdoors. And a lot of the people didn't dance, but they would come to observe, and they would see some funny things, and, of course, they would listen to the band. And we played quite a few of those.
: Was -- because of your broadcasting --
you said WBBM in Chicago -- Yes. Yes.
-- which was a pretty powerful station, wasn't it?

Yes, I used to get quite a bit of fan mail from all over in that section. And I used to weigh the fan mail and see how much I had from different -- from how many states and what not. This is how we would figure out our best one nighters. This is the way we'd do it, and it would pay off that way, you see. We'd get quite a bit of fan mail.
So they did know the band because of the broadcasts. What about recording? Were you doing much recording? Now, we're still talking about this Swingland time, 1937.

I think we had just begun on the tail end of that for recording. This is when I made this 'Ginger Bell' and things, you know. Because we had moved on from Swingland -- if I'm not ahead of myself -- (unintelligible) to the 5100 Club.
I have that -- let's see, you went at the Savoy in Chicago.
Yes.
And then also Grand Terrace in 1939 and later the 5100 Club.
Later the 5100 Club, because this is where we were more or less discovered by the recording studio.
There was a guy that had a recording studio in Chicago. He had excellent equipment, named Bill Putnam. Remember him?
I don't think so.
He had excellent equipment there.

(Inaudible) In fact, the bands from all over used to come to Chicago to record there out on Ontario on the north side. And this is where I made my OKeh and Decca recordings. Fletcher also recorded, if I remember correctly, in this particular studio, too.
During this time, again late thirties, Fletcher was in Chicago some of that time, wasn't he? At the Grand Terrace?
Yes. In fact, we used to run opposition to each other, you know? Even on the air, he used to broadcast too, you know.
Did you actually feel any opposition? I mean, other than just sort of friendly rivalry or --
Just a friendly rivalry.

I also have here that in early -- or no, in December of 1940, that you got the band together again. Apparently, there had been a time when you didn't have the band, and this time you were using personnel from Nat Towles -- is that it -- or Towles? I'm not familiar with that --
There was a band leader, a big guy, named Nat Towles out of Omaha, Nebraska. He had some excellent musicians with him.
Anybody of known name, or --

I don't think there was anybody that was too famous. Yes, I'll take that back. There was a guy named Harold Johnson that's with Duke Ellington's son's band now. We call him Money Johnson. Now he was out of Nat Towles' band, and he was just through here recently, in Denver, and played the Warehouse, and I talked with him. Now he was also a member of -- you remember a guy that had a band named Bull Moose Jackson?
Right. Yes.
And his Bearcats?
You bet.

Harold Johnson was in that band, in Los Angeles. And Nat Towles had some great musicians. Another guy named Lee Pope, a very good saxophone player. Another excellent tenor saxophonist named Bob Dorsey. Man, he could play. He was a character, but he could play. And I'll tell you what happened. This has just come to me. There was a guy that always has been instrumental in helping musicians secure jobs, or get recordings for them, and he's always been a very good friend of mine, been very helpful to me. He was helpful to Fletcher as well as other musicians. John Hammond.
Oh yes.
Well, John Hammond was a lover of Israel Crosby the bassist in Chicago. Israel Crosby was in my

band. He also liked Emmett Barry, the great trumpet player. Well, John Hammond had me get Israel Crosby, Emmet Barry, and myself together. We flew out to Omaha, Nebraska, and -- I hate to say it -- we raided Nat Towles' band because he wasn't doing too much, but they could play, man. They were together. But we stayed in Omaha about two weeks, and I rehearsed in a house there where I was staying. John Hammond financed us this whole thing for me, and we got together and rehearsed, and he flew us to New York City to record us. I had a drummer named Debo Mills. We called him Danny Bo. Man, he could drum. He's one of the few drummers that could make triple beats on a bass drum at any tempo that you played. Clear. I mean clear. And there was a little story behind him.

There was an all girl revue band called the International Sweethearts of Rhythm. Well, the leader of this particular band was a girl named Anna May Winburn. Well, this was his wife, and -- I'm saying this to say that we made a recording in New York, and he sang also, and he sang some lyrics to Anna May, you know. It was a blues. It was a great thing, and the record sold pretty good.

But John Hammond, getting back to what he did for us, he came out to Omaha after I had kept him, you know, well -- what shall I say -- he wanted to know, let's put it this way, what was going on, and so after two weeks of rehearsing I was keeping him -- what's the word I want?
Informed?

Informed. I'm a little off. I've been up all day today. He would be informed of just what was happening and how the band was progressing on the arrangements, and all, and he said because we want to come into New York and cut these sides, and after I'd thought that the band was well rehearsed and we had the arrangements down under our fingers, so to speak, I called John up and I said, "John, I think we're ready." So he flew out, and he heard them, and he said, "Yeah, you are ready." So he took us to New York, took the whole bill, got us -- the whole band -- rooms in a hotel there, and we went down and we recorded.
This was when? Do you recall?
You had something there (inaudible) about Nat Towles; It was during that era.
Okay. I've got some recording lists here in 1940. This would be for you, and this would have been some on Okeh -- let's see -- Chicago, May 8, 1940.
This was in the Forties.
Okay. Now here's one date in 1940 -- October 23, 1940 in New York for Okeh.
This is it.
Okay. And you've got on here Emmett Berry, Nat Bates, Harold Johnson, Leo Williams, Archie Brown, Howard Johnson, C.Q. Price.
Excellent alto saxophonist.
Bob Dorsey.
Bob Dorsey.
Lee Pope.
Lee Pope.
Leonard Talley on baritone.
Leonard Talley was on baritone saxophone. Yes.
Horace Henderson, Israel Crosby.
Right.
Debo Mills, and -- here, listen -- Sir Charles Thompson.
Right.
Lucky Thompson.
Sir Charles Thompson. Not Lucky.
Oh. That's right.
Sir Charles is a great organist.
Yeah. That's right.
He wrote a tune called 'Smooth Sailing' which we recorded. Man, that was the jumpiest thing, and he made the arrangement for me.
It's listed here. There are four tracks you have, or you don't -- let's see -- 'You Don't Mean No Good.' That must be --
That's the one Danny Bo sang to his
wife. That's the blues. John Hammond was a blues fiend, as you know.
Oh yes.
He loved Bessie and Clara Smith.
Right.
He thought that they were the greatest blues singers that ever lived.
And you have "Smooth Sailing," "Ain't Misbehaving," and "I'll Always Be In Love With You."
Right.
Yeah. So those were the four dates there.
That's the time that we were (Inaudible) -- just discussing.

Then in -- earlier that year, you had apparently three or four different dates in Chicago with some -- I guess the earlier band, probably before you went to raid Nat Towles band. You have February 27, several things for Vocalion, I guess --
You have (Unintelligible) "Chloe" on there?
Let's see.
Or "Ginger Bell?"
Titles, you mean?
Yes.
Yes. "Chloe." That was done May 8, in Chicago.

Of course, you know that was part one and part two. You know the band on the other side was John Kirby and that great little outfit that he had. Now we made a slow version of that with the big band, and John Kirby had the swing side.
I see.
That was on... (Unintelligible) Okay.
That was Okay. And then --
You should have a tune there that featured Israel Crosby on bass called "Flinging a Whing Ding." (unintelligible)
There's -- I don't -- oh yes, that was in August of 1940, recorded in Chicago, and Israel Crosby -- yeah.
That was a classic. Then you should have one by Ray Nance, that he played his violin on. John Hammond named this tune, and I can't -- for the love of me, I can't recall it.

Well, some that are listed here for that date of August are "When Dreams Come True," "I Still Have My Dreams," "Turkey Special," "Coquette," "Flingin' a Whing-Ding." Then earlier in May -- or no, July, there's "Sultan" Serenade, "Ginger Bells," and "Do Re Mi."
"Do Re Mi" was an original.
It has you -- original by you?
Yes.
Uh-huh. Okay. And in --

This was a take off on Honeysuckle Rose that Ray Nance was playing the violin. Instead of using the regular chords to Honeysuckle Rose, to make it different, I used diminished chords, and he would run them on his fiddle. It was a great thing. I've got it! Kitty on Toast!
Okay. That was recorded in February.
Yes.
John Hammond named that tune. Kitty on Toast. It just came to me. I've been trying to think of that for four or five days.
And that's based on Honeysuckle.
Based on a take off on Honeysuckle Rose.
I notice that some of these arrangements -- most of them indicated in here are by you, although one or two, like you did I Got Rhythm in February of 1940, and that was Fletcher's arrangement.
-- of I Got Rhythm.
Let's see now. This is interesting. Yeah. And there's another one in here where it says Fletcher Henderson conducts Horace Henderson and his orchestra. That
was "Oh Boy, I'm in the Groove."
Oh yes. I had a little singer with me named Viola Jefferson, a girl. Does it state that on there?
Yes, it does.
Yes. She went to Europe, and was quite successful there. She was the girl that outsang Ella Fitzgerald on "Tisket-a-Tasket" with that 5,000 people in the Savoy Ballroom in Chicago.
What do you mean she outsang her? She --

She took her own number that she made famous and brought the house down. Not because of the fact that she was a local girl, but she really did a job. But she sold, you know, Ella just stood up and sang at that time. This little girl -- "Tisket-a-Tasket" -- did (unintelligible) motions with it. It was a funny thing, you know. We knew that she didn't have the voice or the potential that Ella, but this little girl had drive. She was a saleslady, we'll call her. She knew how to put a tune over. She stayed with me quite a while. She was quite a vocalist.
Do you have any of these recordings, any of these 78's?
I don't have them. My sister has them in Georgia. She's quite a storage person, you know.
Are they pretty well preserved? I mean --
Yes.
She has taken care of them?

She takes things. Very good care of them. Plus I left 500 78's with very good friends of ours in Minneapolis, Minnesota, which we intend this summer, the first week we're off, take off. We're gonna go and get those.
Yeah. You really ought to.
And we hope they still have them.
It's difficult to say.
Well, we keep in touch with each other. Every now and then my wife mentions about them, 'Say, we're gonna come get our records one day.' I hope they are still there.
Do you have some of these arrangements in the arrangements that you have?
Yes, I have some downstairs.
The originals.
The originals.

That's great. Okay. Apparently, right before you went in the army, which was November of '42, then you played with Fletcher's band again. Tell me about that. How did it really work, if you want to say? LIke if

you came to a point where, for one reason or another, you didn't have a job or your band had, you know, stopped a gig or something, did you often automatically go to Fletcher's band, or how did that work out?

Well, we always, as you know, were in constant contact with each other, being in the same city. Fletcher during that time used to exchange arrangements -- write arrangements -- even for Basie, you know, Basie had his great Kansas City band during that time. He had Buck Clayton in that band and Harry Sweets Edison, and Basie was making his little tours up through there, and he would come in and stop at the same hotel right down where Fletcher was playing at the Grand Terrace, you know. And a lot of times, Fletcher would be broadcasting, and it was pretty difficult to broadcast (unintelligible) and direct and play too. And I knew this, and he said whenever you -- you know, 'If you ever take off, you know, close your job, or and you're gonna have a few weeks off, why don't you come in and help out,' you know, one of these things. And I was always there, you know, because I wanted to get all the playin' time and experience in that I wanted. Of course, being around these great guys like Roy And Choo -- in fact, one time when the job closed, the band was out of work for quite a few months. And this is when Crosby went over to Fletcher from my band. Israel Crosby, the bassist.
Yes.

So this is -- and then I went along too, and of course Fletcher liked that. He wasn't lazy or anything like that, but he knew he had to do a lot of writing and a lot of playing, and it was a difficult thing. Man, you know with a big band. It wasn't like a four piece combo, you know, where you can get by with sketches, you know, so this is what transpired.
What did he do during the times that you weren't -- did he just do without having extra hand there?
Yes. A lot of times I've even come in where he was playing, and he was just standing up sometimes through the whole arrangement directing.
Without a piano.

Without the piano, and of course, if there was an important thing where the piano had to play chimes, or bells, or make modulations, he'd do that and jump right back up from the piano. And he had a guitarist with him that was an excellent guitarist -- John Collins. Do you remember that name? He was a legend, and he's still in New York, and he had another guitarist that -- I just scrapped a 'Down Beat' here the other day -- his name is Lawrence Lucey, and he has a music studio and he's teaching chords and all that stuff now. Well, he was with Fletcher's band during that time. But even having the guitar, it wasn't like -- you still had to play the piano, you know. And it helped the bass a lot too, you know, in those
days, you know, the string bass. But it was missed, but he had to do it, and I knew this, and it kept him busy.
When he conducted, what was he actually doing? I mean, was he bringing in, like, you know, like the sax section and so on.

Different sections, (Inaudible) yes. And he used to have a little baton, and he was cute using it, and he had a little steps he'd do it from, you know. He would like this -- please believe it, Tom -- you know, he'd like to show off in front of the band, you know. He'd cut his little step, you know, cause the band would get to swingin', you get that beat, you get that feelin', you know. But most of all, getting back to the musical end of it, he was directing. He would like to draw the chords out, you know. He would have this little motion, you know, and the band would follow him. Shading, as we would call it. So he would like that. Well, he couldn't do it from the piano, and he got so he would love to see me walk in, you know. He'd call me right over there. Point.
Right. Right.
Sometimes --
Right in the middle of a job?
Right in the middle of a job, and sometimes he'd be broadcasting, and he would have to be up, you know, to cut the band off on certain notes, even if someone

-- you know, to come in, and then he would keep the beat going. would be singing (Inaudible). It required this, and he would make some intricate things in his arrangements that actually would require directing, because there weren't in tempo. Maybe an introduction would be an ad lib thing that needed conducting. Maybe somewhere to make the arrangement interesting, cause you know, on the ending. There might be a retard there, and then after the retard, the cut off, and then go back into tempo. Well, that's got to be directed.
Right.
-- to keep from being ragged, as we call it. So these are the things. And I liked this, because I knew later on it was gonna come in handy for me. So that was it. (TAPE 6)

The other day, we talked a little bit about recording, and we were talking mainly about your first recording experience back in the mid-twenties, and then a while ago we were talking about the records you made with your band and with Fletcher's in -- towards the late thirties, and I just be sort of interested in what -- was there much change in the technique -- recording techniques, and the way they set the band up, and such things as that?
Well, let's see. If I remember correctly, we're talking about the era of Christopher Columbus.
Yes. That's like 19 --
-- I've got March 27, '36. I think
Did they use separate microphones for each group?
Yeah. They had mikes suspended over the artists, and you know, having recorded then and the way they do now, it's quite a bit different.
Oh yeah. Generally, before you went to record something, did you have it pretty well rehearsed, or did you go into the studio and then rehearse the arrangement?

No, they would rehearse before the band got to the studio, because I think, Tom, the sessions at that time, they had to -- they were paying union scale or something by the hour, and if you hadn't rehearsed the arrangement before you got there, and had to clean up things, this was on the man's time, so they say, and so they kind of used to beef on that. So usually, the arrangements were pretty well rehearsed before they got there, and the only thing that

might happen in rehearsal, the time element might have been a factor. They might have had to either extend it or cut something out, and that way, after the arrangement naturally had been made, with a big group, you've got to mark the arrangement, where to cut, and what to leave out, you know, and where to come back in again. That might take up a little time, which -- they allowed for that, but as far as getting the arrangement down so it'd be smooth, no way.
Were the recording sessions pretty businesslike, or did you still have a lot of fun, pretty relaxed, or what was the general atmosphere?
Yeah. The band was relaxed, especially if the tunes that they were gonna record were groovy things, you know.
Yeah.

Excuse me. Then you wouldn't mind really blowing. Some of the -- some great things were played during that time, cause you get the beat, and if the set up, again, like you said before, if it was correct, you could hear everything, the rhythm and all, then you'd get a good sound. Some of those old 78's prove that, you know.
Sure. When -- did you often go into record new tunes especially, or simply recorded things that you had in the book and you --
Well, there was some of both. For
instance, like I think -- if I can remember correctly -- a session constituted four numbers.
That's what it seems to be according to --

Yeah. Four numbers, and sometimes that fourth number -- you wouldn't know what it was gonna be, maybe they might change it then, see. They'd have probably three numbers set, and the fourth number -- it would be some hidden thing in the books there, and a funny thing about it, sometimes you would record a tune that's supposed to be the hit on one side, and just put a back up on the other, and it turned out sometime that the back up tune was the hit. It was a funny thing, you know. I wish I had the little book here. I could, I guess -- It's pretty obvious though. I explained it like it would be. But sometimes a guy would come up and say, this is our hit tune. This is gonna be a hit, one of those things. What are you gonna back it up with? Oh, play anything. Put anything on the back. The anything on the back turned out to be the swinger. That was funny. But That's music.
Did the sessions -- what time of day did they normally occur?
We always did a lot of things in the morning. They figure that, well, either the musician has been out all night, and regardless of the fact if he's tired, he's still gonna play.
Yeah. He's gonna be pretty loose and ready to go.

Later on in the evening, they always find out they're lazy, you know, and want to go to bed or get sleepy. Their playing isn't as clean as it would ordinarily be. If I remember correctly, I found out that the morning sessions were mostly the best. But I'll tell you another thing that helped though, the fact that a lot of the sessions were in the mornings -- like on Monday morning after your day off on Sunday. You've had a little time, you know. (unintelligible)
I'd hate to have heard them on a Saturday or Sunday morning.
After all week.
Yes.
Or a big Saturday night, huh?
Right.
Did the -- I lost track of what I was going to say --
About the sessions?
Yeah. It was something about that. Can't think of it right now.
Well, maybe it'll come to you.

I don't know why I lost that. Well, maybe we can get back to that. The other day, we talked a little bit -- I'm leaping ahead now to the early Forties. We had talked about the fact that John Hammond had helped you get

this recording session together using some of the musicians from Nat Towles' band, and that apparently took place in late '40 and -- 1941 and so on. Then in 1942, you did go into the army, and we talked about that the other day, and according to my information here from November '42 to August of '43, you were in the army and you were the leader of the 732nd Military Police Band.
Right.
And you said that was in Illinois -- where?
That was in Joliet, Illinois.
Joliet.
Camp Desplaines. And that was under Wayne King's supervision. He was the one that --
Was he stationed there at the camp?
He was in Chicago. He was connected with the armed forces at that time.
So he probably had a number of different bands in different posts that were --
[I was approached -- disposition.]
(Unaudible) It was first offered to Louis Armstrong, and he turned it down -- as the bandmaster, you know.
Oh, really.
And he recommended me to Wayne King.
So Wayne King came out to see me and said, 'We're gonna have a

camp in Joliet, Illinois, and they needed a leader that would be made bandmaster, you know, so this is exactly what happened. So I played all the service clubs and what not, and we had this great 42 piece band.
Were there any name musicians in that band?

Really, not outstanding, no. But I did have musicians from some great bands, like Fats Waller's band. I had his first saxophone player, Jackie Fields out of New York City that he was drafted as 1A. I don't know if we mentioned this a few days ago, but during that time there was such a thing in the army requesting a guy, if he was 1A and a musician, and you were given a letter of authority where this guy was coming from the service center right directly to you, and man, I began to get letters from all over the country from guys who were 1A. "I'm a saxophonist." "Please call me."
Yeah. "Please call me. I want to get in your band. I know I'm gonna be drafted. I'm 1A, and I'd like to do this, you know, so we found quite a great group there in Joliet.

Following that time then, you played again off and on for a couple of years -- '43 and '44 -- in Fletcher's band, and then I note here that you reformed your group -- smaller group, and from time to time you were

Yes. Along that era, I believe I was doing quite a bit of arranging for Charley Barnet and his great band, you know, and Billy May was in that band, the great arranger and trumpet player. Course Charley had some great guys that could play, and of course, I think that Cliff Leeman, drum --
Drum, yeah.

He was in that band when I was connected with it, and of course, that is where I ran into Lena Horne. Charley Barnet was in New York City, and he had a trombone player with him at that time that played trombone with a valve -- a bass trombone where you could hit that low note with that key, you know, and his name was Ford Leary. A big guy. He had four trombone players, and Ford Leary was the guy that Barnet featured singing Shadrack.
Yeah.

So I never will forget this. Charley was booked to go in the Paramount Theatre, and Dinah Shore was on the bill as extra added attraction. Well, I'm a little ahead of myself, but to get the band set for this particular engagement at the Paramount in New York City, he took a job in a theatre uptown in the Bronx called the Valencia Theatre. So

Charlie called me, and he says, "Horace, I don't know what we're gonna do. Ford Leary, my trombonist and vocalist, has suffered a severe case of laryngitis." He says, "You think you could find me a singer? Go down to Harlem somewhere, down to the Apollo Theatre, and find me a singer." I said, "Well, I'll try." So I got in my car and I drove down, and to make a long story short, after enquiring around, guess who I came back with?
MR. : Must be Lena.

MR. HENDERSON: Lena Horne. She had just come in from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania having been divorced from her husband, so there's a little theatre in New York City -- there was, I don't know if there is now or not -- called the Regent at 116th and Seventh Avenue. So I went back stage in the Apollo Theatre, and they told me that Lena Horne had just left there, but she was going to this particular theatre, the Regent. So I immediately went to the Regent, and I had her paged, and I got her, and I talked with her, and I wouldn't tell her what I wanted, but we got in the car, and I asked her was she available to sing. And we talked and everything, and she said, "Yeah." "Well I won't tell you. I've got a surprise for you." So we rode on up to the Bronx, and we got almost to the Valencia Theatre, and out on the marquee was Charlie Barnet and his band. So she says, "What is this?" And I began to tell her what's happening. So I introduced her to Charlie, and

Charlie told her what was happening. They went downstairs, and rehearsed, and she said, 'Well I don't have any gowns, or anything.' She said, 'I just came to New York to visit,' so he gave her some money to go out and get a gown, and she went in the next show. And broke it up of course, and we rehearsed a couple of things downstairs, like 'The Captain and His Men,' and some other great things. She ad libbed a few things. So to make a long story short, we were set for the Paramount Theatre. So we went to the Paramount Theatre, and Lena Horne was his vocalist there, and we broke it up. And a funny thing about Charlie. This -- I've got to inject this.

Charlie always liked to play the horses. He had a wire on the back stage to the race track, and he won, and came across the stage and threw hundred dollar bills at the guys, and all this kind of stuff. He was quite a guy. He was funny, you know, and anyway, Lena went on and broke it up there, and of course, the scouts saw her and she went to Hollywood to the Trocadero out there. I don't need to say anything else about it, except I later joined her as her pianist and arranger and we toured all over the RKO theatres, all over the United States. I had a lovely time with her. She's quite a girl. We played a lot of the army camps, and we lived in a plane, man. That's the only thing I didn't like. My stomach couldn't take it, you know. We even went to Camp Joseph Robinson in Little Rock, Arkansas, and jumped from
there to Fort Dix, and all these places, all in a day. You know, we played sometimes -- it was a great experience for me. So this is what Charley Barnet did for me.
How was she to work with?

She was a princess. We played the Chez Paris in Chicago, and I got a group together to back her, and (unintelligible) was terrific. And then we began to rehearse to go into an MGM House, the Capitol Theatre in New York City, and Xavier Cugat, Robert Walker, and Lena Horne on the same bill.
Wow.

So when Lena heard Xavier Cugat's band was gonna play for her, she said, 'Hom, I don't know if this is gonna be -- we called each other Hom, you know, that was a little slang expression.' 'I don't know if this is gonna work or not.' She says, 'Why don't you go ahead and get a small group together to back me,' you know. So I went ahead and went to New York, and you know, the personnel that I got -- do you wanna hear it?
Tell me.
I got Big Sid Catlett on drums. I got a bass player named Billie Taylor, not the pianist. I got a guitar player named Al Casey.
I think I've heard that name.

Yeah, he was great around New York. That was my rhythm section. I got an excellent little trumpet player named Dick Vance on trumpet. I got Benny Morton on trombone. I got Earl Bostick on clarinet and saxophone, and who was the other guy? Edmond Hall for the other clarinet player.
That's far out.

So I had two clarinets, a muted trumpet, and a trombone, and played light things for Lena, and it swung. And All I had Xavier Cugat's band do during our four weeks stay was on the end, when we finished playing, was to hit the chord.
Final chord, yeah.

And this was it. But it was a great thing. You know what that band -- financially, you know what those eight pieces cost? But MGM had to pay for it. They were a little sore, but we played a lot of theatres, and Lena got good money for all the theatres that we played, like the Balabay and Katz BMK in Chicago, (inaudible) and all around, but the Capitol Theatre was an MGM house, and she couldn't go in there on a percentage, she had to take a flat salary, and this is rather Catlett teed her off a little bit, what (unintelligible) so she didn't feel anything about these salaries. Sid Kaplan got $500 a week. Benny Morton asked for
$350, and guys got $400 and all like that. This little They piece band, but it costs $3,000, you know? A week.
Wow.
Boy, were the heads (Unaudible) really mad about it, but she didn't care.
Sure.

It was a great thing though. Lena had a great sound. We played light behind her. We had light swing and it moved, because she was so soft, the way she sang, and commanded an audience, you know. It was just beautiful. Then on the end, the great Xavier Cugat's band with the big chord. So that was that.
We talked one evening about a short period where you worked with Billie Holiday. Do you want to tell me a little bit about that?
The great Lady Day.
You bet.
Yes. That was in New York City. I made quite a few things for Billie.
Arrangements, you mean?

Arrangements, and I played piano for her. I followed a guy that's an excellent pianist. He was with her for quite some time -- Bobby Tucker who now is Billy Eckstine's Eckstein's pianist. He's been with him for quite a few years. Well, he was with Billie Holiday previous to that, so he left

Billie Holiday, and went with Billy Eckstine, so I took his place, and she came down to hear my group where we were playing, and we were playing a theatre, and what knocked Billie out, I think, where I'm concerned -- where I was concerned, rather, is the fact that she had some music, and it was for a big band, and it hadn't been condensed where six pieces could play, so what I would do, I would look at all the parts, and where there would be seven bars out, with this particular horn, what's important, you know, I would suggest to fill that in with the other guys and make it full, and that knocked her out. She says -- she turned round to her husband, John Levy, and says, "See John, this is it. This is it," you know. But she liked that. She had her faculties, you know, and I made some things for her like "Strange Fruit." And Bobby Tucker had made a swinging thing for her that I had to condense called "Them Their Eyes," Lady Day. And I really had a ball with her, and it was a different experience from Lena Horne. Just -- they were two different personalities.
Was this after you had worked with Lena Horne?
Yes.
So this would be somewhere in the forties?
Right. We had to play up in New England, up in Boston, around that vicinity. She had some one

there -- then we jumped from there to Detroit, Michigan in a beautiful nightclub. And She was quite a girl, and the only thing about it, she had no conception of the time of day. Like in her contract, if she had four shows after she did her first show, she would take her little dog, her little chihuahua, which was given to her by Xavier Cugat, by the way. She'd take her little dog for a walk, and she'd walk up the street, and the first convenient bar that was open that she passed, she'd go in and sit at the bar, and she'd just sit up there and be friendly with people, and she would forget that in another hour or 45 minutes, she had another show to do. And if you didn't stay with her, she was there. And so, you just had to stay with her, you know, but she was so friendly and nice, and once she got on stage, Lady Day did her thing.

And I remember once in Boston, Massachusetts, her husband always tried to work a psychological on her, which I never approved of, but I couldn't do anything about it. He always made it a habit of making her mad five minutes before she got ready to go on stage to perform. He would walk in and peep in the door and call her a name or something, and she'd take her shoe off and throw it at him and start swearing, and start crying. And at the same time, she's putting her evening gown on, but she would go out on that stage with tears in her eyes, and give one of the greatest performances that Billie Holiday has ever given, you know. And mad with John Levy, her husband. But (inaudible) nobody knew it.
I just thought this -- it happened once, you know. But I found out it was a regular thing.
How was she to work with? I mean, for instance, like when you're rehearsing, or --
Oh, she was beautiful.

She would sit back and listen, you know. If she knew you knew what you were doing, she would never interfere, you know. And if you did something that really pleased her, and have the band do something, you could like at the expression on her face, and you could tell that she tell you thank you that way, you know. As long as you got the right tempo for her, she was fine, and I used to start the band out, especially the big bands that we would use -- she would wear these long dresses, and her feet would keep tempo. She'd just do like that, and she had the beat -- she would never drop time or anything else, and she always had presence of mind. If something went wrong, a guy was too loud behind her, one of those things, she'd go right on through the performance. Then after, she'd come and tell me -- "Have the trumpet player turned a little bit." You know, It's in my ear a little bit. Just bothers me -- just a little." But she was so diplomatic in even asking that
Did -- was she drinking a lot at that time, or --
Well, she drank, let's put it this way. She drank, and some other things, you know.
Yeah.
But --
Was she pretty spacey or was she pretty much there? I mean, when you talked with her, did she --

She had her faculties. It didn't seem to bother her. It seemed like she really needed this. It got so she depended upon it. But it didn't affect her singing, like I've seen it affect some people, you know. And it was a pitiful situation, but you were afraid to deny her these things, because you don't know what it might have done, you know, to her. So as long as she performed and did a great performance, you just couldn't disturb her.

This sort of brings up a topic. As a band leader through the years, how did you make out with regard to guys drinking on the job, and so on? Was that a major problem in just being responsible, getting to jobs on time and being there with the right clothes on, same colored socks, and so on?

I was fortunate in our band. I never had that trouble. I just had a couple of guys that I remember that would drink like that, but there were so many musicians in that time that you could get to replace these guys if they acted up, And jobs in big bands at that time -- Good jobs, I'm talking about were hard to come by, and especially steady jobs, where a year or a year and a half -- you know, the way you stay on the -- those are careers now.
Yeah. For sure.

So there were a lot of guys in Chicago just waiting for guys to goof, you know, and I only had one. There was a little guy named Hubert Dodson. He didn't become famous, but he was in that era along with Gene Ammonds, he came along with -- but he was an excellent reader, and he could play first, second, or third trumpet. He played beautifully, but he was weird, man, upstairs, you know. I remember one time, he was playing a solo, and he idolized Roy Eldridge, and he could play and he had good chops. And I remember one time, we were playing "After You're Gone," and we were playing it like Roy did with Krupa, you know, and when you got to the break in the bridge, he snatched his horn down, and instead of playing the break, he jumped to the mike. He says, "I'm not gonna play another note." And the guys, you know, thought it was funny. And he stood at attention. He was weird. I don't know. So he kept saying, "I'm not gonna play another note." So he kept saying it, so I begin to get a little peeved about it. I said, "Well, that's right, you're not. You're not gonna play another note. You're through." So I didn't even give him a notice, or one of those things. And this is when I got Gail Brockman, the guy that recorded with Gene Ammonds. Remember me telling you of "Redtop," and Gail took his place, and of course it was quite an addition to the group, because he was an excellent reader too. He could play. He had a beautiful style. But I never had any trouble with guys not

showing up on the job, getting drunk, or one of those things like -- I don't know. The guys wanted to play, I think, in those days, you know. They took it serious. It was a little bit different in my brother's band in that way, of course. But the guys knew how to hold their drinks. I shouldn't even say that. They knew how to hold the drinks. But playing in places like the Roseland on Broadway, you don't goof up jobs like that. So, I don't know if that answers your question or not, but the drinking thing didn't get out of hand. Didn't get out of hand. It was pretty well music.
Would you say that was pretty true with most all groups?

No. Number one, I had in those days what we would call an organized band, because we stayed together, the same personnel, for over a year. Then you gotta be classified as organized, you know, and with two or three sets of uniforms. But the guys in some groups figured that you had to drink that stuff to make you think you were playing up a storm, you know, and one of those things. I disagree with that. A lot of times, you might think you're doing it, so there's no way. But I have seen some musicians, though, that they really drank and could play. It's very seldom though that the two go together.
Let's continue a little bit here
just on our chronological forward movement. In mid 1945, this is after you had worked from time to time with Lena Horne, again you reformed a big band and you played at the Plantation in Los Angeles.
That was with Fletcher, of course.
It does say that you were also with Fletcher's band. Now was that his band or your band or what was the deal there?

No. Fletcher was booked out in Los Angeles from Chicago. He played 31 one nighters going into Los Angeles. Of course, the Plantation was out on 108th Street and Central Avenue where the people used to dance and what not. It was more of a dance place, and Fletcher got some California musicians to join his key men that he brought out there. Have you ever heard of a trumpet player in Los Angeles named Jake Porter?
I don't think so.

Well, he was an excellent player. He's an official in the union there in Los Angeles now. But he was a great trumpet player, and Fletcher got these particular guys to augment his band, and I think he played the Plantation for three weeks, or something like that, then he started back East. And this is when I decided to stay in California, and this is when I joined Lena Horne as her pianist and arranger, and we made a tour. We started our tour -- we first went to

San Francisco, played (unintelligible): the theaters and all. Fletcher said, "Do you mean you're not going back East?" I says, "No." I like California. I like this, and I'm gonna stay." I had no idea what I was gonna do. I was just gonna take a chance. I liked it. And I happened to have been staying at a place in California with a guy that's got quite a name, and he played with a name band and that was Juan Tizol, the great trombonist --
Oh yes.
-- with the late great --
Ellington.

-- Duke Ellington. I was stopping at his home, and I knew his wife Rose Tizol. She was quite a comedian, you know, natural comedian. I don't mean like a professional comedian. She was funny, and she and Lena Horne were very good friends, and Lena often came over and this is how I ran into Lena. I hadn't seen her since the days of Charley Barnet. And she came over one day to see Rose Tizol, and incidentally, she had a two room apartment over the garage in the back that she was renting to a movie star. Guess who? You remember a guy named Willie Best that played the funny parts with the big goo-goo eyes and the comical things?
Right. Yeah.
Well, Willie Best had that apartment, and we used to talk. Well anyway, Lena came over to visit Juan Tizol's wife, Rose, one day, and I was in the house

talking, like we're talking, you know, and she wanted to know what I was doing there. I told her (unintelligible) I got here with Fletcher, and I was getting ready to leave, and she says, "What are you gonna go back?" she says, "I'm getting ready to make a tour," she says. "Why don't you join me?" And I was a little quiet, you know, because it took my breath. She thought I was thinkin' about it. This is funny. So she said, "Come on, let's go in the room and talk." So she took me in the room, and we talked, and she said, "Listen, I'm gonna make a tour of theatres, RKO, all of the United States, and then I'm going into Chicago to the Chez Paris," and she says, "I'd like for you to be my pianist and arranger, and I'll pay you for each arrangement you make, make as many as you want to, wanna, and one of those things. I'll pay you for the recordings, and all these things, and I was so dumb-founded, I couldn't talk. She thought I was --
-- debating.
-- debating over the thing, you know.
So she says, "I'll double your salary."

So she asked me, was. How much money I wanted, you know. I didn't say anything. So I'm glad I didn't, because what she came out with, and I don't want the Internal Revenue to be listening, but what she came out with -- it was far more than I would have asked. And man, I didn't say anything, that got me then. She says, "Well, I'm gonna give you extra for
so and so when I get it." (Inaudible) So, man, I still can't talk; I'm silent. (LAUGHTER)
: (Inaudible)

So I had to check my head, you know. It wouldn't come out. So man, it was a lovely thing, and I made a lot of scores for her, and she paid me for all of them. I supervised her recordings, and on one of the sessions, guess who I had playing piano for me, and I was the conductor? Nellie Letcher.
: Oh really? I know Nellie, yeah.

Because we had something that needed to be directed, and I couldn't get back to the piano. So I had Big Sid Catlett Kaplan on the date, so it was decided that we would get a piano player, so I could conduct, you know, certain things, so I said, "Geez, I don't know anybody." Well, Big Sid Catlett Kaplan says, "Well, why don't you get my girlfriend?" I said, "Well, who is your girlfriend?" He says, "Nellie Letcher. Let me get her on the phone." Boom. That was it. So she came down in an hour.
: Was this in Los Angeles?
Los Angeles. We were recording. We had the session, and it went beautiful.
: About how long did that -- how long were you working with her on that tour?
Well, I stayed with Lena almost four

years. We would tour, and then we'd come back to Los Angeles, and then -- well, she was great in every way. More than financially, you know. I'll tell you one thing she did. You know, she was a starlet, you know, at that time at MGM. So she did something. I don't know what it was, and there was a little suspension there, but it wasn't bad, but nevertheless she told me that she was gonna take off some time, about four or five months. Do you know, she paid me three months in advance? She said, 'I want you to be around when I come back. I'm going out of the States.' This is when she married Lennie Hayton.
Oh yes.

So she and Lennie took a little tour, and she said, 'I want you to be available when I come back.' So, she was supposed to have been gone about three months. Well, she was gone about six. Well, I begin to get restless, so I used to hang around down on Central Avenue at a place called the Club Alabam, with a great band, swingin' band down there, and you must have known this guy. A guy named Johnny Otis.
Oh yeah. He's still doing a thing today.

Johnny Otis was playing the Club Alabam, and there was a band down there called Harlan Leonard and his Kansas City Rockets. They were there in California. So I happened to have been down there one day, and just foolin'

around. So here's a guy comes in from Twin Falls, Idaho. Here's a little story for you. And he walked up to me, and he said, "I'm lookin' for a four piece band to go to play about five months in Twin Falls, Idaho. I can pay $600, room and board." I said, "Come this way, sir." And this guy -- this really happened. So I had my group I was rehearsing, because I was getting restless. I accepted that job. You know, we went to Twin Falls, Idaho, and it was a beautiful thing, and this is how I started my group, my small group, and while I was in Twin Falls, Idaho, playing this date -- I think it lasted about five months -- Lena Horne had come back to the States, and she couldn't find me. And this is one of the reasons why I didn't get the part in The Benny Goodman Story." They couldn't locate me.
They didn't know where you were.

Fletcher's wife tried to find me, and I wasn't a good writer anyway. So they took Sammy Davis, Sr. to play in The Benny Goodman Story, instead of me. They looked all over for me. Nobody knew where I was. I was in a little obsolete town, Pocatello, Idaho, you know, which you had to get a magnifying glass to find on the map. But this is what happened.
Now, when was this? Do you recall what year, or -- probably late forties?
Yeah. Well, it was a year before the picture came out, you know.
I don't remember.

Benny Goodman tried to find me. They all tried to find me, you know. But I was happy with the group back in again, and this was a nice salary, with room and board. I had a little saxophone with me from Boston, Massachusetts named Smiley Thompson. He could play. A little bitty guy, but he was tight financially. And I got to tell you, this is real funny. And the guy that we played for was the President of the Cattle Owners' Association of the State of Idaho. And we had nothin' but steaks, you know, food. Anything we wanted at this particular club. It was called the Turf Club. Smiley, the saxophone player, picked up about 35 pounds. He couldn't get into any of his clothes. He had to buy new wardrobe.
Eatin' all that beef, yeah.
He had to spend about $500, man, to buy everything new. His shoes got too small! No shirts would fit him. No underwear, or nothin'. It was a fun thing, you know. Boy, and we fell out. There.
This was in Twin Falls or Pocatello?
This was in Twin Falls, but he had another club in Pocatello, so we played both places. But man, that was a great experience. And then I came back down to Los Angeles, but it was too late.
: Yeah.

I got a job down there working at a club right on Central Avenue, and I'll tell you another lady was on the bill -- Ethel Waters was the star attraction. So this could go on. But these things happened. It sounds like fairy tales, but it really happened.
: Ethel Waters had been around a long time, actually, cause she was very big in the mid-twenties.
My brother, you know, started her out --
: That's right. on the Black Swan label
(Unaudible) for Pace and Handy, music company, on the Black Swan 78 label in New York City.
: Yeah. He was musical director for that label when they first started.

Yes, Fletcher was musical director for that. (Unaudible) And he had such singers as Clara Smith, the blues singer, Bessie Smith, another Henderson, Rosa Henderson. He had the late Bert Williams on there, The comedian, and who else? I was a little stinker then in school, but I used to look forward to come and joinin' him then, but those were great days. And then Fletcher had his own band. This is how he began to start these bands to going. That was a great thing.
: Actually, in later interviews, I'm gonna get back to a number of different people. I've been making a list here, and we'll talk about individuals, but
leaping back into the late forties here, you played in the Million Dollar Theatre in Los Angeles?
Right. I was the house band there.
Was that a big band, or a small group?

It was a seven piece band, but it had a guy in there that I'm sure you know. You're talking about names, and he's still playin' trumpet. He looks like Louis -- Teddy Buckner. He's still in L.A. with his own group, and I had a little saxophone player. His original name was Curt Kirk Bradford, but he goes by the name now of Mustafa Hashim. But he was the first alto player after Jimmie Lunce Ford. Willie Smith with the great (unintelligible). Yeah. Curt Bradford. Excellent saxophonist. He was in the pit band, and we used to play for the different acts that came in, and one of the acts that came on stage during that time -- when we had two bands -- was Charlie Ventura.
Oh yeah.
And he had Benny Green playin' trombone with him.
Right.
And Roy Kral and Jackie Cain (Inaudible).
And Jackie (inaudible). Yes.
Oh, that's a group.
Yeah. I remember hearing that
group. Some of those -- That was the house band at the Million Dollar Theater.
(Inaudible) for a year. It was a beautiful thing.

Yeah. Then you got back to Chicago in late '49, 1950, according to my reports. One thing -- I basically just have information during the 1950's that you had your own group, small group, mainly in Minneapolis and Vegas, and various places.

Minneapolis was the base -- the jumping off place, I should say, with Billy Williams. Billy Williams brought his Charioteers to this particular Key Club where my band was housed, and he loved this group that I had so much so that he said to me one day, "Hey man, I've got a date in Vegas at the Riviera Theatre." He said, "Would you like to go?" I said, "Oh yes, sure." He said, "Well, it's comin' up in about three months," He says, "I'm gonna play a couple of shows down in Kansas City, and I'll get back to you." Well, I heard these things so much before --
Sure.

-- I took it with a grain of salt. But one morning, at five o'clock the phone rang, and he says, "Hey man, this is Billy Williams. You ready to go to Vegas? We open up in two weeks." And man, this was three months afterwards. So I had to go talk to the boss which was Hank [Sabis.] He brought attractions in his club like Sarah Vaughn,

Slappy White, Billy Eckstein, the all these guys played there, you know, and my band backed these guys, you know? Redd Foxx was there. Redd Foxx came there and broke it up, man, just like he is doing, you know. So I had to get a leave of absence from the owner. I wanted an eight-week absence -- leave of absence to go play with Billy Williams. I'm still on that eight week absence. I never went back. But we went to Vegas and played the Riviera and the Starlight Room, six different times. First time, we went there for four weeks, and we stayed six months. That's a career.
Oh yeah.
Had a great band. We had a revue, and this is -- we were one of the first revues that ever played in --
In Vegas.

-- Vegas. Then comes the George Young Revue, Harry James and Betty Grable in their revue. They all started there, you know what I mean. Revues I'm speaking of. But we broke it up. I had a quartet with me called the Four Dukes, and had a fat boy weighed 350 pounds that sang Mack the Knife. Tore it up. So we went on from there, and I had a good trumpet player named Clora Bryant who sang and played like Louis Armstrong. A woman.
Clora, you say.
Clora Bryant.
: Bryant.
She made some records with Billy Williams, man, she could play. We had an arrangement called Angel Eyes.
: Yeah.
And she could hit high F's all night long, and she wasn't like the average woman, you know, (inaudible) As the night progressed, she got stronger. This could go on.

: Yeah. Well, I'll tell you what, time being what it is, why don't we call it quits. But I'm intending to do on some of the next sessions is get down to some details about various people we have all ready, like with Hawkins and so on. But there's some others I'd like to talk about, and we'll, from time to time, get back into just some of the musical things, and also, I want to spend some time -- I've got it here from various lists I've acquired, that you -- and we've already talked about some of this -- that you arranged of course for Fletcher, some times, for Benny Goodman, Charley Barnet, and one account said you arranged for the Casa Loma Orchestra. Is that correct?
No.
: It's not correct.
That's incorrect. I did something for Jimmy Dorsey.
: Yeah, I've got Tommy Dorsey here. Not Tommy?
Not Tommy. Jimmy.
And Earl Hines? Did you do any arranging for him?
No. I didn't do anything for Earl.
Okay, then we'll knock that out. How about Jimmy Lunceford, cause that's down too.
Oh yes. I did a tune during the war called 'Jeep Rhythm' that I'm still drawing royalties off.
Really?
(inaudible) Had Jimmy Lunceford record it.
That's 'Jeep Rhythm'?
'Jeep Rhythm'.
Okay. Well, we'll talk about that. And Red Allen?
Oh yeah. We recorded a lot of things.
And some for Meredith Wilson?
Yes. I was with the Armed Forces Radio Service in Hollywood, and I did a lot of things for Maggie Whiteman.
Mel Tormé?
Oh yes. Mel Tormé.
Yeah. He's a great guy.
Oh boy. You know, that guy knows a lot about harmony.
You want me to tell you a little

story here? How I got started in music? When I was a kid, I remember seeing a movie with him in which he didn't sing, he played drums, and I was so knocked out by his drum playing, that I decided that I want to be a drummer, and that was the first thing. That was Mel Torme.
Isn't that something? He can play the drums.
Oh yeah.
He can sit down and play you some chords on the piano too. You remember the Meltones?
Yes.
That group. Oh man, now, he wrote a lot of stuff for them.
Well, 'The Christmas Song,' you know --
(Whistling)
-- is his song.
Oh yes. We've got to talk about Bob Crosby and his Bobcats. I made some things with them too.
Okay. Great. Well, we'll get into those next time around.

Eddie Miller. They were great guys. I met Bob Crosby when I was with Billy Williams at the Riviera. He came right up to me while I was rehearsing. He didn't know who Billy was. He walked right past Billy and says, 'Where's Horace Henderson?' and so and so? He knew me. He came over. Oh boy.
So you did some things for him?
Oh yeah.
Great. Okay, we'll get 'em next time around then.
Well, it sure has been a pleasure.
(END OF PROCEEDINGS AS RECORDED)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Interview with
Horace Henderson
Reels Seven - Thirteen
Interview by Tom MacCluskey

Washington, D. C.
April 16 - 27, 1975

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
This is April 16th, I believe, 1975, again interviewing Horace Henderson, third interview.

Horace, I made out a list of a number of the performers that you've mentioned, basically name performers that you've mentioned and some that I gleaned from various writings, and I thought today perhaps we could focus on some of those people. Now we have already in some cases, and I've tried to leave out names that we have discussed, but there may be some duplications here.

So I'm just going to name names and let you go on them, whatever you have to say, but I'm particularly interested in well, specifically about, you know, how you came to know them, what, especially most of these people either played in your band or Fletcher's band. I'd like to know about their musicianship, about their personality in their -- with regard to playing in the ensemble, you know, how they got along with the guys, whether they did or not, were they really sociable or were they pretty exclusive and stayed on their own, that sort of thing.

But just let your mind flit back to those people and those times, and we'll go from there. We have talked about Rex Stewart, of course, several times here, and I'm not sure if there's more that we can say, but I'll just bring his name up.
Well, you're going to talk about some real characters in some of these fellows, --
Great.

-- but actually it was a great experience for me because they all had different personalities; yet they were great musicians, and, of course, starting out with Rex Stewart, I was fortunate enough to have Rex Stewart in my band with the Wilberforce Collegiates, along with Benny Carter.
Right.

And Rex was playing the cornet at that time, and he was always an aggressive sort of fellow. He wasn't one of the greatest sort of what you call sight readers in the world, but he had quite an ear, and, of course, in my band as well as in Fletcher's band he more or less played third trumpet, you know, and, of course, as you know, not playing the lead, you can skate a little bit if you've got a good ear, you know, what I mean by like-skate.
And, of course, on the solos he was terrific, and he was one of the few trumpet players --
(Inaudible portion) INSERT
So this was what the people ate up.
Did he hit those notes intentionally?
No. No. No.
He'd just miss them.
INSERT TO p. 3

... that I ever had the pleasure of working with or hearing, for that matter, that could make a sour note, which we call a blure, and sell it, and it would sound good. Not on the recordings, of course, but when we would play to a packed house, like in the Graystone Ballroom in Detroit, Michigan, for instance. I know we had a battle of music there, the Wilberforce Collegians and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, which was quite a band in those days. And we had a battle of music out in the garden where had had about five or six thousand people. And Rex could sell, and he would play this little cornet. And he looked real funny, because he was a hefty guy anyway, and playing the little horn, it looked like he was taking advantage of that horn. And he would scream on a note, and it probably had the original intention of being a C, and he made it a C sharp or out of key deal that had no relation to the chord at all. But he sold it.

It was he just -- the force that he put behind his horn and he didn't have the correct schooling like most first trumpet players, you know, so I mean he had to make it up by being a salesman, and when he would play, he would do something in music in what we call -- rather -- he would pump, see, you know. It was funny to watch, you know, and the people loved that. They didn't even pay attention to what he was playing, what was coming out of the horn. They were looking at the individual, you know.
I see. He was moving his body and --
Oh, he was funny. You could see his stomach moving in and out. He -- why he drew laughs and everything and applause too, you know. So this was Rex Stewart.
As the leader, did it bother you, like in the beginning when he was hitting these clinker notes, or did, you know, it immediately appeal to you, or how did you feel about that?

Well, I tell you, there weren't that many clinkers that he hit. Just when he would snatch for high notes, you know, reach for the high notes, we call it. But he had an uncanny ear, and you played something down once, an arrangement, he's got his part. He might even put in a few weird notes that weren't on the paper, for harmony, you know? And as long as it would sound pleasing to him, one of those
things, or pleasing to me, I would, you know, accept it. But he was a salesman and he was a hard worker at all times. Now this all happened in my band.
Right.

And when he was with Fletcher's band, Roseland, he would hit those clinkers right on then, and he would sell -- the band was a little larger, of course. and I've got to inject a funny thing here once, what happened. Coleman Hawkins and that bunch were with Fletcher during this time, and Benny Carter and Jimmy Harrison, the trombone player, and Rex, one night on the bandstand and in Roseland in New York City, said, "Smack -- that was Fletcher's nickname, you know. "Could I request a number without comment?"
So the guys start to laughing, you know, and Hawk was a devil, you know, Coleman Hawkins, and they started laughing right away. He said, "Fletcher, I said without comment."
(Laughter)

Fletcher said, "Why sure, Rex." He says, "What is the tune you want to play?" Well, the title is, "Is My Face Red?" and, boy, that's all he had to say. The guys fell out. Of course, his face was red. It was the color of your black shoes that you have on. This was Rex.
(Laughter)
And, boy, it was funny, and, oh, could he swell up and get mad!

And when he would get mad, he would play at his best. Isn't that funny? As if to say, 'I'll show you guys laugh at me, you know? Fletcher would call the tune because he would know him that well. And, he'd call the tune that would feature Rex. And, man, he would blow and blow, and when he'd get through, he'd snatch his horn down and just -- the expression on his face -- oh, he would look like he was mad with any 60 people, you know?
(Laughter)
The guys would laugh kind of quietly, then, you know, because they had him mad, you know -- no fights, nothing like that, just verbal things, you know. So that was a little story on Rex Stewart.

Uh-huh. As a leader, did you -- were you pretty much a stickler for people playing very close to what was written, or was there quite a lot of freedom in the style or what they did with the notes or, you know, the types of attacks or such things as that?

Well, in those days I think I gave the individuals more liberty, especially after I found out the extent of their ability musically. I would simplify the arrangements, and I would make a lot of times what we call a skeleton arrangement, you know, and I would probably write out a riff, you know, for the first chorus. Then the solos would come in between. And a lot of times if we wanted to change

keys, and we were in a a little interlude, I'd probably take a four bar for, you know, change keys within that four bars on the piano, or either the drummer might take four bars, and we'd make an abrupt rough modulation going to the out chorus, and, of course, I always had my key men that could read real well have the lead, you know.

And it worked out real fine that way, and I found out that it made the band more relaxed because they weren't struggling, you know. So this is what I more or less leaned to in that era. But as things progressed and we got good -- I'll say better musicians reading --
Better readers, yeah.

-- yes -- then I began to make the arrangement full. You know, I -- instead of making it sound more like a jam deal after the first goes off, chorus and all. We actually had an interesting pattern laid out in the arrangement that we could follow because it didn't take long, number one, to rehearse this particular thing, and everybody could read. So as time marched on, this is what we did.
How was Fletcher as a leader, as far as, you know, being very tight about what he wanted, or was -- again, did he allow the musicians a certain amount of freedom, or how was that?
Well, as you know, Fletcher always had great soloists. When I say great soloists, I mean

individual artists that could play you 32 bars all night long and not repeat. But they still had to know how to read, especially in the keys Fletcher wrote in, B natural and D natural and things. You had to know your horn pretty thoroughly to do it. But he wouldn't cramp them. He would -- for instance, like a lot of times, as you know, being an arranger, too, you don't burn wearing your trumpet player out by not giving him a few bars to rest.
Right.

You know? And this is where the seesaw would begin with the reed section, and the brass might have little figurations and all, and then if the arrangement was made pretty intricate, why someplaces in the arrangement you'd have seven bars out, you know, where the trumpet player could rest his chops so that he would -- eventually toward the chorus outcourse he wouldn't be worn out. He'd be strong then too, if he could.

Then in the bridge of the chorus outcourse, you give the trumpet a break for that last eight bars, and then the ending, you'd have Hawk or somebody step in in the bridge, you know, just a little small figurations, 'it's tuh,' you know, little spot, just enough not to tire them out and have their chops up -- chops -- what I mean is your lip.
Yes.
(Laughter)
How was Fletcher to work for? Was he easy going or was he, again, pretty --

Oh, he was too easy a lot of times. You know, I can cite an instance in -- actually one time when I was playing with Fletcher's band, we were playing a series of one nighters up in Massachusetts, and this was when Fletcher's band was traveling by individual automobiles instead of a bus. And we had guys in the band like John Kirby, Coleman Hawkins, Louis Armstrong, Kaiser Marshall, Elmer Chambers and guys like that during that era, you know.

And they all had individual cars, and all Fletcher would tell them when they left New York, "We're playing up in Fall River, Massachusetts. It's on highway so and so.. We hit at 9:00 o'clock, and we're wearing such and such a thing." And he'd tell them this the night before. Okay, we don't see the guys no more.

Well, I remember one time Fletcher was driving his Packard, it was one of those old long roadsters, funny things, Maine, and I was riding with him, and he always kept his books in the -- there's a compartment on the side where he could put six on one side, and they'd just fit. Six on the other.
Yeah, I remember those. Yes, I do.
Anyway, this is where he used to carry them. Of course, the boys in the band carried their own horns. So I remember one time we were playing up in

Massachusetts, and it was 20 minutes of 9:00. There was nobody in the house, as far as the band was concerned, except Fletcher and myself. And he seemed just as unconcerned about, you know -- me, I was worrying to death.
(Laughter)

I went outside and was trying to look down the highway to see if I could see anybody, you know. I'd go back in and Fletcher's sitting at the piano just fooling around, playing. This is honest, the truth; this has happened more than once. And I was -- man, I was worrying so much, I was -- I should have been in bad health, you know, from worrying. But anyway, he never worried, and the guy didn't bother him, so -- well, about quarter of 9:00 here comes Coleman Hawkins in. About ten minutes of 9:00 here comes the drummer, ten minutes of 9:00 -- the drummer!
: To set up, yeah.
(Laughter)

To set up -- John Kirby was such an erratic roadsign reader that he went through the town which that we were going to play in and went 15 miles on the other side. And he asked somebody, 'What direction is Fall River?' They said, 'Back down the highway here the way you just came, 15 miles,' and all this thing, so he got in about 9:20, the bass player, so it happened that about 9:45 we had a full band, and the people were coming in, you know.
And Fletcher would start off with four or five musicians, man, and it worried me to death.
(Laughter)

We talked to the promoter that was running the affair, and he told them maybe they had a flat or something, you know, one of those things, you know. Finally, about 10:00 o'clock we had a full band. And the guys played after they got there so hard, you know the guys in some instances didn't cut any money off the contract. They honored the full contract because the house was full, and they always played a little bit overtime.

But when they got there, they played, but man -- it was -- oh, man, you were on edge. Not Fletcher! He didn't worry. And he never reprimanded the guys for it, you know. They were easy going, but they would seem as if they would play harder, you know. He was too easy on them. But I've often heard him say, 'Well, you don't ride your musicians,' you know. 'You tell them what you want done. If they don't do it, then you try to look for a capable replacement, if you can find one.' This was his answer.
I see.

So this was his pattern. Everybody knows Smack is an easy going guy, and the greatest harm he ever did to anybody was to himself by being too easy with these guys. But anytime he had a battle of musical jazz,

he didn't worry. I remember one time Fletcher played a battle of music. I'd like to insert this. Against the Casa Loma Band. This happened in Michigan. And this is a funny thing. He was quite a judge of what we call battling with bands, you know. Okay, this happened in the Greystone Ballroom too. That was a prominent place in the old days, you know, for different things. Well, anyway, there was a band on that side -- Glen Gray Casa Loma Band, two bandstands -- Fletcher on the other side.
So here's Glen Gray and his band, and he had great musicians in that band, you know, --
Oh, yes.

MR. HENDERSON: -- like Kenny Sargent, and Sonny Dunham played trombone and trumpet. Oh, those were great guys, man. And Peewee Hunt and that -- in that era. Okay. Those guys would play, man, and open up. They would generally be the first band to start. They would open up, and they would play like mad, you know what I mean, and swinging the whole crowd, four or 5,000 people there. Okay.
Now Fletcher had -- I think I told you this before -- had a book, had two sets of books. He had one for arrangements.
Stocks, right, and his specials.
MR. HENDERSON: (Inaudible) Then he had his specials like A, A1, A2, A3 -- I want you hard to remember this, but because I
want to tell you this. So after Glen Gray played his 45 minutes, then Fletcher started. Fletcher started calling number six, 14, 12, those stocks, simple things, and they just blew.
(Laughter)

And, man, he was building up something. The guys in the band knew they weren't the best arrangements. He did this to his band for two sets. And generally, you know, when you have two bands playing in a ballroom, the crowd will shift over to the next band, you know --
Right, back and forth.
