Well, after Fletcher played his first set, and it was just a mediocre deal with the stocks, he had the crowd in front of him. Then they went back to Glen Gray. Glen Gray shot his best shot with the Casa Loma Band the second set. Okay. The next set Fletcher called stocks out. And the people -- just a few came over. The majority stayed over with the Casa Loma Band. Okay, the Casa Loma Casinoma Band played the third set, played like madmen. By this time everybody had -- Hawk had his arm back of a chair, just playing there, and they had their heads down.
(Laughter)

and Rex Stewart -- next to him was so mad, just fuming, you know. And Buster Bailey was in that band. So the third set they were getting ready to reach over for stocks, you know, like he was going to call them. Fletcher says, A6. The guys in the band begin to
Getting ready here.
(Laughter)

And he'd call X2. Hawk would say, bl-dl-dl-dl, trumpet player would say tl-tl-tl-tl-tl. They'd get ready. Man, they were so mad until these arrangements never sounded so good! They blew everything they ever knew --
I see.

-- in that one set. And the people, when they started to playing this stuff, they ran across the floor, and this was the -- I'll never forget it as long as I live, and afterwards, too, two hours. They ran across the floor and, man, they started to swinging, man, to things like D Natural Blues. -- I mean -- but Fletcher was the judge of the stuff. Glen Gray had played all his best numbers.
Yeah, he shot his wad.

He was played out, see. And, man, Fletcher went on from there all night long, and when Glen Gray got back to start again, the people didn't move. They stayed there by Fletcher's band. The guys were so mad, man, they could hardly talk.
(Laughter)
But it was a great experience for me to watch this, you know.
But he was great at that, see, and he won many a battle like that. So I wanted to inject that.
Yeah, that's great. How about -- how was Fletcher at rehearsals?

He was pretty thorough at rehearsals because, even with his own band, they knew his style, you know, and it wasn't any hard thing to do, but just if he -- he would write skeleton things too, you know, and he would explain where to jump, and I wanted to insert this, but I didn't have time to do this, and so on, because he was always busy. Benny kept him busy too, even while he was playing with his own band. And, of course, he rehearsed Benny's band, too, and he was pretty thorough, and he knew what he wanted. He didn't have to write a conductor's sheet. He did for Benny because a lot of times when Fletcher couldn't make Benny's rehearsal -- if he was on the road -- he'd send a conductor's sheet, and so having known his style, Benny, it would be easy for him to rehearse these things, see.

But with his own band, unless there was something, just as I said before, he wanted to insert one of those things. They knew his style, and it was easy, and they knew it was going to be in one of those weird keys, you know, so they had gotten used to that. And, of course, Coleman Hawkins, the reason I've marveled at him all along through my

musical career is the harder the key, the prettier he played. Keys meant nothing to him, you know. He could play in A natural and C sharp and F sharp and all those things, just as -- and I mean run the chords, but he knew what he was doing. He knew his instrument. So this is why I rate him as a genius, you know. Benny Carter's another one. Keys meant nothing, you know. When you get down, if you have Benny on that list, I want to tell you about a little guy.
Oh. Why don't we go ahead. He's just a couple down the list, so we might as well.

Well, this happened in Michigan too. It seems like everything is Michigan. This was a jam session after the job. I'll never forget, Benny had his alto. He wasn't playing something then. And he very seldom jammed, but on this particular night he didn't feel like going to bed. He wanted to go out, and the guys told him, well, there's a club band that's open late, you know, and the guys jam down there, so we'll go.

I can't recall the club. It's not important, I guess, but nevertheless they had a little piano player there. I remember his name was Guy Rodgers. He was a local little boy. And he had a few pet keys he could play in, and, of course, he did not know Benny Carter. He didn't know him musically. He might have known his name, but he didn't know that Benny was a genius. So he wanted to play one of those standard

tunes. I don't know, but it was something like "Sweet Sue," It's been so long now, It's been so long now, but all I can remember is the incident. But they started out playing in G, you know, and they went to F and one of those things. He told Benny, say, "We're going to change keys now, says, let's go to C sharp." Benny says, "Well, I don't know. I'll try." Putting him on, you know.
(Laughter)

But the more -- and, you know, And the little guy thought he was so and so. So Benny played one in D flat and struggled through it, but, you know, purposely. And then the little guy says, "Well, I'm going to A natural now. You know, if you get lost, --"
(Laughter)

I'm sitting there, man. -- "If you get lost, you know, just lay out, and I'll pick you up, one of those things, see. So when they got there, he didn't have to -- this little piano player played. Benny started to come down. He played A natural. But when he finished the, by the time he got to his 30th bar over a 32 bar chorus course, Benny said, "let's go to F sharp." Benny got in F sharp and started to -- the guy looked about and one of those things. He played all through F sharp. Piano player couldn't even find the chords in F sharp. Benny says, "How about E natural, concert, one of those things. Won't you start playing. Why Benny was playing a solo by himself.
Then when they got through, this guy says, 'Who's this?' He says, 'That's Benny Carter, one of the greatest arrangers in the -- and the guy wanted to go through the floor.
Yeah, I'll bet.
That was one of the funniest things, man, and I sat there and just howled. And it was all in fun, you know. But we had a little fresh guy that knew a couple of pet tunes --
In some --
-- in some pet keys.
Right.
So I think that cured him.
(Laughter)
Benny showed him. Yeah.
So that -- these are funny things you never forget.
Uh-huh. Had Benny had some formal training in a sense in arranging or --

Oh, I think he did have some in Pittsburgh, but I know in his later years -- like right now and a few years back from the current year. Last time I talked to Benny, he had gone to school in California. I don't know to what institution -- to study arranging and to learn more about the violins because he made a lot of things for MGM for the
Studios was out there.
Yes, he was doing some TV things.

Yes, TV things, and it involved, you know, when you cut your sound tracks, like for 105 musicians, one of those things. I was fortunate enough to be in on some things that the great Russian composer and arranger, Lennie Hayton, Lynn Haven, you know, Lena Horne's husband -- I sat in on a lot of his sound tracks for MGM and the way he rehearsed the band, you know, and all, and I knew he was well versed in all those things. And that was the first time that I had seen a big band rehearse with the big sheets in front of them, and they didn't -- like, for instance, when we make an arrangement, we would have letter A, you know, letter B and C. Well, at the studios they'd have everything by numerals -- bar 74, bar 150, and, man, he could hear somebody make a bad note way down there even at 105, he'd stop the band and he would say, like, 12 violins, four of them playing first, four playing second, four playing third. And they would have maybe 16, you know, another playing fourth.

And I asked Lennie Benny one thing. This is very interesting. And this was -- with politics going on. I guess I can say this, but I says, 'Lennie, Benny,' I said, 'Why is it so necessary to have four first violins or, second four violins?' He says, 'You really want to know?' I said, 'Why, sure.' He says, 'Well, we've got a lot of politics here, and we have something in the

studios, what they call the blues and the greens, you know, those syndicates,|| you know, one of those things. And -- plus the fact that the number third -- the third number one violinist was so horrible. He was a cousin of some executive there, and this is how he gets in. And the other thing -- so you got to have that many deep to cover up the other guys because they sould like -- he says, "I'll show you what I mean sometime."

So one day he did -- not Ben then -- but he told me a lot of other things. So they were rehearsing something, and he stopped the band, and he looked at me, and I knew he was up to something. So he -- about 105 guys, you know -- Murray MacEachern McKeckny, you remember the trombone player?
Murray --
MacEachern McKeckny.
I don't believe so, no.

I don't know if I pronounced it right. I know you know this guy. He's a great trombonist and alto saxophonist, great arranger -- he's made -- but he was in this particular band. Anyhow, he stopped the band, and he said, "Number three violin in the third chair, bar 84, go back a little bit and start playing it, bar 84, 85, 86, 87. Seems like something's wrong." This guy, nervous as he could be. Man, you could see perspiration coming on him because he wasn't -- he was a cousin of some executive there, and they

put him in, and, man, you should have heard him. He sounded like a high school kid, a beginner, you know. And Lennie Benny looked at me. He says, "Okay, fine. Now we can take it back from there." You know, he covered up good. But those are the things that happen. When he got to me it, he says, "You see now why we have to have that many deep?" I said, "Yes, I do."
I see. Yeah.

So those things happen. You never know. The public doesn't know these things. They go to the theaters, and hear these sound tracks, if there's some trash, you know, behind the star and music interludes, you know, all that. But these are the things that happen, and it was real interesting to me, so that's that, you know, was

Yeah, I'm sure of that. One thing I've always noted about Benny Carter whenever I've seen him or talked with him, that he always seems to be such a gentleman. He just -- you know, he's always got that smile on his face. You'd never know even for sure what he's thinking or how he's feeling or whatever because he looks -- he just comes across so nicely that way. Is he always that way?
Sometimes that smile can be deceiving, you know?
That's what I've wondered, you know.
Yeah, it can be deceiving.
That's really what I've wondered.

He's very thorough in rehearsal of the band. He's another Don Redman. When he rehearses a group, they are well rehearsed. He gets out of you all you've got. but he knows how to explain what he wants...
(Inaudible portion) INSERT

It meant exactly -- you've got the difference between the two smiles if you've worked with Benny. But he was a thorough musician, and he's another genius. I admire him tremendously and we are very good friends.
We've talked a little bit about Freddy Jenkins, but really not too much. I know he was with the Collegians and then later, of course, he was with Ellington.

Yes, Freddy was with me in Wilberforce, and he was quite a showman. He always carried that label, even into Duke Ellington's band. He could play, and he was a good reader. He was a good reader. And he never complained about a sore lip. That's one thing, you know. Trumpet players, a lot of them have trouble with their lips. He never had a sore lip. The only thing that -- you know, just to get on him about -- I think I mentioned it before -- he played more or less -- to an empty house he played better than he did to a full house. Full house, he didn't feel like playing, because next night you're on a percentage, and you weren't making any money, he'd blow the roof off, you'd go on a little I

... in his arrangements, and how he wants them played, how he wants this phrased. And if you don't get the idea of what he's talking about, he'll take his horn and show you. His marks are very thorough, how he wants you to do his correct shading, and there he was a dinger at having the right tempo for his arrangements. And he'll play them back. When you finish with that particular arrangement, you could almost play it with your eyes closed -- he was that thorough.
Then you would see the smile that meant satisfaction. Otherwise, if you weren't doing the job, you saw another type of smile, and it wasn't welcome.
never could understand that.

But he was quite a little guy, and I haven't heard of where Freddy is or know his whereabouts in the last four, five years, and it's bothered me. I've asked quite a few musicians, did you ever run across Freddy Jenkins. The last I've heard of Freddy, he was -- what do you call these guys that go about and promote records for the recording companies? PR man?
Promo or --
Yeah, public relations or A & R or promotion or PR or something.

I don't know. But anyhow, he was connected with a recording company in Texas, and he came through Denver, and I got to talk to him, and this was his last venture, as far as I'm concerned, what he was doing. I don't think in the past few years he was active, because he was considered more or less as a scout for talent for this particular recording company he was associated with.
Yeah, that would be A and R then.

Yeah. You know he was with Duke in those early years when Sonny Greer was in the band, and Duke had all those little sharp uniforms, and Freddy Jenkins used to stand up and sell. He was another salesman like Rex. Although In those he didn't hit the blues and sell them years if the blue wasn't selling, he was selling -- just he would get through playing and flip his horn over, you know, and twist it around like a baton, you know, and all this. It
would come right back up to the valves and everything. People would eat that up. That was Freddy Jenkins.
How were these people to travel with?

I mean not when you were just playing, but, you know, I've been in bands where everything is really great. Everybody loves everybody -- and other bands where it just seems like a very unhappy kind of crew, and sometimes it's due to one person.
Well, are you speaking of my band now, Fletcher's or just generally?
Well, specifically I suppose we could deal with each of these people that we've talked about or some of the other people we will talk about, but --
Well --
-- like sometimes one guy will turn out to always be the comedian, and another guy will always be the straight man and that sort of thing.

Yes. Oh, I see. Well, I'll tell you, I think the fellows in Fletcher's band liked to travel because of, number one, a lot of the guys were single, and a lot of the guys that weren't single traveled so long that they became single.
Yes.
(Laughter)
You know what I mean.
Yeah, it is

Sometimes you were out for two or three years, you didn't see your family. You didn't have any, in fact, you were served papers, you know, one of those things. They had a saying once, join John Fletcher Henderson's band, see the world and be a bachelor, you know. So this is what actually happened. But he paid them -- like you would have 31 one nighters, you would get a nightly salary, you know, which was far more equivalent according to working, you know, week stands, where you got, you know, a flat salary for a week, you know, plus the fact that a lot of guys used to like to travel and meet the girls and all this kind of stuff, and they'd look forward to it.

He'd have one or two in the band that would be home boys. They would miss their families, you know, and this is where you would have to inject quite a bit of humor or comedy to keep the guy from being so lonesome, like Henry Red Allen, you know.
(Laughter)

He hadn't traveled much when he joined Fletcher's band. And I had one or two guys in my band the same way, but the same procedure existed. My band too, the same way, we played the one nighters, and, naturally, you -- like, for instance, if you played at a job for a week's stand, you might get $800.00 or $900.00 for the week for the entire band, you know. Well,

you can get four, five or $600.00 a night for one nighters, or you might have it on a percentage, you know, 60-40 or 70-30 with a guarantee of so much. You could come away with -- I know of sometimes you'd have two, 3,000 people, you're owing us $1,500.00. That's good, so guys, that was an incentive, you know, to keep going, you know.
So these are the things, the one nighters, you know, and a lot of guys hated them, but --
Did you find as leader that you had to play mother from time to time, I mean that you had to really look after them or were they -- were --

Well, they were pretty well on their own. In the beginning you probably had to tell them a little -- a few things because, especially if we were taking a southern tour. A lot of -- we had some eastern boys that had never been south, and in that time things weren't like they are now, you know. There were certain restaurants that you couldn't go in, and the guys would ask why, you know? Then you had to go through a long bag and explain to them, you know, this is the reason why. They say, Man, I don't dig this."
(Laughter)
Yeah.
"I'd as soon as go back home," you know, one of those things. So you had to shoot your best

shot and talk them out of it, you know. And then a lot of times when you have a good night, though, down there, and sometimes it -- the guy would pick up $50 or $60.00 for his stand on one night. That would kind of compensate for the inconvenience, you know? A lot of times I know we played one nighters, and, you know, when a musician gets through playing at night, he's hungry, you know. He wants to go eat in a restaurant. Sometimes there were no restaurants open. This is when you had the problem. The guys are hungry, and you had to get in a bus, and sometimes maybe our next stop would be 300, 350 miles, you know, 350 miles and the next available eating place would be that.

So the guys began to get wise, and they started to getting their little sandwiches and things early, -- this, you would gather experience as you went along, but the handicaps, you know, that the one-nighters are for at that time, you know. And then there was such a thing as lodging, and where you could stay and where you couldn't stay, you know, and maybe the first time around, it was a rough deal, and after you went back again, you'd always know, these keep -- your notebook.
You know the place.
-- was the most, handiest thing to have, was like your Bible on the road, you know. Every town that you go in, you always write where you stayed, the

address, telephone number, the name of the person you stayed with, so if you ever went back to that town, you wouldn't have to go through that hassle that you went through originally, see. So I'd say the second and third time around, why it began to be easy. But that first one, you had to sell, you know, and so it was a little gruesome, especially to the guys that never traveled like that, one-nighters, before. Is this what you were asking me, did it help?

Yes. Did you -- when you were in these situations, especially in the South, and I'm talking more about like the late '20's and the '30's, did you all talk about this thing? Was it -- did you have a strong feeling of resentment of, you know, the black-white situation or just did most everybody at that time pretty much accept it and not think about it very much?

Well, the guys, you know, had read something about it -- there were some fellows in the band that had actually gone through the ordeal, you know, but they came out all right, and they begin to convince some of the eastern boys that had never been there that it wasn't as bad as they pictured it to be, you know, so you just be a gentleman and do your thing, you know. You were there to play; you were there for one night; play your little riffs; get your bread; mind your own business, and get out, you know, and be careful if you are lonesome. Be careful who you're talking to and who

you're with, you know, one of those things. So the guys caught on well, so it got to be either to -- it began to be pretty well routine, and there were no incidents. You see, we didn't have any incidents. We had probably some potential things, but they were stopped.

And, of course, after the musicians began to play, and they got on the bandstand and we saw these people that might have tried to heckle you a little before, that diminished. You began to play these things, and the guys were so good, until, man, these same guys began to get with it, you know, and get the beat and all those things. And a lot of them would come up, the same guys that tried to heckle you a little bit maybe in the beginning, some of them actually put their arms around your shoulder. "Boy, you were great!" You were always "boy." You never grew up. If you're 55, 60, you're still boy, you know.

So this is another thing, the -- some of the musicians in the band that had been there or were from the South, they said, "Now you got to accept being called that. If they call you boy, don't be insulted. So what's the difference?" We had one or two guys that -- they were a little hefty, but they came off of it, after they saw that the other guys were falling in line and no trouble, and they just sort of -- they toed the mark like everybody else, see. This is what happened.
Uh-huh. Shelton Hemphill.

Shad Shell -- Shelton Hemphill was from Birmingham, Alabama, out of a high school that turned out quite a few great musicians from a great band leader down there -- we called him Fess Watney, and Shelton Hemphill graduated from that school, and he was an excellent reader. He had big shoulders like Cootie Williams, Woodchop, you know, and when he would play, he would sit down, he would actually pump. He was the first trumpet player in anybody's band, and he was in my Wilberforce Collegians band, one of the original, and Shelton stayed with me for quite a spell. Benny Carter was in this band, and Shelton Hemphill and Rex Stewart was in that -- this was the group.

And he was in that group that we played the battle of music with the McKinney's Cotton Pickers Kenny Scott in Detroit, and we also went to New York at the Savoy, and so forth, ballroom, The Home of The Happy Feet, down there on 143rd and Lenox Avenue. And Shelton was great, and the band that we played against there was the great Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, and getting back to saying a little bit about Shelton, Shelton was an excellent reader. He was what you call a sight reader. And he wanted to continue in music, especially after going to New York, he got that bug, and he stayed in New York. And in fact he was with Duke Ellington's band for quite a spell, and he did an excellent job there.

And he was with a band before that, that Lucky Millinder and Mills Rhythm Blue A Band, he was also in that band. And there were quite a few name bands that Shelton had played in after the Collegiates, but I think his greatest triumph was when he was with Duke because he always wanted to get with the great Duke Ellington. He always also talked Duke when he was with the Collegiates. And he made it, and I just read recently in the DownBeat where he passed, so I was real touched on that because I knew him just like a brother. Of course, he was with Fletcher's band too, you know, did some things. He's quite a little guy.
How about Ben Webster?

Let's see. I'm trying to think of that nickname we used to call him. Ben had two or three. Ben was quite a guy. He had those big cueball eyes, and he could work them too, you know. And he always carried that big tone, and, of course, Coleman Hawkins was his idol, as far as playing. He carried that big tone with him all the time. And Ben Webster went to Wilberforce University. He wasn't one of the Collegians, as far as playing a horn was concerned, but he was our band valet, believe it or not. But that lasted only a year because we left school, it seems to me disintegrate during the summer, and, of course, everyone went their own way.
And we didn't see Ben the next year. It was about

a year later he came back to Wilberforce with a horn, tenor, and he could blow blew it. And he did join my band then, and we went to New York. Those were the trumpets -- Roy Eldridge, Red Harland and Jack Sprat. Then Russell Bowles and Archie Hall were the trombones, Van Sherrill, Cleve Mack were alto --
Two Alto players.
Right. Cleo Good --
Tenor --
Right.
I don't know how they left him out.
And Joe Thomas, (Unaudible).
They don't have him listed either this time.
I had four saxophones.
Uh-huh. Yeah, that would seem strange you'd have two altos and one tenor.
Yeah, right, Wait a minute, I (unintelligible).
Luke Stewart again on --
Banjo.
Banjo -- they have it listed as guitar. And Bill Howard is drums. Who did you say before?

Do you know, that is correct. Bill Howard -- he was out of Columbus, Ohio. Instead of Jimmy King. Jimmy King preceded Bill Howard. That's correct, Bill Howard, little short guy out of Columbus, Ohio, Bill Howard. That is correct.
Okay, so Bill Howard probably again was on that job in Columbus. Maybe you picked him up there or something.

That's where I got him, in Columbus. Now this particular job that they quoted there in this book of Buffalo, I think is incorrect because we played and stayed in a place there called the Vendome Hotel.
The Vendome.
Vendome -- was owned and operated by

a guy named Bill Clore, C-l-o-r-e, which actually turned out to be a legend because we starved to death in that town, and that man let us play for our rent and everything else. And right behind us another band came and started with Jimmie Lunceford, because Willie Smith, the great alto saxophonist told me this, and they stayed -- everybody in two rooms, that big band.

Right there at the Vendome Hotel, and Clore let them play their thing off too. Jimmy Lunceford this was followed behind me, and this particular place where this book has me listed as playing, that's incorrect.
It says the Paramount Inn. You don't --
No, I never heard of it, that wasn't it.

Uh-huh. Okay. Good, we've cleared up some things here. Okay, they have -- we're talking now in 1929 in late spring where you played in Huntington, West Virginia, and according to this your trumpets were Roy Eldridge, and it says Matthew Harles, but that probably was Harland.
Harland.
Right.
Yeah, Red Harland.
Okay. Then it says B. Morton, trombone. That probably was Benny Morton -- not Benny Morton.
(Not unintelligible) Benny Morton.
Oh, no.
That's an error.
Excuse me. They have inserted here -- the writer has inserted trombone in parentheses with a question mark, but it has B. Morton, Guy Jackson and Cleo Good, Alfred Gibson as saxophone players.
Alfred Gibson is correct. He's out of Cleveland, Ohio.
Uh-huh. Are -- let's see who would that B. Morton be?
What instrument did you say it was?
As a sax -- as an alto player. They probably got this information from the local 362. Maybe you filed a contract or something like that at that time.
I don't recall that B. Morton.
Huh. It doesn't show any trombones listed, as a matter of fact, here. It says Roy Eldridge, then Matt Harland, trumpets.
Russell Bowles was still in that group.
Russell Bowles was still playing? Uh-huh. Guy Jackson -- maybe the reason you -- they weren't listed is because of some union problems or something.
It could have been at that time. Something of that (unintelligible).
(Laughter)
Yeah. We all do that.
A lot of times if guys in those days weren't union, you still wanted to use them, you know?
Yeah. It has Luke Stewart and Sylvester Lupin. That probably was Turpin.
Turpin. Bass.
Yeah. And --
In fact, He played tuba and string bass.

Here's something that might be interesting to talk about. Let's see. It's -- I'm not sure -- oh, yeah, this is November, 1930.
