If Fletcher was indeed cooperating with some of his special arrangements, meaning that he was providing some of his arrangements to you, which I think you did tell me that the first day. "If Fletcher was indeed cooperating with some of his special arrangements, it might have been -- it might not have been all voluntary. In late November, 1930, Fletcher's band went into Connie's Inn a few blocks down 7th Avenue, and Sandy recalls that he, Horace and Talcott Reeves would go down to Connie's in the afternoon and copy off Fletcher's
charts onto their own manuscript paper. Of course, they would never those borrowed arrangements when Fletcher himself was listening." Do you have any comment about that?
I don't recall this, truthfully, because I, number one, I wouldn't have had to do it. All I had to do was ask for it.
Yeah, that's what really seemed strange to me when I read it.

Because why would he have given me anything I wanted before this and always did? I wouldn't have to do that. Or either I'd tell him if I was going to do it. I wouldn't have to slip, so I don't know where this information came from.
Oh, I could see you -- let's see. It was who that said this?
Did you say Sandy Williams?
Right, yeah.
Sandy must have -- you know, Sandy was another one of those guys like Coleman Hawkins, you know, that was in that band.
He liked to play games, yeah.
So I think Sandy was putting somebody on.
Could have been, easily, because you could see where that could grow out of somebody just joking about it.
That's not true.
But what would we have done with something like that, you know, just a few parts? No way. I don't buy that.

Okay. Here's one other personnel thing you might be able to clear up. "In the spring of 1931 Horace's band was appearing regularly at the Rockland Palace in Harlem. The personnel was pretty stable. The local 710 would -- Washington, D. C., reported Butler, McClung, Sandy Williams, J. Williams, Cole -- "
MR. HENDERSON: John Williams. saxophone.
MR. : John Williams and Cole --
MR. HENDERSON: Rupert Cole.
MR. : Rupert Cole. Then it says a Joseph Smith, and in parentheses it says it "is not known whether this was the famous trumpeter or a saxophonist."
MR. HENDERSON: Joe Smith was from the three Smith brothers that played with my brother.
MR. : Yeah, I remember.
MR. HENDERSON: Trumpet -- used, a plunger with a human -- sounds like a human voice. But he wasn't in this group.
MR. : He was not in this group.
MR. HENDERSON: He might have come by one time as a guest or something like that, but Joe Smith never played with me. He played with Fletcher. And they have the name of
the place wrong. It was the Dunbar Palace.
It wasn't the -- oh. Yeah, I remember we talked a little bit about that before.

Yes. In fact I've got a picture of it right over there in that book, and it has my group and me sitting on a railing with the guys (unintelligible by me), and it was taken at the Dunbar Palace Ballroom. So that name is incorrect -- whoever wrote that down
This is reported in the International Musician in May of '31. There's also a person's name in quotes here -- Clarence -- I can't even read it. Looks like Ysiquirre. Siquirri or something.
Actually, it's YsiquirrE.
YsiquirrE.
Bass player. That's -- his name is actually -- we called him Bobby YsiquirrE. Bobby YsiquirrE is the one that I told the story about, that John Kirby took his place. It's Bobby YsiquirrE.
Is that correct spelling?
Yes, YsiquirrE is his -- the way he spelled it. He was a foreigner.
I see. Uh-huh.
And he played with me a little while, but he joined Fletcher.
Yeah. And who is M. Johnson?
MANZIE? 111
Mancy Johnson, a great drummer. He and he played with was a drummer in this particular band, Fats Waller.

Okay. "To summarize"-- I'm quoting here --"there were five essentially different groups which accepted engagements either using Fletcher Henderson's name or implying his sponsorship." Here's one, "Fletcher Henderson and his Rainbow Orchestra, led by violinist Ellsworth Reynolds, spring 1925 into 1926." Does this mean anything to you? I couldn't quite understand it.
It doesn't ring a bell with me. Where did they play?
It doesn't say where.

The only time that I know something like this transpired, and I think I'm pretty well correct in it. Fletcher wouldn't give anybody permission to use his name for a long period of time. I know some things that have happened like this. Fletcher has had two jobs in one night, casuals, when he has designated some guy to front the band until he could get there, but this was an agreement made between the promoters and Fletcher. But for a guy to play a regular job stating -- no way. No. Because I've done the same thing, I've had two jobs, in one night, too, and you've done it, too.
Oh, yeah.
(Laughter)
I remember New Year's Eve, man, in Fort Collins.
Sure.
Vernon Andrade's Andratti's orchestra possibly working under the name Dixie Stompers.

No, that's incorrect, 1000 percent incorrect. Vernon Andrade's Andratti's was the house band always at the Renaissance Ballroom at 138th and 7th Avenue in New York City, and he played for different club dates. This was all he did, and he was the banjo player in the band. And the leader -- and he had a regular group there that played all these things, all these jobs with him, and his band didn't record, and they went under the same name of -- as Vernon Andrade Andratti's and his Renaissance Ballroom Band.

Uh-huh. I see. Okay. Here we have Horace Henderson's Wilberforce Collegians, which we've talked about, sometimes billed as Fletcher Henderson's Stompers. Now it says here, "Basically, Horace's college band with Rex Stewart, Benny Carter, Freddy Jenkins, et cetera, about 1925 to spring, 1928." I remember asking you about this before, and you said that the Stompers was a name that was used for recording purposes.
Right.
And that it did sometimes involve a combination of your personnel and some of Fletcher's.
Fletcher's, correct.
Yeah. Okay.
But we never went by that name steady. We didn't drop the agents Collegians (unintelligible), but the Stompers, the reason we arrived at that name is because it constituted the members of both bands.

Yeah. I see. Then here it says, "Fletcher or Horace Henderson's Stompers, with a new personnel of Midwestern musicians, including Syd Valentine, Roy Eldridge, et cetera, reorganized in the fall of '28 on into '29 and 1930." That's just -- apparently what they're doing is they are stating these are five essentially different groups. Okay. Horace Henderson and his orchestra with the revamped personnel, Jack Butler, Sandy Williams, Rupert Cole, et cetera, at the Dunbar and Rockland Palaces.

The Rockland Palace, they are confusing. That was either at 155th or 158th and 8th Avenue, which was a huge barn which hired bands just for one nighters. It wasn't a steady thing, like a night club or one of those things. The Dunbar Palace was a night club.
STeady gig, yeah.
(Unintelligible) It was a steady job, weekly.
Yeah.

The Rockland Palace is where they had roller skating, you know, and all that stuff going on there, so I don't know how they got that confused. Fletcher used to come up and play the Rockland Palace after the

Roseland. You know when you're finished at night? Sometimes they'd have a breakfast dance, and I've been up there with them when they played the breakfast dance, but it was only a one nighter, extra job. Good old Rockland Palace, skating rink.

Uh-huh. It says, "By this latter time, which would be '31, Fletcher was no longer interested was no longer interested in such activities; however, there were at least four subsequent occasions when he again became involved for short times. Late 1932, early January, 1933, he fronted the Benny Carter Orchestra for engagements in Reading and Philadelphia, Pa., while his own band toured the South." Now I guess that is Fletcher that they're talking about there.
This I didn't know.

Apparently that's reviewed on a couple of other pages in the book, which I don't have copy here. "May-June -- May to June, 1933, Fletcher Henderson's Blue Harmony Boys, perhaps a vocal group?" Is that -- do you remember that name?

I've heard that name before. The -- excuse me -- the only conclusion I can arrive at about these different names, you know, in recording, just like Benny Goodman has a contract with a certain record company, and they say clarinet, Joe Blow. You see? So these are the way some of these things, like Red Allen had a contract. So if he

recorded with Fletcher, when they gave the personnel of the band, Fletcher's band, they couldn't use Red Allen. They'd have to say Red Smith or anything, to keep Red from getting in trouble with his contract, all this way, so I know this to be a fact.
(unintelligible)
Uh-hub. I remember seeing one time Izzie Goldberg for Dizzy.
Yeah. See, things like that.
(Laughter)
So if guys want to make that extra bread, they just go under fictitious names.
Here's another one, "February, 1936, he fronted the Baron Lee Band for a short tour of New England, while Horace directed his own band at the Grand Terrace. Now again, I don't know --
Never in my life.
Never.

He always was at the Grand Terrace for a number of reasons. He was broadcasting from the Grand Terrace, plus the fact that one of us had to either play piano or the other directed the show, or either I had to direct the show and he'd play the piano on certain things. So both of us were essential to be there, so Fletcher never did that. So where that information came about, I would like to challenge that.

Okay. Here's another one -- "March 1942" -- clear up in the '40's -- "he took over the Jimmy Murray Band from Pittsburgh and played dates in Albany and Washington. He had fired his 802 band, but there seems to be a period of overlap when the latter" -- meaning the 802 band -- "played Baltimore, probably under Horace's direction."
No way.
(Laughter)
I don't know. Where does this information come from?
This is from Hendersonia.
I'm very happy to hear this. I am very happy to hear this. This I'm going to challenge.
Okay. Well, we can -- I don't have a copy of the book. Do you have a copy of the book?

I did have a copy of the book. There was one here in the library. This gentleman that published this book wrote me several months -- when I say several months, I mean a lot of months ago -- and wanted my permission to -- two, three years ago this was -- to publish this book. I didn't give the permission. So he went down South where my sister is living, and I understand he tried to romance her to get her permission, and of course she never does anything without checking with me. She didn't give it. I've checked with her. So where he got the authority to publish this book without our permission, I don't know. The only letter
I've gotten since this book was out is if I wanted the book, I could send him $10.00, and he'd send me one. Which is a great thing.
(Laughter)
Thanks a lot, huh? Gees!

He made a couple of remarks in there about me that I'm going to challenge also, from 802. He said that I was playing a job in Harlem somewhere under the scale, and I was taken before the board. I'm going to challenge that too.
I remember reading that, yeah.
And I --
In fact it's right at the top of this page.
I'm not at all pleased with that.
Page 211, right at the very top, it says-- he covered himself by stating 'Horace was reportedly brought up before the local 802 board for accepting less than scale and was fined by the union.'
Huh. That I'm really going to challenge.
Yeah. Didn't happen.
That it was the first thing I saw in that book, and I became really a little upset about it. We're going to really check -- my attorney's going to check into quite a few of these things.

Might be worth it. This -- again I'm using a Xerox copy, but I believe this is probably from Leonard Feather's Encyclopedia that I'm quoting now. This is concerning you. It says, "He" -- Horface -- "is acknowledged to have been a more swinging piano soloist in the Earl Hines manner than was Fletcher." You want to make any comment on that? That's putting you on the spot.
(Laughter)

Fletcher was a great pianist, and he always liked more or less to play things that had a fast beat, just the opposite of what Ben Webster was like. And it showed off his execution, and, of course, when people came out to see Fletcher, naturally Henderson, in this way he could be flashy in playing the piano, like I know one of his feature numbers was Honeysuckle Rose, but at the tempo that he played it off, it showed him off well on the piano. And I just used to like things like "Sweet Lorraine," you know, where you --
Middle funky beats?

Yeah, funky beats and (unintelligible) you could play in the right hand, if you wanna octaves, you know, (unintelligible). That was the difference. We had different styles, but it's just all in the matter of the way you thought, you know, and he thought his way, and I thought mine. A lot of things we thought alike, and -- but I idolize his way of thinking because he was successful. You don't fight find success; you just join it (unintelligible).
That's right. Then it goes on to say here, 'His arrangements were also more,' quote, 'modern for their time.' This -- your arrangements were more modern than Fletcher's.

That's a matter of opinion, and I'm not being -- you know, because of the fact he's my brother, but I don't know -- it all depends upon a person's taste, you know. Maybe I was given a certain style of arranging to do, which required the swing thing, but Fletcher made things like King Porter Stomp. They don't swing any more than that, man! Sometimes I'm Happy -- there's a beautiful thing he and I made together. Benny Goodman did this thing. Fletcher did it for Benny. And Fletcher had played it before in his band too -- 'Sometimes I'm Happy,' and the reed chorus was a legend, you know.
(Singing)

It flowed, you know. Okay, so he wrote this early in the morning. He wrote the 16 bars. So he called me upstairs, and I was asleep, and he asked me if I'd come down and finish that, and I wrote the brass chorus, where it comes in --
(Singing)
That's me.
(Singing)
Well, I wrote that. I don't know if even Benny knew that until

later on, you know, that it was -- we collaborated on the thing together, unintelligible, you know, but we did things together, and then if he wanted me to do something that was a thing -- he'd always ask me, AAH, 'You want to do this tune?' Well, I'd take and play it, and I'd see if I felt it, you know, and I can play it down, you know, and if I felt the tune had a feeling -- if I had a feeling for that particular tune, I'd say, 'Yeah, I want to do this.'

But he gave me some, he said -- I'd say, 'Smack, I don't think I feel this one, because, see, I might do a corny deal on this.' unintelligible to you. He said, 'Okay, I'll take it,' you know, one of these things, but we always agreed. So it was just a matter of the way you felt about the tune. And I never wanted to write any -- this is why I loved Jimmy Dorsey, you know, because he said, 'Look, if you don't feel like doing this thing, don't do it, you know.'
I'm going to ask you something tough here maybe, and you don't have to make any comment at all.
All right.

This is also from Leonard Feather, I believe. It says, 'Although the two brothers worked together frequently, they reportedly had many differences, and Horace is widely reported as being resentful of being only as Fletcher's brother and of the fact that many arrangements popularly credited to Fletcher were in fact his own.' Do you
want to make any comment on that? In other words, the -- from --
You know... (Unintelligible).
Oh, go ahead.
This came from Leonard Feather?
I believe so, yeah.
This is the first I've ever heard of that, and I'm actually surprised, because Leonard and I are great friends, and Leonard --
I could be wrong. I just have only one page of a Xerox copy, and it --
Well, it's something -- it's there in black and white, and this is what bothers me.
Well, it could be somebody else's. It may not be the Encyclopedia. I can check this out. I don't know what the source is.
Well, the only differences, and I don't mind saying this, that Fletcher and I had didn't involve music.
There were girls, huh?
(Laughter)
Well --
No, I'm teasing.
(Laughter)
No, not girls even. I used to
bawl Fletcher out until I found out that actually he was right. I used to bawl him out, not worrying about whether the guys were going to be there on the gig, like I told you up in Massachusetts.
Right.

Now that bothered me, no end, and in fact I threatened to leave him and all this stuff, you know. These are the only differences I've had. But speaking -- but musically -- differences? I idolized that man. No way -- because he had done too much to help me in college with sending me arrangements which I could never repay him for, so somebody's off their rocker. They should have delved or checked with me and found -- we've had differences, just as I told you, but they weren't about music. No way. No way.

Well, I think that's great to clear up. It says here in the last sentence of this paragraph, "Attempts have been made to contact Horace, but he seems to rebuff attempts to discuss the old days." I would say we've sort of challenged that right here.

Yeah. Well, who has made attempts? I've been living here for the last 12 years. I have a sister that knows where I am every day in the year, so I'm not hard to find. I'm a union musician. I'm listed with the local, so somebody has --
They're making up stories.
Yes, and it's going to be cleared up.
I think that's good. That's one thing, why we're getting this stuff on tape.
Sure.
We're about the end of this tape, and I think -- you've been sitting here -- are you aware you've been sitting here for about three and a half hours, nonstop?

Well, this is great to me for a number of reasons because, first, I love this. Music is my life. These particular people that we've talked about, the things that I have said are 100 percent authentic, and they can be proven by men that are living like Dickie Wells, Benny Morton and the guys that participated in these different activities, and they will verify everything that I've said, and I'm happy about it.
That's great. Well, I think maybe we'll close for this session, but there's still some stuff we can deal with in another session.
Knocks me out -- I've had a ball (unintelligible) doing this.
Great. Me, too.
(Tape 10.)
This is Saturday, April 19, I believe, 1975, and we're at Horace Henderson's home once again

with our fourth interview, fourth interview. And, Horace, I'd like to ask you -- to begin today, I'd like to ask you a number of questions, basically about -- actually, these are just sort of oddball questions, so we'll hit into them one by one, and some of these things we've covered at various times, but I thought I'd sort of like to get them together here. In fact, just a moment ago we were talking about club owners, and so on, some of the problems you have with club owners, especially those who really don't know music and are only interested in making money and want to exploit the band, you might say, for making money, and if they aren't making money, they immediately blame the band, and they fire it, and you get a new band and constantly churning that way.

Do you feel that this has always been this way, or how was your experience, say like when you first started out with the Collegians? Of course, you were probably touring more at that time, but my main question is how were your relationships with club owners and ballroom owners and so on? How did they operate?

You know, a funny thing, Tom, I'm happy you mentioned this. As I think more about this particular situation, which is a drastic one as far as musicians are concerned, but it seems to me, if I remember correctly, in the past, the nightclub operators in the earlier days of jazz were more hip, you know, than the nightclub operators of

today. Maybe a few of them will hear me say this, and I'll get less work. Nevertheless, it seems to be true, though, that back in the days when the Collegians were traveling around or if we had chance to play, oh, a week's stand or two or three weeks, those nightclub operators seemed to have been on the ball, musically. Either that or they loved the music. They didn't have to do like the current operators in some of the clubs. Even here in Denver we have -- I've played two or three places here in Denver where these nightclub operators seem to have a tin ear --
Yeah, dig.
You know what I mean by that.

-- (unintelligible). They don't know whether you're good or bad. They've got to go around and mingle among their customers and say, well, how do you like them? What do you think about them? What do you think? And you could be swinging like mad or playing like mad, and they don't even know this, and so if a situation occurred where the business dropped off, the first thing they would pick on was the band, by letting them out, and the problem actually didn't exist where the band was concerned. It was the inferior help, like the waiters or the bartenders or one of those things, and it probably would go on for months and months before they would detect this particular thing that was happening in the club and the source of the -- what shall I say -- the lack of having a lot of business, I would say,

you know, and right now that's going on, which is a pathetic the very thing, you know, and the first thing they do, they blame the band or they blame the singers or the entertainers, and I think it's an unfair situation, and that's one of the reasons why I have been a little reluctant to play Denver in a lot of clubs which I could have played.

I chose to play the surrounding areas, which seem to me -- which not only seem to me, which is a fact, like up in Estes Park for the past three seasons. I've been playing there summer and winter because of the fact that it is a resort town where we get people from all the states. It seems like they appreciate the band more, you know. Are they more hip or are they just more hungry for that type of music? Same way with a little town of Longmont, and Loveland and Fort Collins and places. They seem to just be more hip than Denver, you know?
Huh. That's very interesting.
So this is why I've been a little reluctant, as I said before, to just play,-- and this is at home.
Right.

But I'd rather drive the extra miles, even in the wintertime, to play for people that appreciate what you're offering, more so than to sit up and play for an audience here that stares at you while you're playing,
and they look at you like you started a world war, you know? (Laughter) Right.
This is the thing that happens here, you know, in Denver.

Uh-huh. Do you -- I'm sure that as a leader at the present time, that you're conscious pretty much of the time when you're playing a job, that you're conscious of what the business, how it's doing and how the club owner feels and that you're making every effort to satisfy your listeners, as well as the club owner. Do you feel that you're more conscious of this now then you were, say, in the '20's or '30's when you had your bands then?

Well, yes, I am because, unfortunately, it's a matter of survival, you know. However, we don't go overboard to do it. What we try to do, and I've talked to my fellows about this, my boys in the band, that is. We usually have quite a few arrangements in the book that -- I won't say the style of the band changes, but we found out one thing. It seems like the people here that go out and support these clubs, we found out -- the real dancers, even in the settled bunch -- they seem to dance by the names of tunes. You know, if they know a tune, and you play a little melody and things like that, man, they used to flow right away. And you can turn right around there and play something else that is a swinger, or either

a great tune, one of those things. If they don't know it, they sit this one out, you know, and they'll applaud after you finish. But as soon as you go into one of the old standards, something that -- like Peg O' My Heart, things that never die, and you play that melody, man, before you get to the first eight bars, the floor's half filled. And it's a great thing. So we found out if this is the type of thing they like, and we hit them with that, we stick with it because we've got a book full of those things.

And then a lot of times we might start out another way, and we found out it isn't getting through to the people. We change the tunes. We try some other things, you know. And whenever we get something where we hit them with it, we stay there, and so this naturally makes the boss happy.
Right.
(Laughter)

And they notice all of these things. But here recently I've been playing some nice clubs where they don't bother us at all. They hired us because they respected my judgment on how to reach the public, and we've been successful in it, and they don't interrupt us, you know. That is the -- one of the reasons why I like to play the surrounding towns, because they do give you more liberties as a band-leader, because they respect your judgment in judging the audience, while here in Denver the night club operators, they

try to run your band, some of them, and they try to -- like they try to run the bartenders and have certain things, which is all right with me, as far as if they knew what they were doing. But I've found out through experience that it just isn't there, and if you follow the pattern that they want, you're out. This is what it winds up -- they blame you. They don't stop to think that they're the cause of these things, you know. So I just try to avoid these guys, you know.

Uh-huh. In the '20's and '30's, did you find that the people who came to the dances, the audiences and the dancers and so on, were they as conscious of names of tunes, you know? Were they strongly requesting things or did they pretty much just dig the style of the band and the fact that it was your band or Fletcher's band, you know, the name band?

Tom, I tell you, speaking generally from back in those days, I hate to say it but those people in those days could dance, man. They would dance by anything. Even the young kids of today. This is one thing that bothers me. I know some clubs that we play right now. I see some of these young kids get on the floor, man, and they can't keep time. They dance all out of time, and they look like they're wrestling on the floor.
(Laughter)

It's honest -- the truth, and I feel so bad about it because right away I think, just as you asked me, back in the '20's and '30's the fathers and the mothers of these kids, they danced, man. I never will forget one time, for instance, that I played -- well, I was with Fletcher when we played this particular -- St. Joe, Missouri. We played a ballroom down there called the Frog Hop, and they did just that. They hopped. They could dance, man, and that's just one example. All through Iowa, Minnesota and all those places, in those days, man, the people danced. Of course, we played a lot of ballrooms and clubs, you know, but the people could dance. They'd keep in time.

Why, now the kids dance so bad, honest to goodness, if I was playing a solo and I was looking out at them, and they danced off beat, man, I'd quit looking at them because they'd throw me, you know, if I let them. You know, one of those things?
Right.

So it's a pathetic thing, and this type of dancing where -- I'm not criticizing, but I'm just telling you the funny things that happened, you know, which you can see from the bandstand, but a couple sometimes -- a young couple will get on the floor. He don't even touch the girl. Man, she's way out on the other end, and there's some-body dancing in between, and they are dancing it out. It's a silly
Uh-huh. Okay. This is sort of switching. You've had some music published, I mean some of your own compositions. Is that correct?
Yes.
What sort of dealings did you have with music publishers? How was that done?

Well, there were a few companies that I dealt with that I sold the originals outright, unfortunately, before I got hip, you know, to what I should have done. There were others that we had a deal where there it was a commission thing going on, you know. And then -- let's see -- there was a company here back that wanted you to sign exclusively with them, and you couldn't write for anybody else, any original tunes, one of those things. I signed a contract with a company like that. I think it was Mills Music long ago, (unintelligible), but I found out that that was a handicap to me because a lot of times you write tunes, and if you didn't record them, they'd put them on the shelf, and they gather

dust, you know, one of those things, and then you'd go down and you'd try to jack them up on it, and there's nothing you could do. You're contracted. So you're just stuck; the only thing is sweat out until it was one of those things. And you would do it until your contract was terminated, you know, and then if they wanted you to sign, you know better. You're crazy (unintelligible) if you did it, you know?

So the next contract, if you'd have any, you'd have certain stipulations in there that, if they didn't do certain things, why the contract would be null and void or you'd have the option to cancel it and go with somebody else. But you had to learn all these kind of things, you know, because you were dealing with some real pros, you know, that knew all the answers. And this is one of the things, unfortunately, that Fletcher wasn't well versed in, you know, because he's the type of easy going guy would take guys at their word, you know, and then they'd, you know, so called -- stick a knife in his back too, you know, so he wasn't able to give me that information in time for me not to be a victim too. But you learn quick.
(Laughter)

Right. Have you ever -- this just comes to my mind -- have you ever had a -- written a song or a piece and somehow it became transferred to somebody else, and that person published it under their own name, has that
ever happened to you that you know of? You know, you hear a record someplace or you hear somebody playing something, you suddenly realize that's your song?

Oh, I've listened sometimes to something that sounds quite familiar to me, you know, especially about eight bars of certain things, you know, that you know you thought up, and some guys just put a few more bars with it, you know. They got the credit for the title and all that. Yes, those things have happened.
Uh-huh. Do you have any idea how many songs you have published -- had -- your own compositions I'm talking about, not arrangements, but compositions?
Compositions -- that's a good question, Tom. Let's see. I imagine 35 or 40, roughly, I would say, tunes that I had some dealings with, you know, with the publishers, the companies.
Uh-huh. What about Fletcher? Did he consider himself a composer or more of an arranger and bandleader?

He started out as more of a composer, but he was soon discovered as a very good arranger, and, of course, by Benny grabbing him so quickly, he had to more or less concentrate on arranging, I would say. Every now and then he would come up with an original thing. You know, he'd get to fooling around with the piano sometimes, and

those things come to you. You have run up on an It was just (unintelligible) how they have 'em, original tunes. This is but of (unintelligible), but as far as him concentrating on just writing originals and -- I think he had to dispense with that because of his popularity being in demand an arranger, and (unintelligible) and as (unintelligible).
Uh-huh. Did you usually work with a lyricist, or did you write lyrics of your own?

No, we would work with different individuals that were very good with lyrics, like Andy Razaf, the late and great Andy Razaf, the guy that wrote the lyrics to (unintelligible) "Honeysuckle Rose" with Fats Walker. And he and Fletcher did a lot of things together, but of course, I had the pleasure of living in Los Angeles, pretty close to Andy Razaf, even before he was confined to a wheelchair. And I wrote a few things, and I used to go over to his house. I would sit down and play the melody note of the things, man, and he could take his pen and just write right along with you, just as he was writing a letter, you know.

I remember one tune called Smooth and Soothing Music. This is the title that he gave a thing that I was fooling around with, and it was a nice little melody. Boy, he wrote 32 bar lyrics in about ten minutes, and it made sense, you know, and it told a little story, you know, and built up to quite a climax. He was a genius. And Fletcher knew quite a few guys that were great songwriters because when he played Chicago and was broadcasting, of course, this is why a lot of -- how

a lot of these guys survived, you know, and, of course, if you could get the lyrics and get your tune on the air, (unintelligible) naturally it popularized the tune, and they would do anything to get those things on, you know. So in those days it was great. That's why I think that there were better tunes written in those days than things that are being written now, you know, with the exception of a few.
Uh-huh. In those days, of course, money was made more from the sale of sheet music than from recordings.
Yes. Yes.
Whereas nowadays, if -- even if you don't ever really publish a song publicly, you can get it recorded and on an album, which most of the groups do, so it's -- it really is a different thing.
There is a different thing, yeah, a difference. (Inaudible).
Did you -- when you worked with, say, Andy or somebody like that, did you normally write the music first and they would put lyrics to it, or vice versa?

Yes, I would come in with a little piano copy, and I'd play it down. He says, 'let me hear this; played through once.' And while I'm playing through, he could see the veins, you know, right away working, you know, and his mind's working -- and (unintelligible). (Laughter) -- fast. Then he says, 'Okay, let's start again from the top, but do it slowly.' And as I played each part, bar, man, he's
scribbling. He's writing.
No kidding.
When I get through with my 32 bars, he'd throw that over to me. He says, 'Here are the lyrics.' "your"
Is that right?

Right. He was like that. But a lot of them aren't like that. They got to think and try to make certain passages rhyme, you know; not Andy nonending. These guys would have to erase something, see. "No" "Well, we'll try this." but he had a pattern, just like, you know, you do in playing, you know. He would listen at the melody real close, and when you play the bridge, so he would just -- his mind would be there. He was a was a genius.

Huh. How was it in those times, again '20's and '30's especially, in working with unions? I know you've mentioned a couple of times various things that have happened, but in general did you feel as much pressure from union or did you feel that the union was very useful or just how was it or did you just basically, ignore it?

Tom, I think in those days, in the early days, the union officials were more strict than they are now. I really do. I'm judging from the international -- of course, they've changed a lot, "and" and their personnel, of course. And Mr. Stanley Ballard, who was located in New Jersey, 220 Pleasant Avenue -- remember that?
Uh-huh.

That was an address that he occupied for years and years. He's just retired recently, but like you'd play one nighters, you'd have to send your tax in, and -- plus the fact that, when you had a big band, and you'd frequently the larger cities, there would be these business agents which actually see if you belong to the union, and if your dues -- if your card was up, we'd say, you know, and your dues were paid, and all those things. And a lot of people would collect the local tax at that time. But now you play a lot of dates, man, sometimes you'd be on a job three, four, five weeks before you even --
See the agent?

-- see the agent, and he doesn't even show up. He reads the newspapers, you know, like in the surrounding towns here. And say that you would get a letter from this particular guy in the jurisdiction that you play in, I'm from local so and so's secretary -- I see by the papers that you're playing the so and so. They're not as strict.
(Laughter)

In fact a job that I'm closing on tonight, the band that played there before me was there for six months, and I met the guys when I first opened there, and they were union. They said -- I asked them, I said, 'What's the tax on this -- it's a different --
Local.
-- jurisdiction that I'm in, (unintelligible).
Boulder local, isn't it?

Yeah, it's Boulder Local, and I said, "Do you know the amount of tax?" They said, "Well, we've been here for six months, and we haven't paid any tax. We haven't -- I said, "Did you file your contract?" No, we didn't file a contract." Well, man, I could picture back in the old days, and they never did, but I was there, played for one week, and I got a letter.
(Laughter)
And so I don't know what caused this thing, but there's a lot of negligence, like you have in Denver. I don't want to talk too much because I still live here, but it's a fact.

I have -- we do have a new administration here now in our local, and they're doing a very good job. And there were some discrepancies back a few years back. They're trying to rectify these things, but I think back in the days that you talked about the union -- the unions, I should say, were more helpful, I think, to the musicians because a lot of times, you know, the booking agents would have to file the contracts before the band entered that jurisdiction, and a lot of times the promoters would have to put up half the amount of the contract, you know, and then the business agent would come out and help you collect, you know. That doesn't happen now, you

know, so unfortunately, it's bad for the musician.
And in those days, as you know, the bands used to move around far more from what they do now, you know, like the one nighters, and they would be four, 500 miles apart, one of those things. In fact, those days you'd be happy to know that there were some union officials around, so you felt more or less protected.
Give you some support.
Yes.

In traveling around, of course, again talking about the '20's and '30's, we didn't -- certainly didn't have the highway system that we have now, and cars didn't have quite the same kind of speed. How was just the physical activity of traveling? Was it really a big problem or did things work out pretty smoothly?

Well, I would say a lot of times it was a physical hazard, because of the fact that, as you mentioned before, we didn't have the highways that we have now, freeways and whatnot. It took you twice as long to get to your destination, you know, and sometimes riding in even the older buses that the bands used to ride on, I don't think they had enough shock absorbers of the right kind during those days when you'd have to take those bumpy roads, you know, and they'd shake you up, and sometimes the distance between the jobs that you play was so great, like 500 miles, you'd ride

the bus all day long, and only thing you'd do is get out to stretch and you stop to eat and get to one of the drive-ins and pick up hamburgers, and you get back in the bus and that shakes in your stomach and all, and by the time you get to the job, you'd have just about time enough to wash up and put your uniform on, and you'd be tired.

And you played all right, but sometimes you didn't play your best. However, if there was a huge crowd and an enthusiastic crowd, you'd forget your bumps and bruises, you know, and go on the play, especially if there were some pretty little girls.
Oh, yeah, that makes a difference, right.
(Laughter)

You'd forget, man, and that would be it. And a lot of times you might play a job that you didn't have as many people, in the and -- that's when it would really show up, you know; you'd be tired, and you just say, "Well, I'm going to go and just play this gig tonight, but I don't feel good." You know, sometimes those things would happen. Of course, after all, you still were human, was (unintelligible).
Did you very often have to do directly from one job to the next, in other words, just finish the gig and get aboard the bus again and take off and drive the next 20 hours and --

Well, that would depend upon the distance of the next engagement. Like if you'd play a place tonight, like say Jacksonville, Florida, and you only had 200 miles to go. Well then, you'd stay all night in Jacksonville after you'd finished the date, which was a welcome sight, a welcome relief, we'll say, and you'd leave the next day around about, oh, 2:00 or 3:00 o'clock, if you didn't have to start playing until 9:00. The bus driver would usually check the conditions of the road that you were going to, you know, travel that next day, and if the map showed that the roads were very good, then you could make good time. We would leave at the latest time possible.

And I noticed a lot of times with Fletcher's band, if they were going to stay all night, Fletcher would say, we leave at 1:00 o'clock and the half hour -- we give you a half hour grace, meaning that you'd pull out at 1:30. And if there wasn't anybody there at that time, you would get there the best way you could. We lost a couple of guys a couple of times. They had to come in -- in fact, I remember a couple of musicians hired a private car to bring them in. They had missed the bus because they'd had such a ball.
Right?
(Laughter)
The night before, you know, in that particular town -- and you just didn't wake up, man. And his
alibi was the alarm clock didn't go off. He didn't have an alarm clock.
(Laughter)
His chick didn't wake him up.
That's the thing, yeah. And his company forgot, you know, sort of, and -- but he was all smiles. He didn't mind paying the dues. Those were great days.

Uh-huh. At that time did you have buses that were especially built or at least furnished for this kind of traveling, or was it just renting a (unintelligible) regular, like a Greyhound bus or something?

No, I tell you, there was a certain bus company that most of the bands that traveled out of New York City used. It was called the Newark Charter Company, and I think the reason for that is because their rate by the mile was so much lower than the Greyhound or the Santa Fe, one of those things, and all the booking agents and the promoters got so that they knew this particular company, and they really gave them a lot of work. And, man, they had plenty of buses; they had, oh, 75 or 100 buses, Newark Charter Company, and they weren't fixed up any different from any other bus, except now I realize they didn't have as soft of seats as the Greyhound, but I guess this is one of the reasons why the mileage that they charged was far less than the Greyhound or

some of the other companies.

But nevertheless, you know, they piled the musicians in there, and they were doing -- put all the instruments in the back of the bus, all back of that last seat, you know, and a lot of things, like the boys', their bags and things would go up on top of the bus, you know, and they'd have a canopy on top, naturally. And mechanically, though, so that you never heard of many breakdowns. The buses always got you there.

One thing for sure, by using the bus, you know that you had your group there all the time and together. If you broke down, you broke down together, you know. Which didn't happen too often.
Did either you or Fletcher ever own a bus?
No, we never owned a bus. We actually did own it by how much we paid.
Didn't have the title, huh?
(Laughter)

But, of course, we didn't have the title. That's it. This brings up a good question, a good statement, rather. I was just reading about a guy that passed here recently. You remember the guy that wrote a lot of tunes called Ivory Joe Hunter?
Oh, yes.

Well, he was a smart guy, man. He bought a bus for his band. Well, he got so many royalties, so much money from the tunes that he had written, of course, he had a lot of hits, and, man, he bought a bus that was quite expensive, and I had the pleasure of going through that bus, and he showed it to me one time. And he had his little office in the bus, had it made up special, and this particular bus that he had, they had their own beds and everything in it. It was really specially equipped. Not like the Newark Charter Company.
Well, that's what I was wondering, if --

It was Specially equipped -- the Newark Charter Company -- and it had 32 seats in it. It was just one of those straight up type seats. They go back, you know, you can lean back, but you're still in a seat. But Ivory Joe had this thing equipped, man, so the boys didn't have the -- when they stayed overnight somewhere, they stayed in the bus, you know.
Yeah. I know a couple of the bands I played on in the '50's, we had buses that way, that were specially built. You had record players and the whole thing.
Yeah, they were really equipped, so that it was an interesting thing, and they had, naturally, air conditioning. They had places to cook and those things.
I know there's another bandleader out of Omaha, Nebraska, Nat Towles. He always had his own bus. And, man, he used to charge the guys so much a month to stay in the buses.
Oh, I see.

Because they had their own beds and everything like that, and if I remember correctly, I had some musicians that joined my band out of his band, and they used to tell us about it, man, that Nat would charge the guys $35.00 a month, you know, like an apartment.
Dollar a night or something.
Yeah, even when he came off the road, he would park the bus, you know, in an area in Omaha where, you know, you could park, and the guys would still stay there. So actually that was quite a deal.
There used to be quite a few territory bands out of Omaha, and a number of them did have buses that way.

Yes. There was another bandleader there named Lloyd Hunter that had a great band, man. There was a trumpet player there -- there is a trumpet player, rather -- I think he's still living in New York City -- he joined Fletcher's band from this particular outfit, and his name is Irving Randolph. I don't know if you ever heard of him.
No.

Terrific trumpet player. He could read. He could play. He went to New York and he made real good. He really did a good job in bands. They nicknamed him Mouse. He looked like a little mouse, but he could play. He came out of one of the Omaha bands.
Uh-huh. I think we may have touched on this, but I can't remember for sure. On your one nighters how often -- or how long were those jobs usually, like from 9:00 to 1:00, 9:00 to 2:00?

I think the majority of the places that we played, the promoters wanted a five hour job, you know, and you wouldn't play like we play now, you know. You play 40 minutes and off 20, like you're supposed to. I don't do that. I play longer, it all depends, and all those things. But in those days, you know, with a big band, you'd play two hours and a half and take a half hour break, you know, and then you go back and you finish the night, you know. This was all you would get. See, so this is what used to happen.
How about in the clubs, was it usually five hours also?

I don't recall too much about it because we didn't play many clubs, Tom, back in those days -- they were little one nighters. Now and then we might play a week stand. I did play a place in Atlanta, Georgia, club, and I think it was like 9:00 to 1:30, and they would actually have to stop
back in town, hit some of the clubs where actually there were jam sessions going on, and the guys would get a chance to play then, you know. Excuse me.
I -- but -- excuse me. But I think it's more common probably for side men to get involved in jam sessions than leaders.
Oh, yes.
I don't know why, but -- I think that's been --

Yes, that's over a period of years, it seems like that's the way it's always turned out, because a lot of times some of the side men didn't get a chance to act hip in the regular band they were playing as they would like to, so they would get those few bars of jazz out of their system after they finished, you know. But the leaders very seldom participated in it. I don't know why.
What about Fletcher? Did he participate much?

No, he didn't do too much of that. In fact, I used to bawl him out sometimes about not getting around to hear some of these other guys, you know, and usually Fletcher would stay in a lot. I would go around a lot, you know. Also the -- you know, I used to come back and report to him, and maybe this is one of the reasons why he didn't go out, because I'd come back and tell him what happened.
Because he had a good reporter, huh?

Yeah, he had a reporter, but I would come back and rave about certain musicians, you know, that weren't working, and I'd keep my little book with me, you know, and like the great Jimmie Lunceford always carried a book. Man, he had a book full of saxophone players, trombone -- had over 3,000 guys in there, so if he ever needed anybody, you know, he could get them. This is where I picked that up, you know, so I began to do it, and I found out it came in handy, because you never know. Maybe a guy might give you a notice, and he might be a great musician, you know, in your band, one of those things, and you wouldn't feel it as much if you knew that you had the address of the guy, and you'd always write whether he was good or fair or excellent, you know, and what his potential was and --
Whether he could read or not.

-- whether he could read, or whether he was a great ad lib man. You'd write all this by the name. This way it was like a dictionary, and it was a great thing to have. In fact, right today I do the same thing, you know. I don't have as much trouble because I've been fortunate enough to keep the personnel the same, which means a lot, you know,, because, as you know and I know, the more you keep the same personnel together, the guys know exactly what the other guy's going to do. That way you get so you can play real, real good blend
together.
Sure. Do you think that Fletcher himself considered himself as a -- what did he enjoy most doing? Playing piano, arranging, being a bandleader, or do you think there was any real differentiation?

Well, it was a combination of all of those, you know, like in arranging. If he had a tune to arrange, and it was a standard or something he knew real well, well, it was no sweat. He enjoyed doing it, and I think he -- sometimes he would turn out terrific arrangements, you know, and, of course, I think in the later years I actually believe Fletcher got a kick out of conducting his band because he used to like to playing with the baton, you know. He didn't go to school to learn to wave it or and one of those things. He had his own style, you know, and it was probably awkward to the thorough baton wielder (unintelligible), but he could do some things with it, and he got results.

And he learned how to cover -- to cut, rather, a few little steps in front of the band, and, man, you looked forward to that. And he liked that, you know. And, oh, man, sometimes the band would get swinging, and, boy, that chorus, outcourse, the band was just -- you could tell he'd feel it. Oh, his shoulders would go up, and he'd get to twisting, and the guys would say, "Yeah, he feels that tonight, you know, one of those things, you know, and he'd like this. He began
to look forward to that, and we could tell by certain tunes at certain time of the night that he would call, he was calling them for Fletcher.
Yes.
(Laughter)

To perform, (Unintelligible), you know. The guys got so they knew this, man, and say, "Okay, Smack, you're on," you know. And he would cut up -- especially if he had a receptive audience, you know. Oh, he'd love this. And, of course, like maybe on Honeysuckle Rose, the arrangement that features him on the piano. He would look forward to doing that tune, and he would like it. And he always liked to play tunes that moved pretty fast because he was at his best then, you know, because of the execution.
Did he like to -- at times when he wasn't on the job or just, say, in his apartment or something, did he like to just, from time to time sit at the piano and goof around?

Yes. Yes. Even Early in the morning, about 5:00 or 6:00 o'clock, sometimes he would be downstairs, and his wife would be upstairs sleeping. Sometimes when I was there, I'd be there the same way and I'd listen, hear (unintelligible) playing the piano downstairs, and he'd be down just fumbling around and thinking of -- and playing pretty chords, you know, and he got so he'd like to do this because a lot of times Benny used to interrupt

him anyway, Benny Goodman. (He) would call him up at that hour of the morning, and it just got so that it was hard for him to get to sleep. And sometimes he'd get to sleep. He said he'd wake up. He had an idea, and he'd come down to the piano and fool around and play it. Then he'd jot it down. He'd go back to back to bed. See? And as you know, sometimes early in the morning the best arrangements are written. Everything was real nice and quiet around, you know; you'd hear a bird or two every now and then outside, you know, and everything else is quiet. So this is the time that I really like to work best.
Did he like to search out when he was at the keyboard? Did he like to search out -- you know, you used the term pretty chords. Do you consider him to have been an innovator with regard to harmony?

Yes, he was more or less bent on playing the open harmony, you know, like the nin-ths -- he would spread them out instead of having them closed sometimes, you know, and he always would experiment. He was always searching, you know, looking for something that would sound different because of the vast amount of arrangements he had to do, but even if he had spare time on his hands, he would still play the piano. And of course, I tell you a lot of things he would do, and, Tom, he would insert a lot of classical passages, you know, in his -- even in his playing
piano in extended the standard tunes, you know.

And as you know, some of the best riffs are the classical things, you know, I know Coleman Hawkins used to (unintelligible) could play a lot of those funny things, you know. And getting back, staying with Fletcher for a minute, he'd play on the piano and he'd -- things like "Humoresque" and all those things. He would spread his chords out and one of those all these things. I know he'd get up and get a drink of water sometimes. He'd stand on the floor and look at the space, and you could tell he was thinking of things. Then he'd go back and then he'd play it a little different, you know, and I think his reason for that is because of the fact that he was trying to make a decision in his mind which pattern should he use, you know.

And I know he mentioned to me a couple of times, "I'm undecided about this," he said, "What do you think?" you know. I'd say, "Well, play it -- let me hear it," you know, one of these things. He'd ask me how I felt, and it was a great thing. And he would that consider asking me I'd say that, one of those things, and he'd play it one way. He'd say, "Okay, that's number one." Then he's play it another way a little different, spread his chords out and say, "Well, which one you like?" And I'd say, "Both of them."
(Laughter)
: No help.
He'd say, "Man, you're no help," for one

goodness' sake, we'd of those things, and held stop, talk a little bit, say, He said, "Well, we in one of my arrangements; we were I thought I'd do this (unintelligible) real close. And it he got so that he would ask me, he said, "Now if you were doing this, how would you do it?" And we'd discuss it, break a chord down, one of those things. He says, "Well, I tell you what we'll do. Let's make about eight bars of it this way and eight bars the other way. We'll take it in." I say, "All right, if you want to do it that way." I say, "We know we've got the benefit of how it's going to sound now because it's get, you know, the " piano here and one of those things. And he said, "Yeah, I just want to look at the (unintelligible) one of those expressions on the guy(s) face; and just see, " you know, you know, so (unintelligible)."

So -- and that way we'd even get the guys interested. Sometimes he'd ask them, "Do you like this?" We'd write a whole chorus sometimes -- it would be one way. Then we'd write it another way. Then we'd take it into rehearsal to the guys in the band and, "Which one do you like, this one or that one?" And, man, there you'd get things started. Maybe we'd have a difference of opinion. So that didn't help any because when we summed it all up, half the guys liked this and half the guys like that. So we went and used both. And injected we checked it, into the this sort of thing, (unintelligible). This is the way we away with it, and everybody's happy. got (unintelligible).
I see. Did he very often revise arrangements after they had been written or was it pretty
much --
Very seldom. Very seldom, because --
Uh-huh. He had it worked out the way he wanted it.

-- a lot of times after you've written so much, you know, you can envision in your mind how it's going to sound, you know, especially if you have the caliber of musicians with the tone, you know, and execution. You can just see that thing, you know, the way it's going to sound. So you don't have to disturb the arrangement once it's written (unintelligible). That way, you know.
That's a good question you asked, because there was a guy that used to write terrific. You remember an old tune, "Chinatown?"
Oh, yeah.
(Singing)

"Chinatown, my China, China-town, one of those things. There was a guy named Nesbitt that did a gang of arranging for McKinney's Cottonpickers. This was even before Don Redman (unintelligible). Nesbitt, he was a trumpet player. Man, he was -- he got real popular, as he was an arranger and everything. And he was the one that brought that old tune back, man, Chinatown, you know. He made arrangements for Fletcher like mad. And then the thing happened. He got so that he was an excessive drinker, unfortunately. This is what

ruined his career.

would need a piano player, you know, one of those things, and I would take the thing, man, just to hear what I'd been missing, you know, from certain guys, and I would hear some great things, you know, and I'd remember those things, and in my next arrangement I used to include some of those things, you know, because I always carried my little notebook with me, you know, and those little riffs that they'd make and some hard things.
