Great trumpet player, Joe Guy -- I did a lot of dates, single dates with these guys, and we'd go as far as up in Massachusetts, you know, play a one nighter and come back. They'd have a 12 piece band, you know.
We had that gig book, you know. It was simplified--
Everybody'd read it right off.
Because you didn't have a chance . . . . But
Everybody read, you know.
Yeah.

It kind of kept the thing from getting monotonous, you know, writing all the time, you know. It kind of kept your fingers a little nimble, you know. Of course, as I said before, you'd always find somebody that played something that you could use, a little bit here, a little group there, you know.
I think I asked you this before.
Do you still have any of those notebooks?
Somewhere around here, I don't know. I don't know if anybody could make heads or tails out of these, except for me.
(Laughter)
It would be interesting to see one of those sometimes.
Well, I'll have to dig up one or two for you.
Yeah, I'd like to. I think we discussed this a little bit before too, but I'm going to ask again, were you normally paid by the arrangement or paid on a retainer, just a weekly salary or --
No, I was salaried.
Uh-huh. What --
This is why I came back to that...
Certain bandleader.
-- certain band --
Bandleader X.

Yeah, bandleader X. It's why I had to do two arrangements a week, whether I felt like it or not, you know. And the same way with Jimmy, I was salaried, you know. And I enjoyed that more. But it seems like after having had the guy tell me this, it seemed like I was always willing to write, knowing that you were writing good for a guy, you know.
Right. That makes a difference.
A little inspiration, you know.
Uh-huh. If I may be so bold, how much money in those days were you paid per week, and again, you don't have to answer if you don't want, but it would be -- I think -- be interesting.
It was a pretty good fee. I think -- because this was a big band -- around two bills, you know. Of course, that's the equivalent of four now.
Heck, yes.
But it was real good. You could do a lot more with it.
That's -- oh, for sure.
Yes, just wonderful.
Uh-huh. Did you -- while you were doing this for whatever band it might be, were they often out on the road, and you'd send arrangements to them, or were you giving -- when they were in town or --,

Sometimes that Here's how it would happen -- if they were pretty close, they would send transportation and I out the band, especially if it was, you know, a little intricate thing that they wanted, you know, a special tune or one of those things. But after -- doing about -- oh, six or seven tunes, and they learned your style and your
pattern, it actually wasn't necessary. I could send it on then, you know. Just on certain tunes, arrangements that I would be there in person.
When you sent the score or gave the score to the bandleader, did you ever keep copies for yourself?
No.
Never did.
No, I just turned the score over to the copyist. And that was their property.
Yeah, uh-huh. I see. So did you ever keep any -- like sketch pads or anything like that that you used?

Yes, I probably did that sometimes because a lot of times you would try to remember not to repeat, you know, certain things, you know, and it was essential that I did do that. You know, I've got a lot of that stuff, Tom, at my sister's home in Georgia now, you know, because when Fletcher passed and his wife passed -- I used to keep a lot of stuff in New York. Of course, they left their home to us in New York, 228 West 139th Street, and when that was sold, we decided to sell it rather, and when it was sold and we moved a lot of that stuff to where I knew it wouldn't be sold, you know. My sister's -- she treasures all that stuff. And I've got a lot of valuable stuff down there. This is one of the reasons why I'm contemplating on taking a little trip,

you know. And I don't know. I would actually like to drive if I had the time, so I could bring stuff back, you know. And a lot of records, and you know we used to cut a lot of those little discs, you know, little records in those days, you know, little experimental things.
Right.

And they were real good, you know. We used to do that even when the guys in the band didn't know that that was happening, you know? And you used to hear some talking, conversation, all those things, and some classics on (unintelligible) there.
(Laughter)
I'll bet there are.

So they're there, and, of course, my sister is well aware of how important that is, and she doesn't let anybody touch those things. This is one of my anxious reasons on this for wanting to go down there.
Uh-huh. You know, sometime for history's sake and so on, it might be worthwhile, if you really wanted to get into it, to get somebody to help you with that and catalog it, organize it and --
Be nice to compile it, wouldn't it?
It really would, I think.
Well, a guy named Tom should be all right on that.
Well, I wasn't hinting or anything,
but just let me know.
(Laughter)
Well, that's beautiful, because it would be interesting, you know, of the things that would be discovered. Just like an easter egg hunt.
Uh-huh. I think it would be especially interesting for you because, you know, everything you're going to pick up is going to be, "Oh, yeah, I remember that."
Yeah, you Always remember the incident after you've run across that thing, you know. Take you a couple of minutes on some of them, but they come back to you.
Well, seriously, you know, if you ever think about it, I'd be very willing to help you.
That's really nice to know. Because well, this is one of the things that I've often wanted to do, but I've just been so busy, you know. When you work like we are now.
Oh, I know, playing six nights a week.

(Unintelligible). It's a rough thing. You don't have time to travel that far. Going by plane, you might as well not go; if you're going to bring that stuff back, you won't get back, financially, you know. Plus the fact that it's heavy.
Uh-huh. Well, we'll have to chat
about that sometime. Tiny Hill.
That was a great guy.
Yeah, he was very -- I played some gigs with him.
Is that right?

Yeah, he used to, every now and then, take a job. While he was here at Fort Luyton, he would book someplace, and he would -- he had a nucleus of Denver musicians that worked for him, although most of the time I was working or writing or something, and so I didn't work steadily, but I'd -- I did a few with him.

Well, as you know, number one, Tiny used to weigh over 300 pounds, you know. He was always heavy. And he was the type of guy that had a great sense of humor, and he was funny, always told jokes, you know, and when he'd laugh, man --
His whole thing just shake, yeah.
(Simultaneous remarks)
-- and shake and whatnot. I tell you what, in -- knowing a lot of bandleaders, he was about the greatest businessman --
That's right. He was sharp.
-- that I ever had the pleasure of being around, man. He was strict -- he was business -- when I say business, he was a good businessman, financially, and,

man, he would pay you right, and he would do a lot of his own bookings, you know, even beside the booking offices, (unintelligible) the, you know, booking offices. He knew a lot of people, and my connection with Tiny was back in Illinois. He used to play a lot of those little, small towns. Boy, they loved that guy. He would get up and sing those --
" : An-gry --"
" Angry Man, " and, you know, those things are hits right now with the people, you know.
: Sure.

And he was far ahead of them. And, man, I used to get up in his hotel room sometimes, and he'd open up his suitcase, and he'd have everything just so immaculate, have his cash there and he had his contracts. He was just a strict businessman, you know, and he had a guy that played tenor with him back there. I hope the guy's still living because he was quite a guy -- named Tod Howard. I don't know remember if you ever met him.
: No.

And he had a great drummer with him, you know. A lot of these names, personnel of that band have left me because, you know, you forget about them, that sort of thing, but he usually carried around ten men, you know, and it was a challenge for me because of the type of music that he played, you know.
: Tenor band.

Yeah. Hillbilly and things like that -- but he was anxious to inject a little swing and have a little versatility in his band, and we became the greatest of friends, and I made some things for him, and I made some arrangements for Tiny on the standards, you know, and he told me, says, 'Jazz them up a little bit, not too much,' one of those things, you know.
(Laughter)

And so we used to sit down and talk these things over, even before I made the arrangements, you know. I said, 'Well, I don't want to get far out,' you know. And I said, 'How do you want this,' one of these things, and I -- he would leave it to my discretion. He says, 'I tell you what you do.' He says, 'Why don't you come down. I'm playing at a little town called Mounds, Illinois, way down in the southern part of Illinois, you know. He says -- naturally, he paid for the transportation and things coming down there, and he wasn't cheap or anything, about it. And they used to travel in cars, and whatnot. And Tiny had a special seat, naturally, big as he was, you know. And he'd have little compartments over there, little nips and (unintelligible) things like that.
: He was just all organized, huh?
You know -- and we'd talk and we'd just go down the highway, and we'd tell jokes, and we would

get the biggest kick out of some things I'd tell him, you know, about what had happened in Fletcher's band, you know, like the things Hawk and those guys used to do. And, man, he'd crack up. He said, "You got to tell this to my guys."
(Laughter)

And we would get in town and the band was never late. He was strict that way, and they knew Tiny. And we used to have an hour and a half a lot of times in the towns, and we kept in the background, the dressing room, and the guys would just have a ball and talk those things, and it was a (unintelligible) and all, and in this particular town like Mounds, Illinois, he'd have me come to hear the band, you know, a lot. In fact, I think I heard the band three or four times before I ventured to do any writing. I got so I would know the individuals and their capabilities quite well before I would write anything, see, and I would take my little book and write down, "this guy -- solo; this guy -- no solo, straight, you know and all that stuff. "Tenor man, vocalists and all that, stuff. (Unintelligible) and all of that. And it made it easier to write after I'd heard them, you know. And then I made a couple of things with Tiny singing, and I knew how he liked to sing, and how he liked so many fill ins, and he didn't like anything, you know, [movements] to get in his way. I remember this and all, you know. So it was easy. So we just did fine. And we became

friends over a period of years, even when he became ill. He was out in Iowa somewhere here, oh, a year and a half ago, and he was connected in some other profession, and I used to get letters from him. He'd always send me little quotes and things, you know.

So here a few months ago, right here in Denver, Colorado, I was playing out, I think, a job -- I think it was out to a town near Villa, and Ike Cole was appearing here for a week. That's Nat's brother, of course. And Tiny heard that my band was playing with Ike there and backing him, and he must have gotten the time wrong because it was a week engagement, and he told me this on the phone -- he went out to hear me, and when he called me up, I almost cried because he had lost his voice, you know. He was real ill and He'd lost so many pounds. And he went to the union and got my telephone number, through the union here, you know, over the musicians' (unintelligible) local. And he called me up, and we talked, and he was telling me how ill he'd been and whatnot, and I felt so bad because I wanted to remember him as the days of when we had fun, you know.
And I talked to the guy like today, and a week later I was supposed to see him, and I read an article in the paper where Tiny Hill had passed. And that hurt me no end, you know.
I can understand.
So we lost a good one, because he was a great guy to arrangers and musicians and everybody, you

know, and he was helpful financially to guys. He had a big farm there, Fort Luyton, Colorado, and at one time he had a 24 hour radio station that he owned. And up until the time that he became ill and he had to move out again I think he sold all this. He moved right down the street here, oh, about eight blocks, at 32nd and Colorado Boulevard. He owned the property there.
Oh, did he?
Oh, yes.
I didn't know that.
He owned -- you know, when -- there was a project going there, and a lot of people bought homes -- they lost them. So Tiny bought up the difference on those things. He was a good businessman.
Right.
(Laughter)
He told me this. And he used to own that gas station right over there.
Yeah, there's a Phillips, I think.
Yeah, Phillips, yeah.
I didn't know that.
And I saw him there one day in his car. I said, 'What you doing here?' He said, 'I own this.'
(Laughter)
How about that?
Yeah.
I didn't know that.
Well, he was -- he was quite a guy.
So --
That's good. You also have here Ralph Marterie.

Ralph Marterie, quite a trumpet player. You know, that guy was real funny. When I say funny, he was comical to me, you know. He was a little busybody, you know, but he knew what he wanted, you know, and he had a swinging band, man. And I made some things for him. I didn't do too much for Ralph. I think I made about, oh, four, six numbers, you know. And I wasn't contracted to him. I just was freelancing. I made these things, and he liked them, you know, and he had a great personnel, and some swing things -- oh, it's just coming to me now. It was a particular arrangement I made, man, and the band went over it a couple of times, man, and I would make a conductor's part so he would know what's going on, you know. Guys like Benny Goodman did the same thing, you know. They wanted to know what was happening. And he got so when the band would be shouting on the chorus, he'd scream in between there, right on those notes. He'd like that, you know. He's real versatile, and I enjoyed the guy because I liked him personally, and he was a likable sort of fellow. I haven't seen him for years, but
it was quite an experience to write for that band.
This was later, wasn't it? Was this maybe in the '50's even?

This was around the '50's because he was doing a lot of one nighters in the ballrooms and whatnot, and, of course, Ralph became quite popular, and he did some good things. Have you heard about that guy lately?
No.
I've been trying to find out where Ralph was because I wanted to get in touch with him, you know. That's the only thing, being here, with all due respect for being in Denver, sometimes --
You can lose touch.
-- you're off the beaten track.
That's true.

It's not like, you know, being in New York or being in Chicago, Detroit and the larger cities where the big bands are coming, you know, California, one of those things. They don't afford that here in Denver. So we just have to try and read, you know. Even getting the DownBeat, it doesn't give you anything, you know.

Yeah. Yeah, I really don't know where he is. There ought to be some kind of a -- like there is a musicians' guide published each year, but it doesn't deal with people in the popular jazz world. It's classical. And
it always gives the addresses of everybody and their -- who their manager and agent, that sort of thing. You can usually keep up to date.
Is it still active or not?
I think so. I can't think what the exact title is, but I've -- up to the last year or so, I believe so.
I sure would like to get one, especially if it's up to date. I know that. DownBeat used to give things in the back of the page where the musicians were playing, you know.
Yeah, but there's so many, man.
(Laughter)
Would take a --

Yes. They used to have the band-leaders, but it turned out, I think, that it had the individuals more or less in there, you know, a lot of combos, see, and it wouldn't justify what I would like to know because most of the combos that it gives, it wouldn't include the big band of the days leaders that we're talking about, you know.
Ben Pollock. There's a historical man.
Yes, there's a lot of history behind that guy, because he had quite a few names that he started out, and Ben would tell you, he's another little active guy too. He would

really talk. He was a drummer, you know, at one time. He used to play drums, and, you know, he'd have that two-week beat thing going, you know, but he had a lot of great names that at one time had started out with him, and he would let you know too -- "I was responsible for this guy."
I got this -- uh-huh.

-- you know, and I think the last I heard of Ben, that he was running a club of his own in Palm Springs, and he just recently passed, and it was too bad because he was a legend. He recorded with his band and whatnot. A lot of people knew him.
When did you write for him? Was that in the early days or --
I think that was the early days, yes, early days. And this was around Chicago. Because... It was --
That's mainly where he was operating.

Yes, right. And, of course, I was a free lancer then, and I made one or two things for him and tried, and it worked out all right, and he says to me, "Well, when you get some spare time, make some more," you know. The guys in those days, they were very encouraging to you, especially if they knew you were pursuing that field; they wanted to help you out. At the same time you were helping them.
Sure.
So it worked out for both parties
in some instances.

Uh-huh. Speaking of that, did you know many of the -- I'm sure you did -- of the -- oh, the old Chicago gang. Of course, they were late '20's more so, but I'm thinking of, well, even Bix. Did you ever meet him?
No, I never met Bix. Bix Buderbecke?
Yes.
No, I never met him. That was -- a little bit before my time. But I knew the history on him quite well, you know. He's a guy that -- "In a Mist"? (unintelligible) miss?
Oh, yes.
Oh, man --
How about some of the other people, like Hoagy Carmichael?

Yes, I met Hoagy Carmichael. And, of course, I think this was in California. I was with Lena Horne at the time that I first met him in person, and he was such a nice guy. Had a heavy voice for such a little guy too, you know. But, oh, boy, that immortal Stardust. I guess that will live forever, you know.
Bud Freeman?
Bud Freeman played great tenor, clarinet, yeah. That was -- now we're getting to Bob Dorsey, right?
Yeah.
And he was with Dorsey on a lot of those --
You mean Crosby or --
Did I say --
You said Bob Dorsey. You mean -- Crosby, yeah. Okay.
Crosby, I'm sorry. [crossed out] Bud Freeman, there's a legend. Man --
Yeah. Well, there -- well, let's see. Bob Crosby was -- oh, the bass player, and I know him really well --
(Singing)
Ray Bauduc?
Well, no, he was a drummer, but -- he's written a lot of those great songs, like What's New and South Rampart Street.
Oh, I know who you're talking about. It's out of that band, though.
He's on the World's Greatest Jazz Band with Bud Freeman and so on. I don't know.
There's another guy in that band -- was a great saxophonist too -- Babe Russen.
I know the name, but I --
Yes, he's in a studio out there; man, he could (unintelligible) play. He was another -- what's the great
saxophonist's name? Russo?
Bill Russo.
Yeah. He was a great man. You -- Matty Malneck talk about guys in that era (unintelligible).
Uh-huh. But now -- well, Russo -- maybe we're talking about something -- Bill Russo was a trombonist, although he was out of Chicago and he did a lot of arranging for Kenton.

Yeah, that Russo. But this is -- what's Russo's first name, for goodness sake? This guy was in Chicago at the Blackhawk during the days when Johnny Scat Davis, the trumpet player, had bands there. Russo -- I should never forget him because he's in Las Vegas now playing.
Are you thinking of Vito Musso.
Vito Musso.
Musso. You bet, yeah.
Did I say? Russo, that's (unintelligible) what threw me off. Vito Musso.
Oh, yeah.
Man, he can play.
Yeah, he was back with Benny maybe, early in those days.
Yeah, he played a lot of things with Benny. In fact, what's this tune -- Tiny Bradshaw even, the days of Tiny Bradshaw.
(Singing)
Vito Musso used to --
(Singing)
You know, that was a great chorus that a lot of tenor players --
They all copped it, yeah.
Vito Musso. What's the name of that tune?
Maybe it'll hit us. I don't know.
(Laughter and singing)
Isn't that something how it gets away from me? The bridge --
(Singing)
That's the bridge. We've got everything but the title.
Gees, I can hear it. Well, we just mentioned Benny, and he's the next one on your list. We've -- actually we've talked a little bit about that previously.
You mean Benny Goodman --
Yes, your writing for him. What about Rubenoff? What did you do for him?

You know, there's a guy in New York City was living on Park Avenue, and he used to come down to Roseland in New York City and listen to Fletcher and that great band, and he told Fletcher one day that he would like to go down in history and have a great jazz band for a change, you

know, and he talked with Fletcher and he talked with me, and he said, 'Your brother here, I understand, is an arranger and whatnot.' He said -- he didn't ask Fletcher about writing, but I guess he figured Fletcher was committed, (unintelligible), you know. And he said, 'How about you doing something for me?' I made some arrangements for him and didn't even have his band in mind, you know. I just wrote something. And he said what his instrumentation would be -- and he said he wanted me to write him some jazz choruses on the fiddle, you know. And, man, I wouldn't dare, you know.
(Laughter)

I wasn't thinking about it, and this guy was a genius, you know, one of those things. But I used to go to his apartment, and just like we're doing now, we would sit and talk. We talked music. And he would outline what he would love to do, and, man, he paid me just for doing things like that, you know. And I say, this is great.
(Laughter)
You bet.

And I said, Phil Rubenoff -- man, I went all over town telling all the musicians, you know, that I was doing some writing. (unintelligible). They didn't believe me. You know, I couldn't either, you know, but it was happening. And he did wind up -- you know, there were a lot of rehearsal halls in New York City, you know, in between the streets, like

Seventh Avenue, between Seventh and Sixth, and they were regular rehearsal halls just for these particular bandleaders that had these particular things in mind. And I know in one instance when they were hiring musicians, they used to have like the first alto player, three deep, you know, would have two other guys sitting on the side, and they'd take one arrangement, and they'd have this guy come and sit in. They would play the arrangement down, and he'd sit five minutes, and -- "Well, let's try this guy," you know, one of those things.

Oh, there were quite a few bandleaders that I was connected with that had the same idea. And Robenoff was one of them. He was getting his group together. And he would talk to me, and he had, oh, two, three other guys, would say, "What do you think? Who's the best? Who's in this chair who's good?" And, of course, it put us on the spot because all eyes were there, you know.
(Laughter)
Yeah, looking right --

And they'd have to go in a huddle, see, in the little office, you know, and we'd mark X for this guy, and, you know, Q for that one and this. He would accept a judgment because this was a new field for him, didn't have any experience in that. Naturally, he was just great by himself, you know, making his concert appearances, and he knew those
things, but this was the experience that I had with Rubenoff.
Uh-huh. Was he using strings?
No, no strings.
Just --
He was the only string.
Yeah. But he had just a regular dance band or jazz band ensemble then?
Regular band -- he wanted to direct, you know. He thought that was a great thing to be in front of a jazz band, it would be something different than what but he was primarily famous for, you know.
Huh. That's really great. We've got a little tape here left. How about Claude Hopkins?

Claude Hopkins. I knew Claude Hopkins from the Roseland in New York. In fact, Claude used to play on Fletcher's bandstand, you know, because they always had two bandstands there in the Roseland right beside each other, you know. Facing This is the ballroom. And like Fletcher would go out on tours or go somewhere else. Then they'd we'd bring Claude Hopkins in, one of those things. This is how I met Claude, our first (unintelligible), and he had a good band. He had a great singer with him called Orlando Robeson. Don't know if you remember -- he sang sweet, and he reminded you a little bit of Billy Eckstine at the time. And Claude had good personnel in his band. He had some

good trumpet players, you know, ad lib men at the (unintelligible). And he later moved up into the Cotton Club up at Harlem at 143rd and Lenox Avenue or somewhere near the Savoy, something (unintelligible), you know, and he was playing for that great review at that time. And I remember Claude real well for one thing. The time that this Christopher Columbus came out. This is the riff that Chu Berry used to play and we talked about me making 32 bars out of. Well, I asked him, "Chu, do you mind me making 32 bars out of this riff you play so often?" He'd damn play...
(Singing)
-- seemed like it was a pattern with Chu, you know. He lifted the band with that. So I put a bridge in the thing and made 32 out of it.
Then I had the trumpets, you know --
(Singing)
-- one of those things. Claude Hopkins was the first band that ever played that.
Oh, really?

For this reason -- when I finished copied the arrangement, and I got in my own score at that time. I wasn't able to have a copyist it copied, you know. I took it up to Claude before I took it down to Fletcher. And his band could read and everything, and, man, they went wild over the thing. and so he said, "Hey, I want this." Well, I says, "Well, okay. pass it in. I'll bring it back, you know, something. I was
on my way down to the Roseland, you know, to take it to Fletcher (Unintelligible) anyway. This is what happened.
I see. I'm going to change tapes here.
(Reel 13.)

Okay, I think we're back on the air now. We were talking about Claude Hopkins, and you had told me about the Christopher Columbus and that his band played it before Fletcher's did even. That was just a read through, right?
Yes, it was.
Did you later give him a copy of the arrangement or --
No.
Probably not.

I didn't get back to him, because (Unintelligible). After I traveled from Harlem down to 51st and Broadway, Fletcher was just going on one of his break, and I had heard the thing and heard how it sounds, you know, and I was real enthused about it, you know, because I wanted to see what the reaction would be from Chu, you know, Berry, the saxophonist that used to play this riff that the tune was written around, you know.
And I told Fletcher about it, and I said, "Hey, Smack" -- I called him Smack, you know -- "Hey, I've got a tune here, I think, that might be all right." I hummed a little

bit of it to him, and I said, -- 'I took it off of a riff that Chu plays all the time,' we're going very shortly. He says, 'Well, if you want to take a break why don't it we run it over very quick. we'll go downstairs and (unintelligible). So he told the guys to bring all their horns downstairs (unintelligible). at the intermission. read excellent in those days. So we Everybody naturally, (unintelligible), took it downstairs, and I passed it out, I had all the parts for the guys. (Unintelligible). Fletcher said, 'What's the tempo on this thing?' So (unintelligible). I kinda snapped my fingers and gave the beat with my feet. So he stomped it off -- I did, rather, I think I (Inaudible portion). did the stomping off.

They started out, man, playing, and it was swinging, and they got to the solos, and everybody in the band liked it. They went back upstairs, it was the first number they opened up with. Man, you should have seen the expressions on the dance people's faces when this thing was up, because they were real hip there. the people at the Roseland, they could dance, you know, and, man, it broke the house up.
I'll bet.
And I felt so good, you know, and, oh, Chu stuck his big stomach out, you know, one of those things. There it was, and the thing turned out to be the theme song of Fletcher, you know.
Right.
And he was broadcasting in those days, from we went on tours. I'm ahead of myself, That's usual there, and tours (unintelligible). "Christopher Columbus became quite a part of it.
Yes. That was recorded, of course.
Yes, by quite a few bands. Unfortunately, Fletcher's band was the last band out of about 60 recorded it.
That's what I was wondering about.
And they got the jump on Fletcher's thing, and it was original, you know, so --
Uh-huh. What kind of record sales could you expect in those days off of what would be considered a hit? How many -- how many records would you --
Oh --

Yeah, it wasn't like the millions they're talking about now. But I tell you, I remember an incident about this particular tune. I didn't have it copyrighted or anything. I just went on and did the arrangement, I was tickled to death with it. know. And, of course, Tom, I was yelling about these things young then. And we had quite a few slick guys in those days, you know, publishers and all this. They knew all the shortcuts and whatnot. So -- in fact, it got around all over Broadway about this thing, you know, and the bands began to play it. Even the band leaders, Man, as it turned out, they recorded it before Fletcher, so it must have got popular, you know.
Well, it got out that Chu Berry wrote the tune. So all this had happened before I was aware that it was happening. So there was a publishing company right there in the Roseland

which was quite convenient. building, right upstairs, (unintelligible). I'll never forget this in my life. Called Joe Davis Music Publishing Company, Incorporated. He got together with Chu Berry as the composer, wrote the tune, and I don't think Chu made any money out of it. He bought it outright from him. In those days they knew rather than take him on a commission all those things and would take (unintelligible) sort of and take a thing, chance on the thing. He bought it outright, and the guy made over $100,000.00 with the tune in a few months.
Gee, whiz.

And he got out of the business. This was another thing -- because he found out as the thing progressed that it wasn't quite the way that it went down. So I don't know if he became nervous about it, one of those things. But it was too late to get an attorney or try to sue or one of those kind of things, because I didn't have it copyrighted, one of those things. So it was just a warning to me for future things, you know.
Yeah, a lesson.

And Chu and I didn't fall out about it. We thought it was okay, you know; we went on, because I did take the riff. But I made 32 bars, while he was playing four or eight. So what I really felt that we could have done was to work together on the thing.
Right, collaborated.
And I think it would have gone farther -- and this is what transpired. So --
Do you -- did you ever have a copy of the published music? I mean did this -- what was his name, Joe Davis, did you say?
Joe Davis is the Music Publishing Company, Incorporated, right in the Roseland building.
Do you have a copy of that, or did you ever have one?
You mean a copy of --
Of the sheet music. It -- was there any sheet music made?
I think he put the stock out on this thing.
Huh. Did anybody ever write lyrics?

No. No lyrics or anything; an instrumental. So this is the way it went down. So the only thing that I got any consolation out of, when I did get together and form a band, I wrote a tune called "Chris and His Gang," which was a part of the "Christopher Columbus" thing. I tell you, a guy who really knows the story on this thing, and I'm telling him -- he'll tell you like it is too, with Roy Eldridge. So we're still friends. So (Unintelligible). Well, I won't say any more about that, because it's water under the bridge now, and I've recuperated from that.
But I've had some near misses on hits, man, you know.

They sat at the bar -- on top of the bar. You know how that is, where the band was playing. We had to go inside the bar (unintelligible) the bandstand. And the band was sitting all
around. So after we'd played this tune once, we had a request with a $5.00 bill to play that same tune again.
I can guess.
So we played it.
Somebody's busy writing it down.

This is exactly what happened. So it became obvious, and we played it the second time. They sent up another $5.00. We said, 'What's happening,' and so we happened to look down. There were two guys, and they was writing (illegible), you know, one of those things. And that's how 'Castle Rock' started. And a few months later here's a recording came out of 'Castle Rock,' one of those things, and my saxophone player came to work one night and he says, 'Man, I heard our riff. They've called it 'Castle Rock' and Al Sears or so and so recorded it and all.' There it was. So that got away.
Son of a gun.
So he made some money off of that tune too. So -- I mean quite a bit. That tune got real popular, you know. So that was that.

Lucky Millender. Now that's a guy that was a real character. When I say character, I mean he was funny. I could tell you some stories on Lucky Millender.

Lucky Millinder had a great band. He always surrounded himself. He didn't know a note as big as this room.
Really?

But he had a great ear, and Lucky could direct a band. This is what he was primarily known for. He could have you make an arrangement for him, which I did. I made an arrangement -- I won't forget this, because I have the score right here in the house now, called "Hallelujah." (Singing) That one -- and I had it up to tempo, real fast. And he had a big band. So the way he would conduct things at a rehearsal, if you had an arrangement, he would get him a chair and sit to the side and tell you to, you know, take down your arrangement and everything, and you'd play it two, three times. And he would sit back and listen. Then he'd come up and tell you, "Okay, let me have it now." And he would get his little baton just (unintelligible) and he'd get the guys ready. Then he'd stomp it off, kick it off. And he would learn those riffs, and he would accent, then, with the baton.
Baton, yeah.
You know? And he was known for this, you know, and he could sell, you know. And he could talk too. Know what I mean? He was a great talker. I'll

never forget one time. Now these are some funny things. You might help a little bit. got to hear this. This is (unintelligible). He was playing theater a field one time up in the Bronx. Okay? He was late one time getting up to the theater. And He could talk, man. He could talk; I mean, and that (unintelligible) and he would write you a check that would bounce higher than a (unintelligible). this building too.
(Laughter)
You know, one of these guys -- but he was a likable guy.

Now, for instance, he would get in a cab. He would have the cab drive him way up in the Bronx, which would run about -- oh, I don't know -- $7.00 seven to $10.00, you know, in those figures. days That was quite a bit because, I guess, the meter would start at a quarter, you know, one of those things, or 20 cents, you know. Well, running up $7.00, you had to go was a lot of around.... I remember one time, he told a cab driver to drive him up to the Valencia Theater.
(Recording interruption)

-- and he says, "I'm Lucky Millender." He says, "Now leave your meter on, he says, "Park your car here in front of the theater. It's all right. It's all right. And just come on in. Just come on in. And he would dedicate this show to him and everything, and would the tell the to fellow, man, would put the spotlight on him and all these things, and when the show was over, he'd tell the cab driver to leave his meters running -- around $25.00, one of those
things. Lucky would go out and get in another cab. Go out of That town and leave the guy, son of a (unintelligible), you know. This is the true slant,

-- and the guys that worked with Lucky Millender that are living today know this as a fact. They were betting two to one that Lucky Millender wouldn't (unintelligible) get hit and--
: Talking
-- would talk himself out of it.

: You've got to be kidding, man.
(Laughter)
I'm telling you, this is what happened. And sure enough, Lucky put a story

So I haven't seen or heard of that guy in years. I don't know -- those guys live forever, though, that do these things. If it were you or if it was me, man, we'd be in the grave, you know. So that's the story on Lucky Millinder. I thought I had to tell that. But that isn't a joke. That's a fact.
Uh-huh. That's great. Really great. What -- did you have any special sort of things in arranging for him or just --

No. No, he left it to your judgment. He wanted you to naturally, like invite other guys, to hear his band, and he wanted you to -- oh, he would specify to give certain solos to certain guys. I don't know if they were his pets or not, but most of his trumpet players could play the part, you know. But I think he favored -- you know, had his favorites, so he would tell you to give so and so the solo on you know -- whether this, and that, so -- but he was impressing me, you know, as to what he wanted, where there was just -- of course, he paid for the arrangements, so that was his privilege.
Sure.
He was quite a guy.
Hal McIntyre.

Hal McIntyre. I did a couple of things for him, not many. He was playing upstate New York in a fabulous nightclub, if I remember correctly. And, you know, he played good sax, he did -- brilliant tone and whatnot. But he wanted -- he didn't want the wild stuff, if I remember correctly. He wanted something, because of the type of exclusive engagements that he played, he wanted something that was not too far out, but yet it had a beat -- I remember him from this, you know. So I made a couple of things for him.

You know, in New York there were quite a few guys during that era, like there was a great arranger named Fred Norman. He was in Claude Hopkins' band, and he was a trombonist and he wrote real good, you know, and -- oh, a guy named Andy Gibson. He was with Charlie Barnett. We were in there together. Now he wrote a lot of things. And -- I'm mentioning these things to say that in those days they had a lot of free lance arrangers, you know, and we used to -- in that thing when I say we, because I was scuffling at that bit too at that time -- and we used to go around and listen at bands, and then we would solicit, see, you know, our writing, you know, the different bandleaders and say, 'Well, I'm an arranger, you know, and go up and meet them.'
Naturally, during those days -- especially when the

bands were broadcasting, they had to have arrangements, and they had to have tunes, so naturally they were interested in, you know, getting as many arrangements as possible, because they had to send their programs in a week at a time to broadcast, so they had to be clear, one of those things.
So this is what the arrangers found out, and naturally we would take advantage of that, you know. This is how we got to do something. So if you do a good job, you --
Yeah, the word would get around.
You'd get more work. --(unintelligible) Yeah, the word would get around, for sure. So this is what happened with Hal McIntyre.
I see.

See, he was a nice guy. And it was in those days easy to write for his band because it was, you know, everybody read. He wanted you to bear in mind, just like I said before, it couldn't be too far out, but he did want something with a beat. That was it.
Uh-huh. I'm going to break in here on this sequence. Did Fletcher do very much -- did he do as much writing for other groups as you did or was he mainly with his own -- and for like Benny and --
No. Between his band and Benny and he was pretty well kept busy. And he used to -- in those days they used to do something that, well, bands don't do now

because, well, we don't have as many of the big bands like we used to have. They used to swap arrangements too, you know. I know of such. They used to swap arrangements with the Dorseys, Tommy and Jimmy. They'd go around and maybe Fletcher might hear a pretty tune that Tommy would be doing, and he said, "Hey, let's swap with you; so and so, and you pick so and so." They would exchange (Unintelligible) no money involved at all. And I think that it made good will among the guys, plus the fact that it made their book a little more versatile, you know.
But in those days a lot of the good things happened that don't happen now, you know.
It's an entirely different world, different business.
(Simultaneous remarks)
Different world altogether. Imagine me going up to one of these seven piece, five piece groups now that -- in fact, they don't have the arrangements.
That's what I was going to say here.

More are four things or our head things, as we call it. We called them skulls, you know, in those days, the skull arrangements. But even so, the only way to get them now is to take them off the record, if they're a recording recorded, you know, one of those things, you know. But it's an entirely different world; you really hit it on the head. You really don't remember it.
Yeah, seems to be.

And Fletcher didn't -- getting back to your question again, I'll elaborate a little more I didn't want to -- he didn't go around much, you know. Now like I used to frequent a lot of clubs where bands were playing because I used to just like jazz and would like the different bands and like the different soloists that came up in those days. In fact, I used to tell Fletcher, I said, "Smack, I went to a certain club last night and heard this band. Man, you ought to hear this trumpet player." This is how Fletcher sometimes would get some great musicians, you know, if the bands would break up, and I'd get the names, you know, and the telephone numbers, and I said, "You want to hear a guy play, man, this can can play," you know.

So he was never one for going out much. He stayed home. He was a good man at home. And he was busy writing, because when he was writing for Benny, that meant from 5:00 o'clock in the morning until 5:00 that afternoon and right on around, because Benny wouldn't mind calling you up anytime, you know. So it took it's physical toll on him, you know, so I think this is one of the reasons why he didn't get a chance to, you know, frequent the places like I did.
Duke Dailey Daly?
Duke Dailey Daly. There's a guy that was a happy go lucky fellow. I did, oh, a few things for Duke, and he was quite a character; however, a sad thing happened. He
just disappeared one day, and nobody's heard of Duke Dailey since, and he was a guy that flew.
Had a pilot's license?

Yes, he flew a lot. And I think his last flight interrupted his musical career, as far as the band was concerned. He was another one like Lucky Millinder, happy go lucky guy, and held tell stories to the guys in his band, and he had a great sense of humor. And a great personality in front of a band, and he didn't play anything, to my knowledge. I didn't know too much about him then, but I was freelancing writing, and he was for one of the guys that we just finished talking about that we would go around and solicit (unintelligible), you know. So that's the story of it, as far as I know, of Duke Dailey.
Uh-huh. What sorts of things did you do for Count Basie?
Well, Count's quite a guy, you know.
There's an easy going guy.

Yes, he is. He's another guy that -- he came up in those days with Fletcher. In fact, before I tell you about the writing part, Count was in Kansas City, you know, and used to be in the band out of Kansas City called Benny Moten. And his brother, Buster Moten, used to direct that band, and he played squeeze box, accordion.
It's Moten, isn't it -- I think.
Yeah. Yeah, and And Count Basie was playing piano, Moten, (unintelligible).
that was a swinging band then.
Yeah, it's well known. There are a lot of good people that came out of that band.
Oh, a lot of great Musicians that -- Big Joe Page, the bass, --
Right. Pres Young was --

Oh, Pres was in that band. That was a great band. And when Count took it over. He wanted to come to Chicago, and Fletcher was instrumental in getting Count in the Grand Terrace. Buck Clayton, the trumpet player, was in that band --Harry and Sweets Edison. Oh, man, those are legends, those guys. And when Fletcher went out on the road, Ed Fox's Grand Terrace was the popular club in Chicago, and Fletcher recommended Basie to this gentleman that owned the club, and went in there and did a terrific Basie was a man that could do the job. And he went right on, man, If course, it was the ambition of every musician and bandleader to get to New York during in those days, you know. If it wasn't for recording purposes, it was for some other reason, because it was popular. And that was that.

And I made a couple of original things for Basie, and I don't know if he recorded them or not, but I'd heard that band, and it was easy to write, you know, and he often told me, he says, 'If you have anything good that you think is good, and you know my style, he said, send it on in to the office. The old man will take care of you.' You know, one of those
things. And I used to take some riffs, fix them up, because he was primarily interested in things like that.
Yeah, that was those that hold a whole Kansas City blues band tradition. Walter Page and Benny Moten.
Those stocks that Joe Stutte came out in those days.
Oh, man, and -- let's see. You know he was living in RedBank, New Jersey, for a long time.
"The Kid from RedBank."
He was from RedBank. Yeah, that's a tune by that was two by their name. And who's that great drummer that was with him from RedBank? Wasn't it Joe Jones?
Yeah, I think so.
I think That was the original drummer that he had.
I believe so. I'd have to check it out, but --
That, or either I'm thinking of Sonny Greer. I think Sonny Greer was from Redbank, New Jersey.
Sonny Greer was with Ellington for a long time.
Yes. But I think he was from Redbank, New Jersey, too, I think.
Was he? Yeah.
I know that they had two guys there. One was the piano player, and the other one was the drummer.
They were from Redbank, New Jersey. But Basie made a lot of great things.
You know, we were talking about John Hammond. I think it was John Hammond that brought Basie to New York.

Yeah. That guy has helped a lot of guys. He brought Basie to New York, and he hasn't looked gone back since. I'm thinking of Lester Young, and Basie had a great tenor player named Herschel Evans that played the sweet stuff, and they left Pres with his crooked neck saxophone. In fact, I think John Hammond was instrumental in getting Basie into the great Apollo Theater in New York at 125th and 7th Avenue, because I remember the first time that I saw Basie's band actually, really playing, you know. They were -- their theme song, of course, was One O'Clock Jump. They were playing this Apollo Theater, and a lot of young kids, you know, even ducked high school and everything to hear the Count Basie, the great when they played, Count Basie's band.
And the Apollo Theater, you know, and they would get behind the curtain and when the band would start playing, the curtain would stay down for, you know, a minute or so, and it went --
(Singing)
-- man, it was rocking before it came out. And when it opened the curtain up, here's this band, and here's Pres

sitting up there with his saxophone's neck crooked at a 45 degree angle, and the guys in the audience would say, "Hey, look at that guy there with a broken neck." You know? And they found out later on about Pres when he would come down to the mike and get his pose, and when he would finish, they would know he wouldn't have a crooked neck. That was his way of playing.

(Laughter)
Boy, he was really an influence on guys, you know, and everybody would -- just like when Louis Armstrong
-- we talked about this once --
With the handkerchief, yeah.

-- come out like this with the handkerchief and all -- "What do you say there, pops," you know? But Pres was playing -- he just lifted that band. He did? I didn't know that.

was funny, you know, because I knew this guy, man, could play. And they regretted it many a day since then, including Fletcher, you know.

But they had some set guys in that band, you know, and they didn't give Pres a chance to stretch out. And, of course, certain tunes show off musicians, you know, better than others, you know, and I think this was actually one of the factors -- but he made up for it finally.

something. He was at the Apollo Theater, and in those days -- I got to mention this and clarify it -- guys had to travel -- one nighters, you know, one of these things. Well, anyway, Reverend Gatemouth Moore was one of those guys, and this is an incident that actually occurred.

Father Hines. Let's see. That takes us back to Chicago, the Grand Terrace, where he used to play, aong with Fletcher, you know. the fighter.
Dancing, uh-huh.

He took charge when Earl wasn't around. You know, and this was the nickname they label you with, like in Count Basie's band here a few years back when Marshall Royal was leading the band, they called him the straw boss, you know. So this is the title that is forced on you, whether you like it or not.

But Earl had a good band, and I made a few things for him, and he also was interested in originals. Seemed like so back in those days, all these guys had in mind that the original tunes would swing more, you know. I think this was the trend.
Well, they'd like to keep the book new and refreshed.

Yeah, that's it. And I think it is a fact that the originals last longer, you know, popularity wise, even if you get tired of playing them, and sometimes you can put them in the back of the book and let them rest for a few months, which they used to do, and then bring them out again, and they're fresh again, you know. And I think this is what they had in mind. But Earl was quite a guy. He's always been my favorite, you know, playing and sitting at the piano directing his band from there with finesse -- (unintelligible) also -- Father Hines. Fatha
Uh-huh. Well, that's quite an impressive list of people with whom you've worked.
It was quite an experience, for me, because the different band leaders on that list were so different.
Uh-huh. That's true.
Especially --
The styles and so on.
-- Rubenoff, man. That was quite a thing, but they were all different, you know. And they'd put things in your mind that you'll never forget. You take them from now on right along with you.

Yeah. Concerning arranging itself, let's see -- by the time you are really starting arranging, they had begun pretty much to shift on over to string bass, hadn't -- they weren't still using tuba or --
Yes. Tuba became obsolete.
And same way with banjo -- was either dropped or guitar.
Yeah, replaced it. It gave it a more mellow sound, plus the fact that the string bass, you know, gave it a better beat, especially if the guy could play, and guys were switching over like mad.
Uh-huh. Did you know Charlie Christian? Thinking of guitars made me think of that, and
Benny.

Yeah, I knew Charlie real well. I knew him when he first came up and joined Benny. And he was another guy that played by ear. I believe had he learned to read, it probably would have impaired his playing because the guy could play. And, you know, he made a thing with Benny and George Auld called "Good Enough to Keep" at that time, and it was later changed to "Air Mail Special." See? The original name for that thing was "Good Enough to Keep." And I've got an old 78 that they made that on, man, and Charlie Christian was weird on that. You know how that thing, in the bridge --
(Singing)
Charlie Christian was just walking through that thing just like that. But that guy, name is that walked through Georgia -- Sherman.
Colonel Sherman -- or General, yeah.

Man, he could play. And he had a lot of soul solos, and Benny knew it, and Benny let him play, you know. That's one thing. If you could play, you could do something, he'd let you do it. But Charlie was perfect. He was steady, steady, and he'd play the chords. He could play chords, man. And you didn't have to write anything for him. He would just use that seventh sense that he had, that musical sense. It would work out just fine.
Uh-huh. Did you ever know of

anybody that was really getting into unusual phrasing? Of course, Louis did quite a lot, but we often think of the very unusual kind of phrasing coming in with Charlie Parker pretty much; that is, you know, carrying phrases longer than the four bars and then beginning the next phrase in the middle of what the usual phrase ought to be, that sort of thing. Do you recall any players that were doing that at all?
You mean other than Charlie?
Yes. Earlier than Charlie.
Earlier than Charlie -- that's a good question, Tom. I don't recall offhand. Let's see. You say earlier than Charlie.
Yeah, this would be like late '30's or even the very early '40's.

I know there were a lot of musicians that would anticipate the progression over into the next bar; they would carry them over. And like the first guy, I think, that used to do that was Don Redman, the great alto saxophonist and arranger, in years. In fact, Don used to make a lot of out of key breaks and come back into the tonic, you know. And he'd experiment. And it would work. And he'd anticipate the moving to the next bar. But he'd always know how to catch up and where to do it, you know, and then I would know some other guys that weren't quite as fortunate, because you had to know your horn in order to do those things, you know. So I
hope this answers part of your question anyway.
In a way, yes. Well, I was just tossing it out there.
And, of course, the great Bird came on and did it up.
Yeah, really did.
He did start something together, though, and Dizzy didn't they?
Yeah, very much so.

I would like to ask you a question, because you are, in my estimation, a great authority on things like this that we're talking about. Do you think that Charlie Parker and Dizzy, having developed that unusual style, do you think that it hurt some of our younger musicians?
Do you mean at that time? Or --
When it first became so popular.
I think perhaps so in the sense that a lot of younger musicians thought that all you had to do was play fast and loud and just, you know, --,
(Bubbling sound)

-- kind of thing, without really knowing what was happening. So I think it would have affected younger musicians that way, and I think that's happened definitely today, where a lot of the young musicians who are maybe coming out of rock or getting more interested in jazz, and so they heard a number of

the musicians during the '70's -- or the '60's, you know, John Coltrane and a lot of these people that knew very much of what they were doing, but it was still extremely involved music, and the young musicians that hear it just hear it and think, all I have to do is go fast as hell.

Well, you see, this is what I wanted to hear from you, because those are my sentiments too. When I said hurt them, I mean hurt them at that particular time, because they weren't aware of the fact that these musicians that were playing these riffs and things knew what they were doing, while these kids, just as you said, thought they could pick up their horns and play something fast and everything and get by, but it didn't make sense what they were doing.
These guys knew how to come out of those passages, you see.
Well, the thing is that those people had the background, and Dizz and Bird and so on had been playing swing, jazz --
They played --
-- prior to that time, and it was an evolvement out of that, whereas the young musicians didn't have anything to evolve from, so --
Right. They just hear a record or hear something, and that's Bird, man. I'm going to get this, something, but they didn't realize that Bird and Dizz
could play legitimate, you know, something that these kids couldn't, so this is what I mean by do you think it hurt them at that time.
Well -- go ahead.
Oh, that's okay. But I think they have become aware of this now, after they found out that something was missing. They had to get down to the fundamentals of it, you know.

Well, that's it. What I was about to say was, obviously, the younger musicians who started that way, if that's all they ever did, they never amounted to anything, and if they did go about learning what they were doing, then they had the opportunity to grow with it.
That's so true.

You know, it just occurred to me, since we're talking about young musicians, for the past decade or so there's been this huge growth of what for a while was called the stage band movement in schools -- in high schools and junior highs, so that almost nationwide every high school has at least one big band jazz ensemble. And I've judged some of these festivals where they -- competitions where they get together, and there are some fantastic groups all around the country, and I was just thinking it might really be neat, again, if you had some arrangements to dig them out simply from their historical value and let some of these kids
see these arrangements and even play them. I think it would be a big thing for them.

You know, Tom, I'm looking forward to that. I would like to bring out some of the arrangements even that were made back in those days, because some of them are still modern. That's how far ahead -- (unintelligible).
That's right. Both your arrangements and Fletcher's -- it'd be great.
I better bring Fletcher's out, (unintelligible). don't know.
No, no, man. I think it's important that -- everybody realize how much contribution you made.
Thank you. Well --
That's what we're doing here.

-- I'll bring one or two along, and I want to see the expressions on the kids' faces because it might be some interesting things in there, and I'm very anxious, since I've heard about just what you said, what their reactions would be, you know, and then I'm looking forward to that because I am going to have a lot of time here very soon, with the coming on, you know, and the only thing about a lot of kids, they'll be out of school, won't they?
Yes, although there are various summer projects and so on, but -- yeah, even though -- if you would just get the whole thing together and decide what ones
you'd want to use and things could be set up so that they could be implemented next fall.
Now let me ask you a question. What would be the instrumentation?
Most of these bands are pretty big, if you get a pretty big high school. They would have five, six saxophones and they're using five trumpets.
(Unintelligible). Good. Oh boy.
Sometimes I see six or seven standing there, these little kids screaming, busting their lips (unintelligible), stuff like that.
Three or four trombones.
Yeah, so they'd have --
Then there's then, that's beautiful. It'd be no sweat, maybe, huh?
-- sometimes three or four percussionists, as well as piano, maybe two pianists.
Well, what we'll have to do is probably make some extra parts especially, you know, like we have two of the same, you know, like in the rhythm section.

One thing I want to bring just before this tape runs out, did you do much writing or did Fletcher for unusual instrumentation? I mean did -- like did you -- the guys double on flutes and occasionally oboes or things like that or --
No, mine was just the basic things.
You know, that, the standard --
Instrumentation --

-- like four trumpets, three trombones, five saxophones and everything. I wrote a little bit for fiddles, but I had to go to school a little bit. In fact, this is what you have to do. But mine was primarily like the instrumentation for the big bands, what they carried, originally had.
You say you went to school -- where and what?
Oh, in New York at Damrosch. I had to find out a few things in But that came in handy.
Our tape is about shot on this one.
